items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has an HBV DNA level of 2 million IU/mL and elevated ALT. Tenofovir is started. Six months later his viral DNA is undetectable, but HBsAg remains positive. His hepatologist explains that therapy will probably be needed long-term because the drug leaves intact the template that persists in hepatocyte nuclei. Which step in the viral life cycle does tenofovir directly inhibit?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding of the virion to the NTCP bile acid transporter

options.label: B
options.html: Cleavage of a viral polyprotein by NS3/4A protease

options.label: C
options.html: Conversion of relaxed circular DNA into cccDNA

options.label: D
options.html: Reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA into viral DNA

options.label: E
options.html: Transcription of cccDNA by host RNA polymerase II

items.explanationHtml:
Tenofovir is a nucleotide analogue that, once phosphorylated, competes with natural nucleotides and terminates DNA chain synthesis by the HBV polymerase acting as a reverse transcriptase. HBV replicates by packaging pregenomic RNA into capsids and reverse-transcribing it into partially double-stranded DNA. Blocking this step stops new virion DNA, so serum HBV DNA falls, but the nuclear cccDNA minichromosome remains and keeps producing viral RNAs and HBsAg.

Takeaway: HBV nucleos(t)ide analogues inhibit reverse transcription; they suppress but rarely eradicate infection because cccDNA persists.

whyNot.A: Entry through NTCP is blocked by investigational entry inhibitors, not by nucleotide analogues.
whyNot.B: NS3/4A is a hepatitis C protease; HBV does not make a polyprotein processed this way.
whyNot.C: cccDNA formation uses host DNA repair enzymes and is not blocked by tenofovir; this is why cccDNA persists.
whyNot.E: Host polymerase II transcription is untouched by tenofovir; viral RNAs and HBsAg continue to be produced.

items.objective: Identify the HBV replication step targeted by nucleos(t)ide analogues and explain why therapy is long-term.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman who injects drugs has known chronic hepatitis B with previously stable liver tests. She now presents with jaundice and an ALT of 1,450 U/L (10-40 U/L). HBsAg remains positive, IgM anti-HBc is negative, and antibody to hepatitis D virus is positive. The new agent can assemble infectious particles only because it uses which component supplied by the coexisting virus?

options.label: B
options.html: e antigen (HBeAg) to block host interferon

options.label: C
options.html: Reverse transcriptase to copy its genome

options.label: E
options.html: X protein to transactivate HDV genes

items.explanationHtml:
Hepatitis D virus is a defective circular negative-sense RNA virus. It encodes delta antigen but no envelope protein, so infectious HDV particles form only when HBsAg from a coinfecting HBV is available. Superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier, as here (IgM anti-HBc negative, so this is not new HBV), often causes a severe flare and frequently becomes chronic, accelerating progression to cirrhosis.

Takeaway: HDV needs HBsAg for its coat; HBV vaccination therefore also prevents HDV.

whyNot.A: HDV has its own ribonucleoprotein (delta antigen) and does not use the HBV capsid; it borrows only the envelope.
whyNot.B: HBeAg is a secreted protein with immunomodulatory effects but is not required for HDV assembly.
whyNot.C: HDV copies its circular RNA genome using host RNA polymerase and ribozyme activity, not HBV reverse transcriptase.
whyNot.E: HBx affects host transcription but is not the dependency that makes HDV defective.

items.objective: Explain the dependence of hepatitis D virus on HBV surface antigen.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation returns from a 3-month family visit to a region with frequent monsoon flooding and limited water treatment. She has 5 days of nausea, dark urine and jaundice, then becomes confused. INR is 2.6 (0.8-1.1). IgM anti-HAV, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HCV RNA are negative. Which virus is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Hepatitis E is a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA hepevirus spread through fecally contaminated water in endemic regions (genotypes 1 and 2) and through undercooked pork or game elsewhere (genotype 3). Infection is usually self-limited but can cause acute liver failure in pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester. Encephalopathy with a raised INR here indicates acute liver failure.

Takeaway: Waterborne hepatitis in a pregnant traveller with negative HAV, HBV and HCV tests suggests HEV, which can be fulminant in pregnancy.

whyNot.A: HAV also spreads by the fecal-oral route, but her IgM anti-HAV is negative, and HAV does not carry the high mortality of pregnancy that defines this case.
whyNot.B: Both HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are negative, which effectively rules out acute HBV.
whyNot.C: HCV is bloodborne, rarely causes fulminant hepatitis and is excluded by a negative HCV RNA.
whyNot.D: HDV infection requires HBsAg, which is absent.

items.objective: Recognise hepatitis E as a cause of fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: Eleven guests at a lunch develop forceful vomiting and abdominal cramps about 2 hours after eating. All had reheated fried rice from a container left at room temperature overnight; none has fever or bloody stools, and all recover within a day. Which organism most likely caused the outbreak?
items.explanationHtml:
Spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking of rice; if the rice cools slowly, vegetative bacteria grow and release cereulide, a preformed heat-stable emetic toxin. Reheating does not destroy it, so vomiting begins within a few hours. Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin causes a similar rapid illness but is linked to handled foods such as salads and pastries.

Takeaway: Vomiting within hours of reheated rice points to the preformed emetic toxin of B. cereus.

whyNot.B: C. perfringens causes watery diarrhea 8 to 16 hours after warm-held meat dishes, with little vomiting.
whyNot.C: ETEC causes watery diarrhea after one or more days of incubation, typically in travellers.
whyNot.D: Norovirus causes vomiting and diarrhea, but its incubation is usually 12 to 48 hours, not 2 hours, and it is not linked to rice storage.
whyNot.E: Salmonella has an incubation of roughly a day or more and causes fever with inflammatory diarrhea.

items.objective: Link incubation period and food vehicle to a preformed-toxin food poisoning.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhea 6 days after starting clindamycin for a dental abscess. Colonoscopy shows multiple raised yellow plaques on an erythematous mucosa. The organism's major toxins act on colonocytes by which mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of guanylate cyclase, raising intracellular cGMP

options.label: B
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of Gs alpha, raising intracellular cAMP

options.label: C
options.html: Cleavage of SNARE proteins, blocking vesicle fusion

options.label: D
options.html: Glucosylation of Rho-family GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton

options.label: E
options.html: Removal of an adenine from 28S ribosomal RNA, halting protein synthesis

items.explanationHtml:
Toxins A and B of Clostridioides difficile enter colonocytes and glucosylate Rho, Rac and Cdc42. These GTPases control actin assembly, so the cytoskeleton collapses, tight junctions open and cells die. Neutrophils, fibrin and mucus erupt from damaged crypts to form the yellow pseudomembranes seen here. Clindamycin is a classic precipitant.

Takeaway: C. difficile toxins inactivate Rho GTPases; the tissue result is pseudomembranous colitis.

whyNot.A: This is the heat-stable toxin of ETEC, a secretory toxin.
whyNot.B: This is cholera toxin (and ETEC heat-labile toxin), which causes secretion without mucosal destruction or pseudomembranes.
whyNot.C: This is the mechanism of botulinum and tetanus toxins, which act on neurons.
whyNot.E: This describes Shiga and Shiga-like toxins of Shigella and STEC.

items.objective: Describe the molecular action of C. difficile toxins and the resulting pathology.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man returns from a week of backpacking during which he drank untreated stream water. Ten days later he develops abdominal bloating, flatulence and foul-smelling, greasy stools that float. There is no blood in the stool and he is afebrile. Stool microscopy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Pear-shaped flagellated trophozoites with two nuclei

options.label: E
options.html: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells

items.explanationHtml:
Giardia cysts in untreated surface water excyst in the duodenum, and binucleate, flagellated trophozoites attach to the small-bowel brush border by a ventral disk. They do not invade, so there is no blood or fever, but brush-border injury causes fat and lactose malabsorption with bloating and steatorrhea. Stool antigen or PCR is more sensitive than microscopy.

Takeaway: Noninvasive steatorrheic diarrhea after stream water suggests Giardia, seen as binucleate flagellated trophozoites.

whyNot.A: Operculated eggs belong to flukes or Diphyllobothrium and do not fit acute fatty diarrhea after stream water.
whyNot.C: Larvae in stool suggest Strongyloides, which typically causes eosinophilia and skin or lung findings.
whyNot.D: Acid-fast oocysts indicate Cryptosporidium (or Cyclospora), which cause watery rather than fatty diarrhea.
whyNot.E: Erythrophagocytic trophozoites indicate Entamoeba histolytica, which causes bloody, invasive colitis.

items.objective: Recognise the clinical pattern and microscopic appearance of giardiasis.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man who spent two years working at a rural clinic in an area with poor sanitation has 3 weeks of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy shows scattered ulcers with undermined edges in the cecum. Which finding is most likely on biopsy of an ulcer?

options.label: B
options.html: Flask-shaped ulcers containing trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Foamy macrophages in the lamina propria filled with PAS-positive granules

options.label: D
options.html: Pseudomembranes of fibrin and neutrophils erupting from crypts

items.explanationHtml:
Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites lyse colonic epithelium and spread laterally within the submucosa, creating ulcers with a narrow neck and a broad base (flask shape). Trophozoites that contain ingested red cells are diagnostic. The cecum and ascending colon are commonly affected, and portal spread can cause a liver abscess.

Takeaway: Amebic colitis shows flask-shaped ulcers with erythrophagocytic trophozoites.

whyNot.A: Intestinal tuberculosis can affect the ileocecal region but produces caseating granulomas, not amebic trophozoites.
whyNot.C: This describes Whipple disease (or MAC infection), which involves the small bowel and causes malabsorption rather than ulcers.
whyNot.D: Pseudomembranes are characteristic of C. difficile colitis after antibiotics.
whyNot.E: This is the pattern of Crohn disease, which can also affect the cecum, but it does not fit an infectious ulcer after exposure in an endemic area.

items.objective: Identify the histopathology of amebic colitis.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has 2 years of migratory arthralgias, followed by 6 months of diarrhea, 12 kg weight loss and new difficulty remembering appointments. HIV testing is negative. Duodenal biopsy shows villi distended by sheets of foamy macrophages containing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant granules; an acid-fast stain is negative. Which organism is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinomycete that persists because of impaired macrophage killing. Infected macrophages crowd the lamina propria and compress lacteals, producing malabsorption, while systemic spread explains the arthralgias (often the first symptom), cognitive change, uveitis and endocarditis. A negative acid-fast stain and negative HIV test exclude MAC.

Takeaway: PAS-positive, acid-fast-negative foamy macrophages in the small bowel of a middle-aged man with arthralgia and cognitive change indicate Whipple disease.

whyNot.A: Cryptosporidium appears as small bodies on the brush border and does not produce PAS-positive macrophages.
whyNot.B: Giardia attaches to the surface epithelium and does not fill the lamina propria with macrophages.
whyNot.C: Histoplasma appears as small intracellular yeasts on silver stain and is usually a disseminated infection of immunocompromised hosts.
whyNot.D: MAC also fills macrophages with PAS-positive material, but it occurs in advanced HIV and stains acid-fast.

items.objective: Distinguish Whipple disease from MAC enteritis on biopsy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man with recurrent epigastric pain is found to have a duodenal ulcer. A gastric antral biopsy shows curved rods in the mucus layer overlying the epithelium. The organism's ability to survive in the gastric lumen depends most directly on which property?

options.label: A
options.html: A polysaccharide capsule that blocks complement

options.label: B
options.html: An IgA protease that cleaves secretory IgA

options.label: C
options.html: Catalase that degrades reactive oxygen species

options.label: D
options.html: Hydrolysis of urea to ammonia that buffers surrounding acid

options.label: E
options.html: Spore formation that resists low pH

items.explanationHtml:
Helicobacter pylori produces large amounts of urease, which splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, creating a buffered microenvironment around the organism. Flagella then move it through mucus to the epithelial surface, where the pH is nearer neutral. Urease activity is also the basis of the urea breath test and the rapid urease test on biopsy tissue.

Takeaway: H. pylori survives gastric acid through urease-generated ammonia; the same enzyme underlies its diagnostic tests.

whyNot.A: A capsule protects against phagocytosis, but it is not how this organism resists gastric acid.
whyNot.B: IgA protease is a mucosal virulence factor of Neisseria, Haemophilus and S. pneumoniae, not the acid-survival mechanism here.
whyNot.C: H. pylori is catalase-positive, but catalase protects against oxidative killing, not acid.
whyNot.E: H. pylori does not form spores; spore formation is a feature of Clostridium and Bacillus.

items.objective: Explain the virulence factor that allows H. pylori to colonise the stomach.

items.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old man has had fatigue, nausea and dark urine for 10 days. He reports unprotected sex with a new partner about 3 months ago. He is alert, with scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
ALT1,280 U/L10-40 U/L
AST960 U/L12-38 U/L
Bilirubin, total5.8 mg/dL0.1-1.0 mg/dL
INR1.10.8-1.1
HBsAgNegativeNegative
Anti-HBsNegativeNegative
IgM anti-HBcPositiveNegative
IgM anti-HAVNegativeNegative
Anti-HCVNegativeNegative

Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Acute hepatitis B in the window period

options.label: B
options.html: Chronic hepatitis B with a flare

options.label: C
options.html: False-positive antibody with another cause of hepatitis

options.label: D
options.html: Immunity from previous hepatitis B vaccination

options.label: E
options.html: Resolved hepatitis B infection from childhood

items.explanationHtml:
In acute hepatitis B, HBsAg can clear before anti-HBs becomes detectable. During this window period IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker. The timing (about 3 months after a sexual exposure) and the high aminotransferases fit acute infection. His INR and mental status are normal, so this is not acute liver failure; most immunocompetent adults clear HBV with supportive care, and repeat testing should later show anti-HBs.

Takeaway: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and IgM anti-HBc positive equals the window period of acute HBV.

whyNot.B: Chronic infection requires persistent HBsAg, which is negative.
whyNot.C: With a compatible exposure, marked aminotransferase elevation and IgM anti-HBc, acute HBV is the expected interpretation, not a false positive.
whyNot.D: Vaccination produces anti-HBs only; it does not cause anti-HBc, and anti-HBs is negative here.
whyNot.E: Resolved infection shows IgG anti-HBc with anti-HBs, normal aminotransferases and no IgM anti-HBc.

items.objective: Interpret a hepatitis B serologic panel showing the window period.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman tests positive for anti-HCV during routine one-time screening. HCV RNA is 1.4 million IU/mL. She has no prior treatment, FIB-4 and elastography indicate minimal fibrosis, HBsAg and HIV tests are negative, and she takes only a daily multivitamin. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Observation with repeat HCV RNA in 6 months

options.label: B
options.html: Peginterferon alfa plus ribavirin for 48 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Treatment-naive adults with chronic HCV and no decompensated cirrhosis can receive a short pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral regimen without genotyping: sofosbuvir-velpatasvir for 12 weeks or glecaprevir-pibrentasvir for 8 weeks. Pre-treatment checks are fibrosis staging, HBV status (DAAs can unmask HBV reactivation), HIV, pregnancy potential and drug interactions. Cure is confirmed by undetectable RNA 12 weeks after the end of therapy.

Takeaway: Chronic HCV is cured with short pangenotypic DAA regimens such as sofosbuvir-velpatasvir.

whyNot.A: Chronic HCV with detectable RNA warrants treatment; delaying cure risks progression and transmission.
whyNot.B: Interferon-based therapy is obsolete for HCV; it is less effective and far more toxic than direct-acting antivirals.
whyNot.C: Ribavirin alone does not cure HCV and is teratogenic and causes hemolysis.
whyNot.E: Tenofovir treats HBV and HIV; it has no activity against HCV.

items.objective: Choose first-line therapy for chronic hepatitis C.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man is admitted with pneumonia and treated with ceftriaxone. On day 5 he has 6 watery stools in 24 hours and has received no laxatives. Temperature is 37.9 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, and the abdomen is soft without distension. Leukocytes are 13,200/mm3 (4,500-11,000/mm3) and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mg/dL). Stool testing is positive for toxigenic Clostridioides difficile. His pneumonia antibiotics can be stopped. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a nonsevere initial episode (leukocytes below 15,000/mm3, normal creatinine, no hypotension or ileus). Current IDSA/SHEA guidance prefers fidaxomicin for an initial episode because it lowers recurrence compared with vancomycin; oral vancomycin is an acceptable alternative. The inciting antibiotic should be stopped and contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene applied.

Takeaway: First-episode C. difficile infection is treated with oral fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin), not metronidazole.

whyNot.A: Fecal microbiota therapy is reserved for multiple recurrences, not a first episode.
whyNot.B: IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colonic lumen and does not treat C. difficile.
whyNot.C: Antimotility agents are avoided as monotherapy in active C. difficile infection; the infection needs specific antibiotic treatment.
whyNot.E: Metronidazole is no longer recommended for an initial adult episode when fidaxomicin or vancomycin is available, because outcomes are worse.

items.objective: Select first-line therapy for an initial episode of C. difficile infection.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had fever, sweats and right upper quadrant pain for 10 days. He returned 4 months ago from 18 months working on a water project in a rural area with poor sanitation. He has no diarrhea now and no history of gallstones, alcohol use or abdominal surgery. Temperature is 38.8 °C and there is point tenderness over the right lower ribs. Leukocytes are 16,400/mm3, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L (25-100 U/L) and bilirubin normal. CT shows a single 7-cm low-attenuation lesion with an enhancing rim in the right hepatic lobe, without daughter cysts or calcification. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A young man with prolonged residence in an endemic area who develops fever, right upper quadrant pain and a single right-lobe abscess most likely has an amebic liver abscess. Concurrent diarrhea is often absent and stool microscopy is often negative. Elevated alkaline phosphatase and leukocytosis are common. E. histolytica serology is the confirmatory test.

Takeaway: A solitary right-lobe abscess after time in an endemic area, without biliary disease, suggests amebic abscess even without diarrhea.

whyNot.B: Hemangiomas are asymptomatic vascular lesions with peripheral nodular enhancement and do not cause fever or leukocytosis.
whyNot.C: HCC occurs mainly with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B and does not present with fever and an abscess-like rim.
whyNot.D: Echinococcal cysts are usually slow-growing and afebrile and show daughter cysts or wall calcification, which are absent.
whyNot.E: Pyogenic abscesses usually arise in older patients from biliary or bowel sources; nothing here suggests that, while the travel history points to amebiasis.

items.objective: Differentiate amebic from pyogenic liver abscess on clinical grounds.

items.stemHtml: The man with the 7-cm right-lobe liver abscess has a positive Entamoeba histolytica antibody test. He is hemodynamically stable, and imaging shows no signs of impending rupture. Which is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Open surgical drainage of the abscess

items.explanationHtml:
Invasive amebiasis is treated with a tissue-active nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole). Because trophozoites and cysts can persist in the colon, a luminal agent such as paromomycin follows to prevent relapse and transmission. Most abscesses respond within days; aspiration or drainage is added for very large abscesses, left-lobe lesions near the pericardium, impending rupture, or no response to treatment.

Takeaway: Amebic liver abscess is treated medically with metronidazole and then a luminal agent; drainage is the exception.

whyNot.A: Albendazole with procedural treatment is for hydatid disease, not amebiasis.
whyNot.C: Surgery is reserved for rupture or failure of medical therapy and drainage.
whyNot.D: Paromomycin is a luminal agent that clears intestinal cysts but does not treat invasive tissue disease.
whyNot.E: Routine drainage is not needed for an uncomplicated amebic abscess, and ceftriaxone has no antiamebic activity.

items.objective: Treat amebic liver abscess with tissue and luminal agents.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with a duodenal ulcer completes 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori. Her epigastric pain has resolved. She asks how to confirm that the infection has been eradicated. Which is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.html: No testing, because her symptoms have resolved

options.label: B
options.html: Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy culture in all patients

options.label: C
options.html: Serum IgG antibody to H. pylori 4 weeks after therapy

options.label: D
options.html: Stool antigen test the day after finishing therapy while on a PPI

options.label: E
options.html: Urea breath test 4 or more weeks after therapy, with the PPI held for 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
All treated patients should have a test of cure because resistance causes treatment failure. Active-infection tests (urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy) should be done at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and bismuth, and at least 2 weeks after stopping a PPI, to avoid false negatives from suppressed organisms. Serology is unsuitable because it stays positive after cure.

Takeaway: Confirm H. pylori eradication with a breath or stool antigen test 4 or more weeks after therapy and 2 weeks off PPIs.

whyNot.A: Symptom resolution does not prove eradication; every treated patient should have a test of cure.
whyNot.B: Endoscopy is not required just to confirm eradication; a noninvasive test is adequate for an uncomplicated duodenal ulcer.
whyNot.C: Antibodies persist for months to years after cure, so serology cannot confirm eradication.
whyNot.D: Testing too early and during PPI use suppresses the organism and can give a false-negative result.

items.objective: Select and time the appropriate test of cure after H. pylori therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has had abdominal cramps for 3 days and now has frequent small bloody stools. Four days ago she visited a petting farm and ate a hamburger at a cookout. Temperature is 37.2 °C; she is mildly dehydrated but tolerating fluids. Stool PCR detects Shiga toxin genes. Hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine are currently normal. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Fluids with monitoring for hemolysis and kidney injury

items.explanationHtml:
Bloody diarrhea with little fever after exposure to undercooked beef or farm animals suggests Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157:H7. Management is supportive, with hydration (IV fluids if needed, which may also protect the kidneys). Children are monitored for hemolytic uremic syndrome (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury), which typically appears about a week after diarrhea begins.

Takeaway: In suspected STEC infection give fluids and monitor for HUS; avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs.

whyNot.B: Antimotility agents prolong toxin exposure and are associated with HUS and neurologic complications.
whyNot.C: Antibiotics do not shorten STEC illness and may increase toxin release and the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome.
whyNot.D: Fluoroquinolones are avoided in STEC infection because of the possible increased HUS risk.
whyNot.E: As with other antibiotics, TMP-SMX may increase the risk of HUS and is avoided.

items.objective: Manage Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection in a child.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old shepherd who tends sheep with the help of several working dogs has a 6-month history of dull right upper quadrant fullness. He is afebrile. Eosinophils are mildly increased. Ultrasound and CT show a 9-cm hepatic cyst containing multiple internal daughter cysts and a partly calcified wall. Echinococcus serology is positive. A surgeon plans definitive treatment of the cyst. Which medication should be given around the procedure?
items.explanationHtml:
Hydatid disease from Echinococcus granulosus is treated by staged procedures (surgery, or puncture-aspiration-injection-reaspiration for suitable cysts) under albendazole cover. Albendazole, a benzimidazole that blocks parasite microtubule polymerisation, is started before and continued after the procedure to reduce the risk of secondary spread if cyst contents spill. Uncontrolled aspiration is avoided because leakage can cause anaphylaxis.

Takeaway: Hydatid cysts are treated with albendazole plus procedural management; avoid unprotected aspiration.

whyNot.B: Fluconazole is an antifungal and has no role against helminths.
whyNot.C: Ivermectin treats strongyloidiasis and scabies but is not effective for hydatid disease.
whyNot.D: Metronidazole treats amebiasis and anaerobic infection; it has no activity against Echinococcus.
whyNot.E: Nitazoxanide is used for Cryptosporidium and Giardia, not echinococcosis.

items.objective: Manage hepatic echinococcal cyst.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old healthy man learns that his roommate was diagnosed with acute hepatitis A 3 days ago. They share a kitchen and bathroom. He has never received hepatitis A vaccine and has no medical conditions. Which is the most appropriate post-exposure measure?

options.label: D
options.html: Serial ALT measurements weekly for 6 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Single dose of hepatitis A vaccine now

items.explanationHtml:
Close contacts of a person with hepatitis A should receive post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of exposure. For healthy people aged 1 year and older, a dose of hepatitis A vaccine is recommended; the second dose completes long-term protection. Immune globulin is used for infants under 12 months and for people who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease (who may also receive the vaccine).

Takeaway: Healthy household contacts of hepatitis A receive hepatitis A vaccine within 2 weeks of exposure.

whyNot.A: Immune globulin is reserved for infants under 12 months, immunocompromised people and those with chronic liver disease; healthy adults should receive vaccine.
whyNot.B: Post-exposure prophylaxis given within 2 weeks prevents infection and should not be withheld.
whyNot.C: There is no antiviral prophylaxis for hepatitis A.
whyNot.D: Monitoring does not prevent infection; prophylaxis is the correct action within 2 weeks of exposure.

items.objective: Choose post-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis A.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man has 8 months of crampy right lower quadrant pain, nonbloody diarrhea and weight loss, and now has a draining opening beside the anus. Colonoscopy shows deep linear ulcers in the terminal ileum with normal intervening mucosa; the rectum is normal. He undergoes resection of a strictured ileal segment. Which finding is most likely on histologic examination of the specimen?

options.label: C
options.html: Inflammation confined to the mucosa with crypt abscesses

options.label: D
options.html: Subepithelial collagen band thicker than normal

options.label: E
options.html: Transmural lymphoid aggregates with noncaseating granulomas

items.explanationHtml:
Skip lesions in the terminal ileum, linear ulcers, stricture and a perianal fistula indicate Crohn disease. Its inflammation is transmural, which explains fistulas, strictures and serosal creeping fat. Noncaseating granulomas are characteristic, although they are found in only a minority of biopsies.

Takeaway: Crohn disease is transmural with noncaseating granulomas; UC is mucosal with crypt abscesses.

whyNot.A: Caseation and acid-fast bacilli indicate intestinal tuberculosis, not Crohn disease.
whyNot.B: This describes Whipple disease, which causes malabsorption and arthralgia rather than fistulizing ileitis.
whyNot.C: Mucosa-limited inflammation is typical of ulcerative colitis, which starts in the rectum and does not cause fistulas.
whyNot.D: A thick collagen band is the hallmark of collagenous colitis, which has a normal-looking mucosa.

items.objective: Recognise the histopathology of Crohn disease.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man with a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis has pruritus and fatigue. Alkaline phosphatase is 410 U/L (25-100 U/L), AST and ALT are mildly elevated, and antimitochondrial antibody is negative. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilations of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. His underlying biliary disease most strongly predisposes him to which malignancy?
items.explanationHtml:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes concentric periductal fibrosis and a beaded biliary tree, and most patients have ulcerative colitis. Chronic biliary inflammation carries a high lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, which is a leading cause of death in PSC. Gallbladder carcinoma and colorectal cancer are also increased.

Takeaway: PSC in a patient with UC carries a major risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

whyNot.B: Fibrolamellar carcinoma affects adolescents and young adults without underlying liver disease.
whyNot.C: Angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride, arsenic and thorium dioxide exposure, not sclerosing cholangitis.
whyNot.D: Hepatoblastoma is a childhood tumour associated with FAP and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
whyNot.E: Pancreatic NETs are associated with MEN1 and VHL, not PSC.

items.objective: Associate primary sclerosing cholangitis with cholangiocarcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis is started on an intravenous monoclonal antibody that reduces trafficking of lymphocytes into the gut wall. Her physician explains that, unlike a related drug used for multiple sclerosis, it carries no known link to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy because it acts selectively on intestinal endothelium. What is the mechanism of action of the drug she received?

options.label: A
options.html: Binds the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23

options.label: B
options.html: Blocks alpha4 integrin binding to VCAM-1 in many tissues

options.label: C
options.html: Blocks alpha4beta7 integrin binding to MAdCAM-1

options.label: D
options.html: Modulates S1P receptors to retain lymphocytes in nodes

items.explanationHtml:
Vedolizumab is a humanised antibody against alpha4beta7 integrin. MAdCAM-1, its ligand, is expressed mainly on gut mucosal venules, so blocking the interaction keeps effector lymphocytes out of the bowel wall without impairing CNS immune surveillance. Natalizumab binds the alpha4 subunit broadly, including alpha4beta1 interaction with VCAM-1 at the blood-brain barrier, and can allow JC virus to cause PML.

Takeaway: Vedolizumab is gut-selective anti-alpha4beta7 therapy; natalizumab is the non-selective alpha4 antibody with PML risk.

whyNot.A: This is ustekinumab, which blocks cytokine signalling rather than lymphocyte trafficking.
whyNot.B: This is natalizumab, which also prevents lymphocyte entry to the CNS and carries the PML risk.
whyNot.D: S1P modulators are oral small molecules, not intravenous antibodies, and act systemically.
whyNot.E: Anti-TNF agents do not act specifically on lymphocyte homing to the gut.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of vedolizumab and contrast it with natalizumab.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman with Crohn disease is to start azathioprine to maintain remission. Her physician orders a blood test first, explaining that people who inherit low activity of a particular enzyme accumulate excess active thioguanine nucleotides and can develop life-threatening bone marrow suppression. Which enzyme is being measured?
items.explanationHtml:
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which is either activated by HGPRT to thioguanine nucleotides or inactivated by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and xanthine oxidase. Patients with low or absent TPMT activity (or NUDT15 variants) shunt more drug into thioguanine nucleotides and develop profound myelosuppression at standard doses. Pre-treatment testing guides dosing.

Takeaway: Check TPMT (and NUDT15) before thiopurines; low activity causes severe myelosuppression.

whyNot.A: DPD deficiency causes toxicity from 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine, not thiopurines.
whyNot.B: G6PD testing precedes drugs such as dapsone or primaquine that cause oxidative hemolysis.
whyNot.C: HGPRT activates thiopurines; its deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and would reduce, not increase, active drug.
whyNot.E: Xanthine oxidase also inactivates thiopurines, but it is inhibited by allopurinol rather than measured before therapy.

items.objective: Explain the pharmacogenetic basis of thiopurine toxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has iron-deficiency anemia unresponsive to oral iron, bloating and loose stools. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Serum IgA antibodies against an endogenous enzyme are strongly positive. That enzyme contributes to disease by which action?

options.label: A
options.html: Activating complement on the surface of enterocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Cleaving gliadin into peptides small enough to be absorbed

options.label: C
options.html: Cross-linking IgA to the epithelial basement membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Deamidating gliadin peptides so they bind HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 more strongly

options.label: E
options.html: Degrading tight junction proteins between enterocytes

items.explanationHtml:
Tissue transglutaminase converts selected glutamine residues in gliadin peptides to glutamate. The added negative charge allows the peptides to bind the pockets of HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 tightly, and gluten-specific CD4 T cells become activated. These T cells help B cells produce anti-tTG antibodies (the basis of serologic testing) and drive the inflammation that, together with IL-15-activated intraepithelial lymphocytes, flattens the villi.

Takeaway: In celiac disease tTG deamidates gliadin, enhancing DQ2/DQ8 presentation to T cells.

whyNot.A: Complement activation is not the central mechanism of celiac disease, which is T-cell driven.
whyNot.B: Small-intestinal brush-border peptidases cannot fully digest gliadin, but tTG's role is deamidation, not cleavage.
whyNot.C: IgA deposition at the basement membrane is not the mechanism; tTG modifies antigen for T-cell presentation.
whyNot.E: Increased permeability occurs, but the enzyme targeted by the antibodies acts on gliadin, not tight junctions.

items.objective: Explain the role of tissue transglutaminase in celiac disease pathogenesis.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has intensely itchy, grouped vesicles and excoriations on both elbows, knees and buttocks. He reports occasional loose stools. A biopsy of perilesional skin is sent for direct immunofluorescence. Which pattern is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae

options.label: B
options.html: Granular IgG and C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction

options.label: C
options.html: Intercellular IgG between keratinocytes in a net-like pattern

options.label: D
options.html: Linear IgA along the basement membrane zone

options.label: E
options.html: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane

items.explanationHtml:
Dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous form of gluten sensitivity. IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase deposit in a granular pattern in the dermal papillae, attracting neutrophils and forming intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces. Most patients have celiac enteropathy even when gut symptoms are mild; dapsone relieves itch and a gluten-free diet treats both skin and gut.

Takeaway: Dermatitis herpetiformis shows granular IgA in dermal papillae and signals celiac disease.

whyNot.B: Granular deposits along the junction suggest lupus (lupus band), not a gluten-related disorder.
whyNot.C: This pattern is pemphigus vulgaris, with flaccid bullae and oral erosions.
whyNot.D: Linear IgA indicates linear IgA bullous dermatosis, often drug-induced (for example vancomycin).
whyNot.E: Linear IgG and C3 indicate bullous pemphigoid, which causes tense bullae in older adults.

items.objective: Identify the immunofluorescence pattern of dermatitis herpetiformis.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman has 4 months of watery diarrhea up to 8 times daily, including at night. She takes naproxen for osteoarthritis and sertraline for depression. Stool studies for infection are negative, and colonoscopy shows a normal-appearing mucosa. Random colonic biopsies are taken. Which histologic finding is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Crypt abscesses with diffuse crypt architectural distortion

options.label: C
options.html: Lipofuscin-laden macrophages in the lamina propria

options.label: D
options.html: Pseudomembranes composed of fibrin and neutrophils

options.label: E
options.html: Thickened band of collagen beneath the surface epithelium

items.explanationHtml:
Chronic watery, often nocturnal, diarrhea in an older woman with a normal colonoscopy suggests microscopic colitis. In the collagenous form, biopsies show a thickened subepithelial collagen band with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; the lymphocytic form lacks the thick band. NSAIDs, SSRIs and PPIs are recognised precipitants.

Takeaway: Microscopic colitis is diagnosed only on biopsy; collagenous colitis shows a thickened subepithelial collagen band.

whyNot.A: These are features of ulcerative colitis, which produces visible inflammation on colonoscopy.
whyNot.B: This describes amebic colitis, which causes bloody diarrhea and visible ulcers.
whyNot.C: Pigment-laden macrophages indicate melanosis coli from anthraquinone laxatives, which does not cause diarrhea.
whyNot.D: Pseudomembranes indicate C. difficile infection, which should have been detected by stool testing and is visible endoscopically.

items.objective: Recognise the histology of collagenous colitis and its drug triggers.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy with asthma and allergic rhinitis has recurrent episodes of food sticking in his chest. Endoscopy shows stacked circular rings and linear furrows in the esophagus. Biopsies show more than 30 eosinophils per high-power field in the squamous epithelium. Which immune mechanism best explains the disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Acid injury with secondary eosinophil recruitment from the stomach

options.label: B
options.html: Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors on smooth muscle

options.label: D
options.html: Th1-mediated destruction of myenteric ganglion cells

options.label: E
options.html: Th2 response to food antigens with IL-13-induced eotaxin-3

items.explanationHtml:
Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic, food-antigen-driven Th2 disease. IL-5 recruits and sustains eosinophils, and IL-13 induces esophageal epithelium to release eotaxin-3, a potent eosinophil chemoattractant. Ongoing inflammation leads to remodelling and fibrosis, producing rings, strictures and food impaction. This mechanism is the rationale for dupilumab, which blocks the shared IL-4/IL-13 receptor.

Takeaway: EoE is a Th2 allergic disease of the esophagus mediated by IL-5 and IL-13.

whyNot.A: Acid reflux can cause a few eosinophils in the distal esophagus, but dense infiltration with rings in an atopic boy reflects an allergic process.
whyNot.B: Esophageal smooth muscle is not targeted by such antibodies; myasthenia gravis affects skeletal muscle.
whyNot.C: Anti-tTG IgA is the mechanism of celiac disease, which affects the small bowel.
whyNot.D: Loss of myenteric neurons causes achalasia, a motility disorder without eosinophilic infiltration.

items.objective: Explain the immunopathogenesis of eosinophilic esophagitis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has fatigue and tingling in her feet. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (12.0-16.0 g/dL) with an MCV of 112 fL (80-100 fL). Antibodies against intrinsic factor are positive. Endoscopy shows atrophy of the gastric body and fundus with a normal antrum. Which combination of findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: High gastric acid and low serum gastrin

options.label: B
options.html: High gastric acid and markedly elevated serum gastrin

options.label: C
options.html: Low gastric acid and low serum gastrin

options.label: D
options.html: Low gastric acid and markedly elevated serum gastrin

options.label: E
options.html: Normal gastric acid and low serum gastrin

items.explanationHtml:
Autoimmune gastritis is a T-cell-mediated attack on parietal cells of the body and fundus. Achlorhydria removes the normal acid feedback on antral G cells, which are spared, so gastrin rises markedly. Chronic hypergastrinemia stimulates enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia and type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours. Loss of intrinsic factor causes B12 deficiency with macrocytic anemia and neuropathy.

Takeaway: Autoimmune gastritis produces achlorhydria with high gastrin and B12 deficiency.

whyNot.A: High acid with suppressed gastrin can occur in other settings but is incompatible with atrophy of the acid-secreting mucosa.
whyNot.B: High acid with high gastrin is the pattern of a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), not parietal cell loss.
whyNot.C: Gastrin rises, not falls, because antral G cells are spared and are no longer inhibited by acid.
whyNot.E: Parietal cell destruction lowers acid; gastrin does not fall in this setting.

items.objective: Predict gastric acid and gastrin levels in autoimmune gastritis.

items.stemHtml:
A 24-year-old woman has 1 year of bloating, loose stools and fatigue. She eats a regular diet including bread and pasta. She has recurrent sinus infections. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference
Hemoglobin10.6 g/dL12.0-16.0 g/dL
MCV74 fL80-100 fL
Ferritin6 ng/mL15-150 ng/mL
Albumin3.6 g/dL3.5-5.5 g/dL
IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase1 U/mLbelow 4 U/mL
Total serum IgAbelow 5 mg/dL70-400 mg/dL

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: IgG deamidated gliadin peptide or IgG anti-tTG testing

options.label: C
options.html: Reassurance, because celiac serology is negative

options.label: E
options.html: Trial of a gluten-free diet for 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Her iron deficiency and bowel symptoms fit celiac disease, and recurrent sinus infections with undetectable IgA indicate selective IgA deficiency, which is more common in celiac disease. IgA-based tests (tTG-IgA, endomysial IgA) cannot be interpreted when total IgA is low. The next step is an IgG-based test, either deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or tTG IgG, while she continues to eat gluten; a positive result is followed by duodenal biopsy.

Takeaway: Always measure total IgA with tTG-IgA; if IgA is deficient, use IgG-based celiac serology.

whyNot.A: Endomysial antibodies are also IgA class and will be falsely negative for the same reason.
whyNot.C: The IgA-based test is invalid when total IgA is absent, so a negative result does not exclude celiac disease.
whyNot.D: Repeating an IgA-based test will remain falsely negative while she lacks IgA.
whyNot.E: Starting a gluten-free diet before diagnosis makes later serology and biopsy unreliable.

items.objective: Interpret celiac serology in the setting of selective IgA deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with ulcerative colitis diagnosed 2 years ago, maintained on oral mesalamine, has 9 bloody stools per day for 5 days with cramping. Temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 112/min and blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. The abdomen is tender without distension or peritoneal signs. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (13.5-17.5 g/dL) and CRP is markedly elevated. An abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilation. Stool testing for C. difficile is sent. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Higher-dose oral mesalamine with mesalamine enemas

items.explanationHtml:
Six or more bloody stools daily with fever, tachycardia and anemia define acute severe ulcerative colitis. He should be admitted and treated with IV corticosteroids, with pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis, exclusion of C. difficile (and CMV if refractory), and avoidance of opioids, anticholinergics and NSAIDs. Response is assessed after about 3 days.

Takeaway: Acute severe UC is treated first with IV corticosteroids in hospital.

whyNot.A: Surgery is reserved for failure of medical rescue, perforation, massive hemorrhage or toxic megacolon, none of which is present.
whyNot.B: 5-ASA escalation is appropriate for mild to moderate flares, not for acute severe colitis with systemic toxicity.
whyNot.D: Antimotility agents can precipitate toxic megacolon in severe colitis.
whyNot.E: Budesonide MMX is for mild to moderate UC and is too weak for an acute severe attack.

items.objective: Recognise acute severe ulcerative colitis and start first-line therapy.

items.stemHtml: The man with acute severe ulcerative colitis has received IV methylprednisolone for 3 days. He still has 8 bloody stools per day, pulse 104/min and a rising CRP. C. difficile testing is negative and the colon is of normal caliber. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue IV steroids for 2 more weeks before deciding

options.label: C
options.html: Start azathioprine and continue IV steroids

items.explanationHtml:
Failure to respond after about 3 days of IV corticosteroids calls for medical rescue with infliximab or cyclosporine, or colectomy. Infliximab acts within days. Surgeons should be involved early; if rescue fails within about a week, colectomy should not be delayed.

TB and HBV screening should be sent on admission so that infliximab is not delayed.

Takeaway: Steroid-refractory acute severe UC is rescued with infliximab or cyclosporine, or treated with colectomy.

whyNot.A: Prolonged steroid exposure without response delays rescue and increases complications and surgical mortality.
whyNot.C: Azathioprine takes months to act and cannot rescue a steroid-refractory attack.
whyNot.D: Methotrexate is not effective for rescue in UC.
whyNot.E: Vedolizumab has a slow onset and is not a rescue therapy for acute severe UC.

items.objective: Choose rescue therapy for steroid-refractory acute severe UC.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman has had ulcerative colitis extending to the hepatic flexure for 5 years, in clinical remission on mesalamine. A recent colonoscopy 1 year ago showed no dysplasia. Persistently elevated alkaline phosphatase led to MRCP, which shows multifocal intrahepatic bile duct strictures, and she is diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis. Which is the most appropriate colorectal cancer surveillance plan?

options.label: B
options.html: Begin colonoscopy 8 years after colitis onset, then every 3 years

options.label: C
options.html: Colonoscopy every 10 years, as for average-risk adults

options.label: D
options.html: Colonoscopy now and then every year

items.explanationHtml:
Patients with IBD and coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis have a markedly increased risk of colorectal neoplasia, often in the right colon. Surveillance colonoscopy should begin at the time PSC is diagnosed and continue annually, regardless of colitis duration, ideally with high-definition or chromoendoscopy. Without PSC, surveillance starts about 8 years after symptom onset for extensive colitis.

Takeaway: IBD plus PSC means surveillance colonoscopy from PSC diagnosis and every year thereafter.

whyNot.A: Stool tests are not validated for dysplasia surveillance in IBD and would be confounded by colitis.
whyNot.B: The 8-year rule applies to IBD without PSC; PSC requires surveillance from its diagnosis.
whyNot.C: IBD with PSC confers a much higher colorectal cancer risk than the general population.
whyNot.E: CT colonography cannot detect flat dysplasia or allow biopsy and is not used for IBD surveillance.

items.objective: Apply colorectal cancer surveillance rules for IBD with PSC.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man with ileocolonic Crohn disease has painful perianal drainage. Pelvic MRI shows a complex fistula from the anal canal to the perianal skin; a small perianal abscess is drained surgically and a loose seton is placed. He is on no maintenance therapy. Tuberculosis and hepatitis B screening are negative. Which is the most appropriate medical therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Complex perianal fistulizing Crohn disease needs combined surgical and medical treatment: drainage of sepsis and seton placement first, then an anti-TNF agent, with infliximab having the strongest evidence for fistula closure. It is often combined with an immunomodulator to improve drug levels. Antibiotics (metronidazole or ciprofloxacin) can be added for symptom control.

Takeaway: After draining any abscess, perianal fistulizing Crohn disease is treated with an anti-TNF such as infliximab.

whyNot.B: Systemic steroids do not heal fistulas, can worsen perianal sepsis and should not be used for maintenance.
whyNot.C: Symptomatic therapy does not address fistulizing inflammation.
whyNot.D: Budesonide targets ileocecal mucosal disease and does not heal fistulas.
whyNot.E: 5-ASA drugs are not effective for Crohn disease, including fistulizing disease.

items.objective: Manage perianal fistulizing Crohn disease.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 3 weeks of fatigue and jaundice. She takes no medications or supplements and drinks no alcohol. ALT is 780 U/L (10-40 U/L), AST 640 U/L (12-38 U/L), total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL) and INR 1.2 (0.8-1.1). Viral hepatitis serologies are negative. ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies are positive and serum IgG is twice the upper limit of normal. Liver biopsy shows interface hepatitis with abundant plasma cells and no cirrhosis. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Raised aminotransferases, high IgG, ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies, and interface hepatitis rich in plasma cells establish type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. Standard induction is a glucocorticoid with azathioprine; budesonide can replace prednisone in patients without cirrhosis. Most patients respond, and long-term maintenance is usually required. Bone protection and TPMT testing accompany therapy.

Takeaway: Autoimmune hepatitis is treated with corticosteroids plus azathioprine.

whyNot.B: Transplantation is for acute liver failure or decompensated end-stage disease unresponsive to therapy, not first-line care here.
whyNot.C: Phlebotomy treats hereditary hemochromatosis.
whyNot.D: Tenofovir treats hepatitis B, which has been excluded.
whyNot.E: Ursodiol is first-line for primary biliary cholangitis, a cholestatic disease, not autoimmune hepatitis.

items.objective: Treat autoimmune hepatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy with eczema and peanut allergy comes to the emergency department after a piece of chicken lodged in his chest. It is removed endoscopically, and the esophagus shows rings and linear furrows. Biopsies from the proximal and distal esophagus show 45 eosinophils per high-power field. There is no evidence of infection or other cause. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.label: A
options.html: Botulinum toxin injection of the lower esophageal sphincter

items.explanationHtml:
Food impaction with rings, furrows and at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field in an atopic adolescent indicates eosinophilic esophagitis. First-line treatment options are a PPI, swallowed topical corticosteroids (budesonide or fluticasone) or an elimination diet, followed by repeat endoscopy with biopsy to assess histologic response. Dupilumab is used for refractory disease, and dilation is added for fibrostenotic narrowing.

Takeaway: EoE is treated first with a PPI, swallowed topical steroids or diet elimination; procedures for motility disorders have no role.

whyNot.A: Botulinum toxin is a temporising treatment for achalasia.
whyNot.B: Myotomy treats achalasia, not an inflammatory eosinophilic disorder.
whyNot.C: Fundoplication treats refractory reflux and does not control eosinophilic inflammation.
whyNot.D: Calcium channel blockers are used for spastic motility disorders, not EoE.

items.objective: Choose initial therapy for eosinophilic esophagitis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man with moderate to severe Crohn disease of the terminal ileum has failed oral corticosteroids, and his gastroenterologist plans to start adalimumab. He has no other medical problems and received all routine childhood vaccines. Before the first dose, which test is most important to obtain?

options.label: A
options.html: Brain MRI to exclude demyelinating lesions

options.label: C
options.html: Interferon-gamma release assay for latent tuberculosis

items.explanationHtml:
TNF-alpha is essential for maintaining granulomas that contain Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB, often as extrapulmonary or disseminated disease. Screening with an IGRA (or tuberculin skin test) and chest radiograph when indicated, plus hepatitis B serology, is required before starting therapy; latent TB is treated before or alongside the biologic.

Takeaway: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting anti-TNF therapy.

whyNot.A: Imaging is not required unless there are neurologic symptoms or a history of demyelinating disease.
whyNot.B: Anti-TNF drugs are avoided in moderate to severe heart failure, but routine echocardiography is not needed in a patient without cardiac symptoms.
whyNot.D: ASCA may support a Crohn diagnosis but has no role in pre-treatment safety assessment.
whyNot.E: TPMT testing is needed before azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, not before anti-TNF monotherapy.

items.objective: Identify required safety screening before anti-TNF therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman has 3 months of watery, nonbloody diarrhea 6 to 8 times a day, including at night. She started lansoprazole 5 months ago. Stool studies are negative for infection, celiac serology is negative, and colonoscopy is grossly normal. Random biopsies from the right and left colon show increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and a thickened subepithelial collagen band. Lansoprazole is stopped, but diarrhea persists after 3 weeks. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Collagenous colitis is a cause of chronic watery diarrhea with a normal colonoscopy in older adults. After stopping possible culprit drugs (PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs), oral budesonide is the most effective induction therapy, with low systemic exposure because of first-pass hepatic metabolism. Loperamide may help mild symptoms. Relapse after stopping budesonide is common, and low-dose maintenance may be needed.

Takeaway: Budesonide is first-line therapy for microscopic colitis once culprit drugs are removed.

whyNot.A: Biologics are reserved for rare cases refractory to budesonide and immunomodulators.
whyNot.C: Mesalamine has not been shown to be effective for microscopic colitis.
whyNot.D: There is no infectious cause, and antibiotics have no role.
whyNot.E: Systemic prednisone is less effective and more toxic than budesonide for microscopic colitis.

items.objective: Treat microscopic colitis.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman has 4 months of frequent watery stools containing large amounts of clear mucus, with weakness and muscle cramps. Colonoscopy shows a 5-cm soft, velvety, sessile mass in the rectum; biopsy shows dysplastic epithelium arranged in long finger-like fronds. Which serum abnormality is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Large villous adenomas, usually in the rectum, can secrete copious mucus rich in potassium and electrolytes, causing secretory diarrhea, volume depletion and hypokalemia (sometimes called McKittrick-Wheelock syndrome). Villous architecture and large size also carry the highest malignant potential among adenomas, so the lesion must be completely removed.

Takeaway: A large rectal villous adenoma can cause mucous diarrhea with hypokalemia.

whyNot.A: Benign adenomas do not secrete PTH-related peptide or cause hypercalcemia.
whyNot.B: The lesion secretes potassium-rich mucus, so potassium is lost and serum levels fall, not rise.
whyNot.C: Diarrheal losses lower magnesium rather than raising it.
whyNot.D: There is no mechanism for phosphate retention; renal function is not described as impaired.

items.objective: Link villous adenoma to secretory diarrhea and hypokalemia.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman undergoes screening colonoscopy. A flat, 14-mm lesion with a mucus cap is removed from the cecum. Histology shows serrated crypts extending to the base, with dilated, horizontally spreading crypt bases and no cytologic dysplasia. Which molecular event most likely initiated this lesion?

options.label: C
options.html: Germline mutation in a mismatch repair gene

items.explanationHtml:
A flat, proximal lesion with a mucus cap and serration reaching dilated, L-shaped crypt bases is a sessile serrated lesion. The serrated pathway usually begins with a BRAF V600E mutation, followed by widespread CpG island methylation that can silence MLH1 and cause microsatellite instability. These lesions are a recognised source of interval cancers in the proximal colon.

Takeaway: Sessile serrated lesions start with BRAF mutation and progress through CpG island methylation and MLH1 silencing.

whyNot.B: MUTYH-associated polyposis produces multiple adenomas through defective base-excision repair.
whyNot.C: Germline MMR mutations define Lynch syndrome, in which cancers usually arise from conventional adenomas.
whyNot.D: APC loss initiates the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence, not serrated lesions.
whyNot.E: TP53 loss is a late event that drives progression to carcinoma in conventional adenomas.

items.objective: Identify the molecular initiation of the serrated pathway.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man has rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy shows several hundred adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. His father died of colon cancer at age 41. Genetic testing reveals a truncating mutation in a tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 5q. The normal protein product of this gene has which function?

options.label: A
options.html: Activating a GTPase in growth factor signalling

options.label: B
options.html: Excising oxidised guanine bases from DNA

options.label: C
options.html: Halting the cell cycle in response to DNA damage

options.label: D
options.html: Repairing DNA base mismatches after replication

items.explanationHtml:
Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by germline APC mutations on chromosome 5q. APC is a scaffold of the destruction complex that phosphorylates beta-catenin and marks it for proteasomal degradation. When APC is lost, beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and activates Wnt target genes such as MYC and cyclin D1, driving proliferation of colonic epithelium. Without colectomy, colorectal cancer is almost certain.

Takeaway: APC normally degrades beta-catenin; its germline loss causes FAP.

whyNot.A: KRAS is a GTPase whose activating mutation promotes adenoma growth; it is an oncogene, not the inherited defect here.
whyNot.B: This is MUTYH, which causes an autosomal recessive polyposis.
whyNot.C: This is p53, whose loss occurs late in adenoma progression.
whyNot.D: This is the role of mismatch repair proteins such as MLH1 and MSH2, whose loss causes Lynch syndrome.

items.objective: Describe the function of APC and its role in FAP.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain. CT shows a small-bowel intussusception with a polyp as the lead point. She has dark brown macules on her lips, buccal mucosa and fingertips. The resected polyp would most likely show which feature?

options.label: A
options.html: Branching cores of smooth muscle covered by normal mucosa

options.label: B
options.html: Dilated mucus-filled cystic glands in edematous stroma

options.label: D
options.html: Regenerating mucosa between areas of ulceration

options.label: E
options.html: Serrated crypts confined to the upper crypt

items.explanationHtml:
Mucocutaneous pigmented macules and small-bowel intussusception indicate Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by STK11 (LKB1) mutation. Its hamartomatous polyps have a tree-like core of branching smooth muscle bundles covered by normal-appearing mucosa. Carriers have raised lifetime risks of gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and gonadal cancers.

Takeaway: Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomas with arborizing smooth muscle; think STK11.

whyNot.B: Cystic dilated glands are typical of juvenile polyps.
whyNot.C: Tubular dysplasia defines an adenoma, as in FAP, not the hamartomatous polyps of this syndrome.
whyNot.D: Inflammatory pseudopolyps occur in IBD.
whyNot.E: This describes a hyperplastic polyp.

items.objective: Recognise the histology and features of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman who has taken a combined estrogen-progestin contraceptive for 12 years has sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg and pulse 124/min. CT shows a 7-cm hypervascular liver mass with surrounding hemorrhage and free intraperitoneal blood. She has no history of liver disease and AFP is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Hepatocellular adenomas are monoclonal hepatocyte tumours strongly associated with long-term estrogen exposure. They contain thin-walled vessels without portal tracts, and larger lesions can hemorrhage and rupture, causing hemoperitoneum and shock. Risk is higher with size above about 5 cm and during pregnancy.

Takeaway: A bleeding hypervascular liver mass in a woman on long-term oral contraceptives suggests hepatic adenoma.

whyNot.A: Hemangiomas rarely rupture spontaneously and are not linked to estrogen in this way.
whyNot.B: FNH has a central scar and almost never bleeds or ruptures.
whyNot.C: Angiosarcoma is rare and linked to vinyl chloride or arsenic, not oral contraceptives.
whyNot.E: HCC usually arises in cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B and often raises AFP.

items.objective: Identify hepatic adenoma as a cause of intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has a 4-cm liver lesion found incidentally on imaging. It is resected because of diagnostic uncertainty. The specimen shows nodules of normal-appearing hepatocytes separated by fibrous septa radiating from a central scar that contains a large, thick-walled artery and proliferating bile ductules. Clonality studies show a polyclonal cell population. Which best explains the formation of this lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Congenital malformation of endothelium-lined vascular spaces

options.label: B
options.html: Hyperplastic response of hepatocytes to an anomalous arterial supply

options.label: C
options.html: Malignant transformation of hepatocytes in a noncirrhotic liver

options.label: D
options.html: Monoclonal proliferation driven by estrogen exposure

items.explanationHtml:
Focal nodular hyperplasia is thought to arise when a localised arterial malformation hyperperfuses part of the liver, prompting a polyclonal hyperplastic response. The central stellate scar carries the dystrophic artery, and the septa contain ductular reaction. The lesion has no malignant potential and rarely bleeds.

Takeaway: FNH is a polyclonal hyperplastic reaction to an abnormal artery, seen as a nodule with a central stellate scar.

whyNot.A: This describes a cavernous hemangioma, which consists of blood-filled vascular channels.
whyNot.C: A polyclonal lesion of normal hepatocytes is not malignant; fibrolamellar carcinoma has large eosinophilic tumour cells with lamellar fibrosis.
whyNot.D: A monoclonal estrogen-related tumour describes hepatic adenoma, which lacks a central scar and bile ductules.
whyNot.E: Diffuse regeneration produces cirrhotic nodules throughout the liver, not a solitary lesion with a central scar.

items.objective: Explain the pathogenesis of focal nodular hyperplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has a 5-cm pancreatic mass found on CT for unrelated reasons. It consists of innumerable tiny cysts arranged like a honeycomb around a central calcified scar. Resection is performed. Which histologic appearance is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: A fibrous wall of granulation tissue without epithelium

options.label: B
options.html: Cysts lined by glycogen-rich cuboidal cells with clear cytoplasm

options.label: D
options.html: Solid sheets of discohesive cells forming pseudopapillae

options.label: E
options.html: Tall columnar mucinous papillae within dilated ducts

items.explanationHtml:
A microcystic honeycomb pattern with a central (sometimes sunburst) calcified scar in an older woman is the classic appearance of serous cystadenoma. The cysts are lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm, and the fluid is thin, with low CEA. These tumours are almost always benign and are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease.

Takeaway: Serous cystadenoma is microcystic, glycogen-rich and benign.

whyNot.A: A cyst wall without epithelium is a pseudocyst.
whyNot.C: Ovarian-type stroma defines a mucinous cystic neoplasm, which is usually a larger macrocystic lesion in the body or tail.
whyNot.D: This describes a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, typically in young women.
whyNot.E: Papillary mucinous epithelium inside ducts defines an IPMN.

items.objective: Recognise the pathology of serous cystadenoma of the pancreas.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has slowly progressive dysphagia to solids. Endoscopic ultrasound shows a 3-cm well-circumscribed hypoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria of the mid-esophagus. Biopsy shows bland spindle cells. Which immunohistochemical profile is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Chromogranin positive, synaptophysin positive, desmin negative

options.label: B
options.html: Cytokeratin positive, desmin negative, S-100 negative

options.label: C
options.html: Desmin negative, KIT (CD117) positive, DOG1 positive

options.label: D
options.html: Desmin positive, KIT (CD117) negative, DOG1 negative

options.label: E
options.html: S-100 positive, desmin negative, KIT (CD117) negative

items.explanationHtml:
Leiomyoma is the most common benign esophageal tumour. It arises from the muscularis propria and is composed of bland smooth muscle cells that express desmin and smooth muscle actin but not KIT or DOG1. Distinguishing it from GIST matters because GIST has malignant potential and responds to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Takeaway: Esophageal leiomyoma is desmin positive and KIT/DOG1 negative, unlike GIST.

whyNot.A: Neuroendocrine markers indicate a neuroendocrine tumour.
whyNot.B: Cytokeratin positivity indicates an epithelial tumour, not a spindle cell mesenchymal lesion.
whyNot.C: This profile is characteristic of a gastrointestinal stromal tumour, which is rare in the esophagus.
whyNot.E: S-100 positivity suggests a schwannoma, which is more common in the stomach.

items.objective: Use immunohistochemistry to separate leiomyoma from GIST.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy has recurrent painless rectal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy show more than 20 polyps in the colon and stomach; each consists of dilated, mucus-filled glands in an inflamed lamina propria without dysplasia. He has frequent nosebleeds, and small telangiectasias are seen on his lips. A pathogenic variant in which gene is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple juvenile polyps define juvenile polyposis syndrome, caused by SMAD4 or BMPR1A variants. SMAD4 carriers can also have hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, explaining the epistaxis and mucosal telangiectasias. These patients need gastrointestinal surveillance and screening for vascular malformations.

Takeaway: Juvenile polyposis with features of HHT points to SMAD4.

whyNot.A: APC causes FAP, in which the polyps are adenomas.
whyNot.B: MUTYH causes recessive adenomatous polyposis.
whyNot.C: PTEN causes Cowden syndrome, with breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer risk, not epistaxis.
whyNot.E: STK11 causes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, with smooth-muscle-cored hamartomas and pigmented macules rather than telangiectasias.

items.objective: Associate juvenile polyposis and HHT with SMAD4.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man with no family history of colorectal cancer has his first screening colonoscopy. The preparation is excellent and the cecum is reached. Two polyps are completely removed with a cold snare. Pathology:

PolypLocationSizeHistology
1Sigmoid colon12 mmTubular adenoma, low-grade dysplasia
2Rectum4 mmHyperplastic polyp

When should his next colonoscopy be performed?
items.explanationHtml:
An adenoma 10 mm or larger is an advanced adenoma. Under the 2020 US Multi-Society Task Force recommendations, the next colonoscopy is due in 3 years. The small rectal hyperplastic polyp does not change the interval.

Takeaway: Any adenoma 10 mm or larger means surveillance colonoscopy in 3 years.

whyNot.A: One year applies to more than 10 adenomas or an inadequate examination.
whyNot.B: Ten years applies to a normal examination or small hyperplastic polyps only.
whyNot.D: A 6-month interval is for piecemeal resection of a lesion 20 mm or larger, which did not occur here.
whyNot.E: This interval is for 1-2 tubular adenomas smaller than 10 mm; his adenoma is 12 mm.

items.objective: Apply post-polypectomy surveillance intervals to an advanced adenoma.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman at average risk has a screening colonoscopy with excellent preparation and cecal intubation. Three polyps, each 3-5 mm, are removed from the rectum and sigmoid colon. All three are hyperplastic polyps. When should her next colonoscopy be performed?
items.explanationHtml:
Small (less than 10 mm) hyperplastic polyps, up to 20 of them, carry negligible risk and do not shorten the surveillance interval. She should return in 10 years, the same as after a normal colonoscopy. A hyperplastic polyp 10 mm or larger would warrant a 3-5 year interval because of possible misclassification as a sessile serrated lesion.

Takeaway: Small hyperplastic polyps only: next colonoscopy in 10 years.

whyNot.A: A 1-year interval is for more than 10 adenomas or a poor examination.
whyNot.C: Three years applies to advanced adenomas or large or dysplastic serrated lesions.
whyNot.D: Five years is not indicated for small hyperplastic polyps; the 2020 guidance treats them like a normal examination.
whyNot.E: A 6-month interval is for piecemeal removal of a large lesion.

items.objective: Avoid over-surveillance after removal of small hyperplastic polyps.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has a right upper quadrant ultrasound for intermittent postprandial pain. It shows gallstones and, incidentally, a 6-cm solid lesion in the right hepatic lobe. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive for 10 years. She has no history of liver disease; liver tests and AFP are normal. Which is the most appropriate next step to characterise the liver lesion?

options.label: C
options.html: Multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI of the liver

items.explanationHtml:
An incidental solid liver lesion should be characterised with multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI (or CT). MRI, particularly with a hepatobiliary agent, distinguishes hemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia and hepatocellular adenoma (and its subtypes) in most cases without biopsy.

Takeaway: Characterise an incidental liver mass with multiphase MRI before considering biopsy or surgery.

whyNot.A: A HIDA scan assesses gallbladder function and does not characterise a solid liver mass.
whyNot.B: Resection before characterisation is premature; the lesion may be a benign entity needing no treatment.
whyNot.D: Biopsy is not the first step: most lesions can be characterised by imaging, and a vascular lesion may bleed.
whyNot.E: Waiting a year without characterising a 6-cm lesion in a woman taking estrogen is inappropriate.

items.objective: Choose the imaging test to characterise an incidental liver mass.

items.stemHtml: The 29-year-old woman's MRI shows features of a 6.2-cm hepatocellular adenoma. She stops the oral contraceptive, switches to a copper intrauterine device and loses a little weight. Repeat MRI 6 months later shows the lesion is unchanged at 6.0 cm with no hemorrhage. She would like to become pregnant in the future. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Percutaneous biopsy to confirm the diagnosis

options.label: D
options.html: Resumption of the combined oral contraceptive

items.explanationHtml:
Hepatocellular adenomas often shrink after estrogen withdrawal, which is why reimaging is done after about 6 months. Lesions that remain 5 cm or larger have higher risks of hemorrhage and malignant transformation and should be resected. Resection before pregnancy is especially sensible, because pregnancy can enlarge adenomas. Adenomas in men and beta-catenin-activated adenomas are resected regardless of size.

Takeaway: A hepatic adenoma persisting at 5 cm or larger after stopping estrogen should be resected.

whyNot.A: An adenoma that remains 5 cm or larger after stopping estrogen carries risks of bleeding and malignant change, so observation alone is not recommended.
whyNot.B: The diagnosis is established on MRI, and biopsy would not change the need for resection.
whyNot.C: Transplantation is reserved for unresectable or multiple lesions with complications, not a single resectable adenoma.
whyNot.D: Estrogen promotes adenoma growth and should be avoided.

items.objective: Manage a persistent large hepatocellular adenoma.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has a 4-cm liver lesion found on CT after a motor vehicle collision. She is asymptomatic and has normal liver tests. MRI shows a lesion with homogeneous intense arterial enhancement, a central scar that is bright on T2-weighted images and enhances on delayed images, and retention of hepatobiliary contrast in the lesion. The surrounding liver is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Focal nodular hyperplasia shows homogeneous arterial enhancement and a central scar that is T2-bright and enhances late. Because it contains functioning hepatocytes and ductules, it retains hepatobiliary contrast, unlike most adenomas. Typical FNH needs no treatment or follow-up, and oral contraceptives do not need to be stopped.

Takeaway: A homogeneously enhancing lesion with a T2-bright central scar and hepatobiliary contrast retention is FNH.

whyNot.A: Hemangiomas show peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement that fills in centripetally, not homogeneous arterial enhancement with a scar.
whyNot.B: Fibrolamellar carcinoma also has a central scar, but the scar is usually dark on T2 and calcified, and the mass is heterogeneous.
whyNot.D: Adenomas usually lack a central scar and are typically hypointense in the hepatobiliary phase because they lack functional bile ducts.
whyNot.E: HCC usually arises in a cirrhotic liver and shows arterial enhancement with washout, not a central scar.

items.objective: Diagnose focal nodular hyperplasia from MRI features.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man has a 3.4-cm cystic lesion in the pancreatic head found on CT for kidney stones. He has no history of pancreatitis, no jaundice and no weight loss. MRI with MRCP shows that the cyst communicates with the main pancreatic duct, which measures 6 mm. There is no solid enhancing component. Which is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A cyst communicating with the pancreatic duct in an older man suggests an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm. Size of 3 cm or more and a main duct of 5-9 mm are worrisome features, which call for endoscopic ultrasound to look for mural nodules and to sample cyst fluid and cytology. Findings of high-risk stigmata or malignant cytology would lead to resection.

Takeaway: Pancreatic cysts with worrisome features need EUS with FNA; high-risk stigmata need surgery.

whyNot.B: ERCP is not used for cyst characterisation and carries a risk of pancreatitis.
whyNot.C: An IPMN with worrisome features carries meaningful malignant risk and needs evaluation.
whyNot.D: Surgery is indicated for high-risk stigmata such as jaundice, an enhancing solid component or a main duct of 10 mm or more, none of which is present.
whyNot.E: Size of 3 cm or more and a main duct of 5-9 mm are worrisome features that require further evaluation now, not delayed imaging.

items.objective: Manage a pancreatic cyst with worrisome features.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man was hospitalised 9 weeks ago for acute pancreatitis related to heavy alcohol use. He now has early satiety. CT shows a 7-cm round, fluid-filled collection with a thin enhancing wall adjacent to the stomach, without septations or solid components. Endoscopic aspiration yields thin brown fluid with markedly elevated amylase and low CEA, and cytology shows inflammatory cells only. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
