items.explanationHtml:
A well-defined fluid collection without solid debris persisting more than 4 weeks after interstitial pancreatitis is a pseudocyst. Its wall is fibrous and granulation tissue without epithelium. Fluid amylase is very high because of communication with the duct system, and CEA is low. Symptomatic pseudocysts, such as this one causing early satiety, are usually drained endoscopically into the stomach.

Takeaway: A collection after pancreatitis with very high fluid amylase and low CEA is a pseudocyst.

whyNot.A: IPMN fluid is mucinous with high CEA, and the lesion arises within the ducts rather than after pancreatitis.
whyNot.B: MCNs occur mainly in middle-aged women, contain viscous fluid high in CEA and are not linked to recent pancreatitis.
whyNot.D: Serous cystadenomas are microcystic with a central scar and have low amylase because they do not communicate with the ducts.
whyNot.E: This tumour occurs in young women and has solid and cystic components.

items.objective: Distinguish a pancreatic pseudocyst from cystic neoplasms.

items.stemHtml: An 18-year-old man known to carry his family's pathogenic APC variant has surveillance colonoscopy. There are several hundred adenomas throughout the colon and densely carpeting the rectum; several are larger than 1 cm, and biopsy of one shows high-grade dysplasia. Upper endoscopy shows a few small duodenal adenomas. Which is the most appropriate management of his colon?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual colonoscopy with removal of the largest polyps

options.label: E
options.html: Total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis

items.explanationHtml:
In familial adenomatous polyposis, prophylactic surgery is needed once polyps can no longer be controlled endoscopically, as shown by high numbers, size over 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia. When the rectum is densely involved, total proctocolectomy with an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis removes all at-risk colorectal mucosa. He will still need lifelong upper endoscopic surveillance of duodenal and ampullary adenomas, and pouch surveillance.

Takeaway: FAP with a heavy rectal burden is treated with proctocolectomy and an ileal pouch; duodenal surveillance continues afterwards.

whyNot.A: Hundreds of adenomas with high-grade dysplasia can no longer be managed endoscopically, and cancer risk is very high.
whyNot.B: NSAIDs may reduce polyp burden but do not prevent cancer and cannot replace surgery.
whyNot.C: Ileorectal anastomosis is chosen when the rectum has few polyps; dense rectal involvement makes proctocolectomy the better choice.
whyNot.D: Segmental resection leaves most of the at-risk colon and the heavily involved rectum.

items.objective: Choose the surgical approach in familial adenomatous polyposis.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman has a 28-mm flat lesion in the ascending colon removed by endoscopic mucosal resection in several pieces. Pathology shows a tubulovillous adenoma with low-grade dysplasia and no invasive cancer. The rest of the colonoscopy, with excellent preparation, is normal. Which is the most appropriate follow-up?
items.explanationHtml:
Piecemeal resection of a lesion 20 mm or larger leaves residual or recurrent adenoma at the site in a meaningful proportion of patients. The 2020 US Multi-Society Task Force advises repeat colonoscopy in 6 months to examine and treat the scar.

Takeaway: After piecemeal removal of a lesion 20 mm or larger, repeat colonoscopy in 6 months.

whyNot.A: CT colonography cannot assess or treat residual tissue at the resection scar.
whyNot.B: Three years applies to an advanced adenoma removed completely in one piece; piecemeal resection needs earlier inspection of the scar.
whyNot.C: Five years is far too long given the high rate of residual adenoma after piecemeal removal.
whyNot.E: Surgery is not needed for a benign adenoma that can be removed and monitored endoscopically.

items.objective: Apply follow-up guidance after piecemeal polypectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with heartburn for 20 years undergoes upper endoscopy. A salmon-coloured tongue of mucosa extends 6 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium containing goblet cells, with no dysplasia. The histologic change in this patient most directly increases his risk for which of the following malignancies?

options.label: B
options.html: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the stomach

options.label: C
options.html: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of the esophagus

options.label: E
options.html: Squamous cell carcinoma of the mid esophagus

items.explanationHtml:
Columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing squamous lining is Barrett esophagus, an intestinal metaplasia caused by chronic acid and bile reflux. It progresses through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus and gastroesophageal junction.

Long segment length, male sex, obesity and smoking add to risk, which is why Barrett is managed with acid suppression and endoscopic surveillance.

Takeaway: Barrett esophagus (goblet-cell intestinal metaplasia) is the precursor of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma.

whyNot.B: MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic H. pylori stimulation of gastric lymphoid tissue, not by Barrett metaplasia.
whyNot.C: GIST arises from interstitial cells of Cajal through KIT or PDGFRA mutations, unrelated to reflux-induced metaplasia.
whyNot.D: Leiomyosarcoma is a rare smooth muscle malignancy with no link to intestinal metaplasia of the mucosa.
whyNot.E: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from native squamous epithelium and is driven by tobacco, alcohol and thermal or caustic injury rather than columnar metaplasia.

items.objective: Link Barrett metaplasia to its malignant outcome.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman is referred for genetic counselling. Her father died of stomach cancer at 41 years of age, and her paternal aunt had lobular carcinoma of the breast. Her own upper endoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa, but random biopsies show small foci of mucin-filled cells with eccentric nuclei infiltrating the lamina propria. A germline mutation in the gene encoding which of the following proteins is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Signet-ring cells infiltrating singly in a young patient with a family history of early gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer indicate hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, caused by germline CDH1 mutation. CDH1 encodes E-cadherin, a calcium-dependent adhesion molecule; its loss makes tumour cells discohesive, so they infiltrate the wall singly rather than forming glands.

Lobular breast carcinoma shares the same mechanism, which is why the two cancers cluster in these families.

Takeaway: Diffuse gastric cancer with lobular breast cancer in a family points to germline CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss.

whyNot.A: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis with colonic adenomas; they are not the cause of hereditary diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer.
whyNot.B: BRCA2 mutations raise breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer risk but do not produce the diffuse signet-ring gastric phenotype seen here.
whyNot.D: MLH1 defects cause Lynch syndrome, in which gastric cancer is usually intestinal type, and lobular breast cancer is not a feature.
whyNot.E: STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation.

items.objective: Identify the adhesion defect behind hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has early satiety and melena. Endoscopy shows a 7-cm submucosal mass in the gastric body with central ulceration. Resection shows spindle cells that stain strongly for CD117 and DOG1. Because of a high mitotic rate, she is started on adjuvant oral therapy. The drug most likely prescribed acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of the programmed death-1 receptor on T cells

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of a constitutively active receptor tyrosine kinase

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of the BCR-ABL fusion protein by DNA intercalation

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex

options.label: E
options.html: Monoclonal antibody blockade of vascular endothelial growth factor

items.explanationHtml:
CD117 (KIT) and DOG1 positive spindle cells in a gastric wall mass define a gastrointestinal stromal tumour, which arises from interstitial cells of Cajal. Most carry an activating mutation of KIT (or PDGFRA) that keeps the kinase signalling without ligand.

Imatinib occupies the ATP-binding pocket of KIT, PDGFRA and BCR-ABL and blocks downstream proliferation signals. It is used for unresectable or metastatic GIST and after resection of high-risk tumours.

Takeaway: GIST is KIT/PDGFRA-driven; imatinib inhibits that tyrosine kinase.

whyNot.A: Checkpoint inhibitors act on T cells and are not the targeted oral therapy for a KIT-mutant tumour.
whyNot.C: The BCR-ABL fusion is the target in chronic myeloid leukemia, and imatinib blocks its ATP-binding site rather than intercalating into DNA; no such fusion drives GIST.
whyNot.D: mTOR inhibitors are used in some neuroendocrine and renal tumours, not first-line in GIST.
whyNot.E: Anti-VEGF antibodies such as bevacizumab are used in colorectal cancer, not as targeted therapy for KIT-driven stromal tumours.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of targeted therapy for GIST.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man has a right colon adenocarcinoma resected. The tumour is mucinous with many intraepithelial lymphocytes. PCR of tumour DNA shows numerous new allele lengths at short repetitive sequences compared with his normal tissue. His mother had endometrial cancer at 46 years of age. A germline defect in which of the following DNA repair processes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Changes in length of short tandem repeats in tumour DNA are microsatellite instability, the signature of failed mismatch repair. Replication slippage creates small insertion-deletion loops that MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 normally correct.

A young patient with a right-sided mucinous, lymphocyte-rich cancer and a first-degree relative with endometrial cancer fits Lynch syndrome, an autosomal dominant germline mismatch repair defect.

Takeaway: Microsatellite instability equals defective mismatch repair; germline loss is Lynch syndrome.

whyNot.A: Base excision repair defects such as MUTYH cause an attenuated polyposis with G:C to T:A transversions, not widespread repeat-length changes.
whyNot.B: Homologous recombination defects (BRCA1, BRCA2) cause breast and ovarian cancer and do not produce microsatellite instability.
whyNot.D: Nonhomologous end joining defects cause immunodeficiency and radiosensitivity, not a familial colorectal and endometrial cancer pattern.
whyNot.E: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum, with UV-induced skin cancers rather than microsatellite instability.

items.objective: Connect microsatellite instability to its DNA repair defect.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has had episodes of facial flushing and watery diarrhoea for a year. He now has a scaly, hyperpigmented rash on the backs of his hands and neck, and he is forgetful. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases with inspiration. CT shows an ileal mass and several liver lesions. A deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely responsible for his rash?
items.explanationHtml:
An ileal neuroendocrine tumour with liver metastases produces carcinoid syndrome: serotonin escapes hepatic inactivation, causing flushing, diarrhoea and right-sided valve fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation here).

The tumour diverts dietary tryptophan into serotonin, leaving less for niacin synthesis. The result is pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea and cognitive change.

Takeaway: Carcinoid syndrome can cause pellagra because tryptophan is diverted from niacin synthesis to serotonin.

whyNot.A: Biotin deficiency causes periorificial dermatitis and alopecia and is rare outside raw egg-white diets or certain genetic defects.
whyNot.B: Cobalamin deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration, not a photosensitive rash.
whyNot.D: Riboflavin deficiency causes angular cheilitis, glossitis and corneal changes rather than pigmented dermatitis on sun-exposed skin.
whyNot.E: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, not a photosensitive dermatitis.

items.objective: Explain the nutritional consequence of carcinoid syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who grew up in a rural area where grain and peanuts were stored in damp conditions has a 6-cm liver mass. He has no cirrhosis, and serologic tests for hepatitis B and C are negative. Biopsy shows hepatocellular carcinoma. Sequencing shows a G:C to T:A transversion at codon 249 of a tumour suppressor gene. Which of the following genes is most likely affected?
items.explanationHtml:
Aflatoxin B1, made by Aspergillus growing on poorly stored grain and nuts, is activated by hepatic cytochrome P450 to an epoxide that binds guanine. The resulting G:C to T:A transversion at codon 249 of TP53 is a molecular fingerprint of aflatoxin exposure.

Aflatoxin and hepatitis B act synergistically, but aflatoxin can cause HCC on its own.

Takeaway: Aflatoxin causes HCC through a characteristic TP53 codon 249 transversion.

whyNot.A: APC mutation starts colorectal adenomas; it is not the signature mutation of aflatoxin-related liver cancer.
whyNot.B: CDKN2A loss occurs in pancreatic cancer and melanoma but is not the codon-specific aflatoxin hotspot.
whyNot.C: KRAS is an oncogene activated by point mutations (often codon 12) in pancreatic and colorectal cancer; it is not the classic target of this carcinogen.
whyNot.D: RB1 loss is typical of retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma rather than this exposure-specific transversion.

items.objective: Relate a dietary carcinogen to its signature mutation.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman has painless jaundice, pruritus and a 9-kg weight loss. Examination shows a palpable, nontender gallbladder. She had two episodes of tender, cord-like veins on different limbs in the past 2 months. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. The oncogene most commonly mutated in this tumour type produces a protein with which of the following functional defects?

options.label: A
options.html: Constitutive dimerisation of a membrane receptor

options.label: B
options.html: Failure to bind phosphorylated SMAD proteins

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of the ability to bind cyclin-dependent kinases

items.explanationHtml:
Painless jaundice, a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) point to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Activating KRAS mutations are present in the great majority and occur early, in pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia.

Mutant KRAS cannot hydrolyse GTP to GDP, so it remains in the active GTP-bound state and drives the MAP kinase pathway continuously.

Takeaway: KRAS, mutated in most pancreatic adenocarcinomas, is locked on because it fails to hydrolyse GTP.

whyNot.A: Ligand-independent receptor dimerisation describes receptor tyrosine kinases such as KIT or HER2, not the small GTPase involved here.
whyNot.B: SMAD4 loss disrupts TGF-beta signalling, a tumour suppressor defect that occurs late in this cancer.
whyNot.D: Increased degradation would reduce signalling; it describes loss of function, not oncogene activation.
whyNot.E: Loss of CDK inhibition describes CDKN2A (p16), a tumour suppressor rather than an oncogene.

items.objective: Describe the molecular defect of mutant KRAS in pancreatic cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man who has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years and drinks a pint of whiskey daily has had progressive difficulty swallowing solid food for 3 months. Endoscopy shows a friable, ulcerated mass 26 cm from the incisors in the mid esophagus. Biopsy of the mass is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrating the wall singly

options.label: B
options.html: Mucin-producing glands in a background of goblet-cell metaplasia

options.label: C
options.html: Nests of atypical cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges

options.label: D
options.html: Sheets of small round cells staining for chromogranin

options.label: E
options.html: Spindle cells staining for CD117 and DOG1

items.explanationHtml:
Heavy tobacco and alcohol use, with a mass in the middle third, is the classic setting for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. The tumour reproduces squamous differentiation: keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (desmosomes).

Hot beverages, caustic strictures and achalasia are other risks for the squamous type.

Takeaway: Mid-esophageal cancer in a smoker and drinker is squamous cell carcinoma with keratinisation.

whyNot.A: Signet-ring cells are characteristic of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma, not a mid-esophageal tumour in a heavy smoker and drinker.
whyNot.B: Gland-forming tumour arising in goblet-cell metaplasia describes adenocarcinoma from Barrett esophagus, typically in the distal third.
whyNot.D: Chromogranin-positive small cells indicate a neuroendocrine tumour, which is uncommon in the esophagus.
whyNot.E: Spindle cells positive for CD117 and DOG1 describe a gastrointestinal stromal tumour, which is submucosal and rarely in the esophagus.

items.objective: Predict the histology of esophageal cancer from location and risk factors.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man who emigrated from southern China 5 years ago has progressive jaundice, itching and pale stools. He often ate raw freshwater fish as a young adult. MRCP shows a hilar bile duct stricture with upstream dilation, and biopsy shows a gland-forming adenocarcinoma in a desmoplastic stroma. Chronic infection with which of the following organisms most likely contributed to this cancer?
items.explanationHtml:
Clonorchis sinensis is acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish in East Asia. The adult fluke lives in intrahepatic bile ducts for years, causing chronic inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia and eventually cholangiocarcinoma.

Opisthorchis species do the same in Southeast Asia. Primary sclerosing cholangitis and choledochal cysts are the other key risks.

Takeaway: Liver flukes from raw freshwater fish (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) cause cholangiocarcinoma.

whyNot.A: Ascaris can migrate into the bile duct and cause obstruction or cholangitis, but it is not an established cause of cholangiocarcinoma.
whyNot.C: Echinococcus forms hydatid cysts in the liver after exposure to dog faeces; it is not a biliary carcinogen.
whyNot.D: E. histolytica causes amoebic liver abscess through faecal-oral spread and is not linked to cholangiocarcinoma.
whyNot.E: Schistosoma haematobium lives in vesical veins and causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, not bile duct cancer.

items.objective: Identify the infectious cause of cholangiocarcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, no personal history of polyps or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer. He has never been screened. Physical examination and a complete blood count are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding colorectal cancer screening?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin screening at 50 years of age

options.label: B
options.html: Begin screening now, for example with colonoscopy every 10 years

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Screen only if he develops rectal bleeding

items.explanationHtml:
The USPSTF (2021) recommends colorectal cancer screening for average-risk adults from 45 to 75 years of age. Colonoscopy every 10 years is one accepted strategy; annual FIT, stool DNA-FIT, CT colonography and flexible sigmoidoscopy are alternatives.

The best test is the one the patient will complete, and any positive non-colonoscopy test must be followed by colonoscopy.

Takeaway: Average-risk colorectal cancer screening starts at age 45.

whyNot.A: Since 2021 the USPSTF recommends starting average-risk screening at 45, so waiting until 50 delays an indicated test.
whyNot.C: CEA is neither sensitive nor specific enough for screening; it is used to monitor for recurrence after resection.
whyNot.D: Routine CT is not a screening test; CT colonography, a different study, is an accepted option.
whyNot.E: Screening aims to find adenomas and early cancer before symptoms; symptoms instead trigger diagnostic colonoscopy.

items.objective: Apply current USPSTF colorectal screening recommendations.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. He takes no medications and has no overt bleeding. His last colonoscopy was 15 years ago and was normal. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (13.5-17.5), MCV 72 fL (80-100) and ferritin 6 ng/mL (reference 20-250). A faecal immunochemical test done by his previous doctor last month was negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Capsule endoscopy of the small bowel

options.label: C
options.html: Oral iron and repeat blood count in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and a right-sided colon cancer is a leading cause. Bidirectional endoscopy (colonoscopy and upper endoscopy) is the evaluation of choice.

A prior negative stool test is irrelevant once a patient has a sign such as unexplained iron deficiency.

Takeaway: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs colonoscopy and upper endoscopy, not stool testing.

whyNot.A: Small-bowel evaluation is considered only after bidirectional endoscopy is unrevealing.
whyNot.C: Iron replacement is reasonable but treating without finding the source can miss a cancer; the cause must be sought.
whyNot.D: Stool tests are for screening asymptomatic people; a negative result does not exclude a bleeding lesion in iron-deficiency anaemia.
whyNot.E: CEA is not a diagnostic test for colorectal cancer and would not change the need for endoscopy.

items.objective: Choose the evaluation of iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, treated to sustained virologic response 3 years ago, has routine surveillance ultrasound. He feels well. Child-Pugh class is A. The ultrasound shows a new 2.5-cm hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe. His previous ultrasound 6 months ago was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI of the liver

options.label: E
options.html: Serum alpha-fetoprotein, imaging only if above normal

items.explanationHtml:
Patients with cirrhosis remain at risk for HCC even after HCV cure and need surveillance ultrasound with serum AFP every 6 months. Any nodule of 1 cm or more needs multiphase contrast CT or MRI.

Multiphase imaging characterises the lesion's blood supply; HCC is fed by the hepatic artery, so it enhances in the arterial phase and washes out later.

Takeaway: A surveillance nodule of 1 cm or more in cirrhosis needs multiphase CT or MRI.

whyNot.B: In cirrhosis, multiphase imaging can diagnose HCC without biopsy, so biopsy is reserved for indeterminate lesions.
whyNot.C: PET is insensitive for well-differentiated HCC and is not the diagnostic study for a cirrhotic nodule.
whyNot.D: Short-interval ultrasound is for nodules under 1 cm; a 2.5-cm nodule needs diagnostic imaging now.
whyNot.E: A normal AFP does not exclude HCC; many tumours do not secrete it.

items.objective: Choose the next test for a liver nodule found on HCC surveillance.

items.stemHtml: The patient has multiphase MRI. The 2.5-cm nodule shows nonrim hyperenhancement in the arterial phase, washout in the portal venous phase and an enhancing capsule. There is no vascular invasion and no other lesion. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is 9 ng/mL (reference below 10). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Accept the imaging diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma and plan treatment

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat alpha-fetoprotein and treat only if it rises

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat MRI in 3 months to confirm growth

options.label: E
options.html: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy before any treatment

items.explanationHtml:
In a patient at high risk (cirrhosis), a lesion of at least 1 cm with arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout, here with a capsule, is LI-RADS 5: definite HCC. No biopsy is needed.

A single 2.5-cm tumour in a Child-Pugh A liver is within the Milan criteria; options include resection, ablation or transplant evaluation by a multidisciplinary team.

Takeaway: In cirrhosis, arterial enhancement with washout on multiphase imaging diagnoses HCC without biopsy.

whyNot.B: Surgical sampling is unnecessary when noninvasive criteria are met; treatment is planned by tumour stage and liver function.
whyNot.C: AFP is normal in many HCCs and is not required for diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Waiting delays treatment of a tumour that already meets diagnostic criteria.
whyNot.E: In a cirrhotic liver these imaging features are diagnostic (LI-RADS 5); biopsy adds risk without changing the diagnosis.

items.objective: Apply noninvasive imaging criteria for HCC.

items.stemHtml:
A 68-year-old man has had progressive yellowing of the skin, dark urine and pale stools for 3 weeks, with a 7-kg weight loss over 2 months. He has no abdominal pain and no fever. He was diagnosed with diabetes 4 months ago. On examination he is jaundiced and a nontender, rounded mass is palpable below the right costal margin. Laboratory results are shown.

TestResultReference range
Bilirubin, total11.2 mg/dL0.1-1.0 mg/dL
Bilirubin, direct9.0 mg/dL0.0-0.3 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase610 U/L25-100 U/L
AST88 U/L12-38 U/L
ALT102 U/L10-40 U/L
Lipase70 U/L0-160 U/L
Leukocytes7,800/mm34,500-11,000/mm3

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: ERCP with stent placement as the first study

options.label: C
options.html: Pancreas-protocol multiphase CT of the abdomen

options.label: D
options.html: Serum CA 19-9 as the confirmatory test

items.explanationHtml:
Painless cholestatic jaundice, weight loss, new diabetes and a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) suggest a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. A pancreas-protocol multiphase CT shows the mass, biliary and pancreatic duct dilation, vascular involvement, and metastases, which determines resectability.

Tissue is then obtained by endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration if needed.

Takeaway: Suspected pancreatic cancer is evaluated first with pancreas-protocol CT, not a tumour marker.

whyNot.A: ERCP is invasive and may later help drainage or tissue sampling, but staging CT should come first because stents degrade imaging and resectability assessment.
whyNot.B: A HIDA scan evaluates cystic duct patency in suspected cholecystitis; it does not define a mass or its resectability.
whyNot.D: CA 19-9 is nonspecific, rises with any biliary obstruction and cannot confirm or exclude cancer.
whyNot.E: The pattern is extrahepatic biliary obstruction with a distended gallbladder, which points to the pancreatic head, not the stomach.

items.objective: Select the initial imaging for suspected pancreatic head cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman has 4 months of epigastric discomfort. Endoscopy shows a flat, erythematous area in the gastric antrum. Biopsies show dense small lymphoid cells infiltrating and destroying gastric glands (lymphoepithelial lesions) and Helicobacter pylori organisms. Immunophenotyping shows a CD20-positive B-cell population. Endoscopic ultrasound shows disease confined to the mucosa and submucosa, and CT shows no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: D
options.html: Rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone

items.explanationHtml:
Low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma is a B-cell lymphoma sustained by H. pylori antigen. When it is localised and H. pylori-positive, eradication therapy (for example bismuth quadruple therapy) is first-line and leads to remission in many patients.

Confirm eradication and follow with repeat endoscopy and biopsies. Tumours with t(11;18) are less likely to respond and may need radiation.

Takeaway: Localised H. pylori-positive gastric MALT lymphoma is treated first by eradicating H. pylori.

whyNot.B: Imatinib targets KIT in gastrointestinal stromal tumour and has no role in B-cell lymphoma.
whyNot.C: Radiation is reserved for H. pylori-negative disease or lymphoma that persists after eradication.
whyNot.D: Combination chemoimmunotherapy is for aggressive or advanced lymphoma, not localised H. pylori-positive MALT lymphoma.
whyNot.E: Surgery is no longer used for localised gastric MALT lymphoma, which often regresses with antibiotics alone.

items.objective: Choose first-line therapy for gastric MALT lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with long-standing reflux has surveillance endoscopy for known Barrett esophagus. The 4-cm Barrett segment looks flat, with no nodules or ulceration. Biopsies show high-grade dysplasia, confirmed by a second expert gastrointestinal pathologist. CT of the chest and abdomen is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoscopic eradication therapy with ablation of the Barrett segment

options.label: C
options.html: Increase the proton pump inhibitor to twice daily and repeat endoscopy in 1 year

items.explanationHtml:
Confirmed high-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus is treated with endoscopic eradication therapy: endoscopic resection of any visible lesion, then radiofrequency ablation (or another ablative method) of the remaining metaplasia.

Continued PPI therapy and post-ablation surveillance follow, because recurrence of metaplasia is possible.

Takeaway: Barrett esophagus with confirmed dysplasia is treated endoscopically, not with surveillance or esophagectomy.

whyNot.B: Esophagectomy carries substantial morbidity and is reserved for deeply invasive or high-risk submucosal cancer or failure of endoscopic therapy; dysplasia is treated endoscopically.
whyNot.C: Acid suppression controls reflux but does not reliably eradicate dysplasia.
whyNot.D: Antireflux surgery does not remove dysplastic epithelium or prevent progression to cancer.
whyNot.E: That interval suits nondysplastic Barrett; confirmed high-grade dysplasia carries a high risk of progression and needs treatment.

items.objective: Manage Barrett esophagus with high-grade dysplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman has bright red blood mixed with stool for 2 months. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated mass whose lower edge lies 6 cm from the anal verge; biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases, and CEA has been drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to stage the primary tumour?
items.explanationHtml:
Rectal cancer needs locoregional staging beyond CT. Pelvic MRI shows the depth of tumour invasion, involved mesorectal nodes and the distance to the mesorectal fascia (the circumferential resection margin).

These findings decide between upfront surgery and neoadjuvant chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy. Endoscopic ultrasound is an alternative for early lesions.

Takeaway: Rectal cancer is locally staged with pelvic MRI after CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

whyNot.A: Barium enema shows the luminal outline but not depth of invasion, nodes or the mesorectal fascia.
whyNot.C: PET-CT is not routine for rectal cancer staging and does not define depth of invasion or the circumferential margin.
whyNot.D: Tattooing helps localise colon lesions at surgery but does not provide local staging.
whyNot.E: CEA is a baseline and follow-up marker; it gives no anatomic staging information.

items.objective: Stage a newly diagnosed rectal cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman has a right hemicolectomy for a stage II adenocarcinoma of the cecum. She is otherwise healthy. Her family history is unknown because she was adopted. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional test on the resected tumour?

options.label: D
options.html: KRAS mutation testing to decide adjuvant therapy

items.explanationHtml:
All newly diagnosed colorectal cancers should have tumour testing for mismatch repair deficiency, by immunohistochemistry for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 or by PCR for microsatellite instability. It screens for Lynch syndrome regardless of family history and predicts benefit from immunotherapy in advanced disease.

Loss of MLH1 prompts BRAF or MLH1 methylation testing to separate sporadic tumours from Lynch; other losses prompt germline testing.

Takeaway: Every colorectal cancer gets universal mismatch repair (or MSI) testing.

whyNot.A: APC testing is for polyposis; a single cancer without many polyps does not suggest FAP.
whyNot.B: HER2 testing has a niche role in metastatic disease and does not identify hereditary risk.
whyNot.D: RAS testing guides anti-EGFR therapy in metastatic disease; it does not screen for an inherited syndrome.
whyNot.E: CA 19-9 is a pancreatic and biliary marker, not a tumour-tissue test.

items.objective: Apply universal tumour screening for Lynch syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man had a sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma resected 2 years ago. Follow-up CT now shows four new lesions scattered through both lobes of the liver, with clear lungs. Which of the following best explains why the liver is the first organ to receive metastases from this tumour?

options.label: A
options.html: Colonic lymph drains directly into hepatic lymphatics

options.label: B
options.html: Colonic veins empty into the inferior vena cava

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatocytes express a receptor that selectively captures carcinoma cells

options.label: D
options.html: Tumour cells spread along the falciform ligament

options.label: E
options.html: Venous blood from the colon drains through the portal vein to hepatic sinusoids

items.explanationHtml:
The sigmoid colon drains through the inferior mesenteric vein to the splenic vein and portal vein. The hepatic sinusoids are therefore the first capillary bed that circulating tumour cells meet, and the liver becomes the commonest site of hematogenous GI metastasis.

Lesions are typically multiple and in both lobes, unlike a solitary primary.

Takeaway: Portal venous drainage makes the liver the first stop for metastases from most of the GI tract.

whyNot.A: Colonic lymph drains to mesenteric and para-aortic nodes and the thoracic duct, not into the liver.
whyNot.B: Most colonic venous blood goes to the portal system; IVC drainage applies to the lower rectum and would favour lung metastases.
whyNot.C: No hepatocyte receptor explains the pattern; the anatomic venous route is the dominant reason.
whyNot.D: The falciform ligament is a route to the umbilicus, not the main path for colonic metastases to the liver.

items.objective: Explain the anatomic basis of hepatic metastasis from colorectal cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has bilateral, solid ovarian masses removed. Microscopy shows sheets of cells whose cytoplasm is distended by mucin that pushes the nucleus to the edge, set in a cellular ovarian stroma. She has had epigastric pain and early satiety for 6 months. The primary tumour is most likely located in which of the following organs?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral ovarian metastases composed of mucin-filled signet-ring cells are Krukenberg tumours. The commonest primary is diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma, which spreads transcoelomically (and also by lymphatics and blood) to the ovaries.

Her epigastric pain and early satiety point to the stomach; colon, appendix and lobular breast cancer are less common sources.

Takeaway: Krukenberg tumour: bilateral signet-ring ovarian metastases, usually from the stomach.

whyNot.A: Endometrial carcinoma forms glands and does not usually produce bilateral signet-ring ovarian metastases.
whyNot.B: High-grade serous carcinoma of tubal origin forms papillae and slit-like spaces, not signet-ring cells.
whyNot.C: Renal cell carcinoma has clear cells rich in glycogen and lipid, not mucin-filled signet-ring cells.
whyNot.E: Thyroid carcinomas rarely spread to the ovary and are not mucin-producing signet-ring tumours.

items.objective: Identify the usual primary of a Krukenberg tumour.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with weight loss and early satiety has a firm, nontender, 2-cm lymph node above the medial end of the left clavicle. Biopsy shows metastatic adenocarcinoma. Which of the following anatomic facts best explains the location of this node?

options.label: A
options.html: The left gastric vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein

options.label: B
options.html: The left vagus nerve accompanies lymphatics from the stomach to the neck

options.label: C
options.html: The phrenic nerve carries tumour cells from the diaphragm to the neck

options.label: D
options.html: The right lymphatic duct drains the abdomen and lower limbs

options.label: E
options.html: The thoracic duct enters the venous system at the left internal jugular-subclavian junction

items.explanationHtml:
Lymph from the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs reaches the cisterna chyli and ascends in the thoracic duct, which empties at the left venous angle. Tumour cells moving retrogradely or lodging near the termination enlarge the left supraclavicular (Virchow) node.

It is classically a sign of gastric cancer but can occur with any intra-abdominal or pelvic carcinoma.

Takeaway: A Virchow node reflects abdominal lymph flowing up the thoracic duct to the left venous angle.

whyNot.A: The left gastric vein drains into the portal vein, and venous routes do not explain spread to a lymph node.
whyNot.B: The vagus nerve does not transport tumour cells; perineural invasion spreads locally, not to supraclavicular nodes.
whyNot.C: Nerves are not a route of metastasis to cervical nodes; the phrenic nerve explains referred shoulder pain.
whyNot.D: The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper quadrant of the body (right head, neck, arm and thorax).

items.objective: Explain the anatomic basis of the left supraclavicular node sign.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman had a 2.1-mm-thick melanoma excised from her back 6 years ago. She now has fatigue and intermittent cramping abdominal pain. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL (12.0-16.0) with low ferritin. CT shows a jejunal intussusception with a lead-point mass. The resected mass consists of large atypical cells with prominent nucleoli that stain for S-100 and SOX10. Which of the following best describes this lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
Melanoma is the tumour that most often metastasises to the small bowel, spreading hematogenously and sometimes appearing years after the primary. Deposits bleed (iron-deficiency anaemia) and can act as a lead point for intussusception in an adult.

S-100, SOX10, HMB-45 and Melan-A identify melanocytic differentiation.

Takeaway: Melanoma is the commonest metastasis to the small bowel and can present late with bleeding or intussusception.

whyNot.A: Lymphoma is positive for CD45 and B-cell markers such as CD20, not melanocytic markers.
whyNot.B: GIST is a spindle-cell tumour positive for CD117 and DOG1.
whyNot.D: Primary adenocarcinoma forms glands and stains for cytokeratins and CDX2, not S-100 and SOX10.
whyNot.E: Neuroendocrine tumours stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin and form nests or trabeculae of uniform cells.

items.objective: Recognise metastatic melanoma in the GI tract.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman treated 8 years ago for breast cancer has early satiety. Endoscopy shows a stiff, thickened stomach without a discrete mass. Biopsies show small cells infiltrating the lamina propria in single-file cords. The cells are positive for estrogen receptor and GATA3 and negative for E-cadherin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Metastatic ductal carcinoma of the breast

options.label: D
options.html: Metastatic lobular carcinoma of the breast

items.explanationHtml:
Lobular breast carcinoma loses E-cadherin, so its cells infiltrate in single file. This pattern spreads to the stomach and bowel more often than ductal carcinoma and can mimic linitis plastica.

Estrogen receptor and GATA3 positivity identify a breast origin and separate it from primary diffuse gastric cancer, which matters because treatment is endocrine and systemic therapy for breast cancer.

Takeaway: ER/GATA3-positive, E-cadherin-negative single-file cells in the stomach indicate metastatic lobular breast cancer.

whyNot.A: MALT lymphoma is a B-cell infiltrate positive for CD20, not ER and GATA3.
whyNot.B: Neuroendocrine tumours stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, not ER or GATA3.
whyNot.C: Ductal carcinoma retains E-cadherin and forms glands or cohesive nests rather than single-file cords.
whyNot.E: Diffuse gastric cancer also lacks E-cadherin, but it would not be estrogen receptor and GATA3 positive.

items.objective: Distinguish metastatic lobular breast cancer from primary diffuse gastric cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with known gastric adenocarcinoma develops progressive abdominal distension. CT shows thickening of the omentum and nodules on the peritoneal surfaces. Paracentesis shows ascitic albumin 2.9 g/dL with serum albumin 3.4 g/dL, ascitic total protein 3.8 g/dL, and malignant cells on cytology. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this fluid accumulation?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased hydrostatic pressure in hepatic sinusoids

options.label: B
options.html: Increased peritoneal capillary permeability and blocked lymphatic drainage

options.label: C
options.html: Leakage of chyle from a disrupted thoracic duct

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia

items.explanationHtml:
The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 3.4 minus 2.9, or 0.5 g/dL, which is below 1.1 and excludes portal hypertension as the main cause. High total protein and positive cytology define peritoneal carcinomatosis.

Tumour-lined peritoneum leaks protein-rich fluid (partly VEGF-mediated), and tumour plugs subdiaphragmatic lymphatics that normally clear peritoneal fluid.

Takeaway: Peritoneal carcinomatosis causes low-SAAG, high-protein ascites through permeability and lymphatic obstruction.

whyNot.A: Sinusoidal hypertension gives a SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more, but this patient's gradient is 0.5 g/dL.
whyNot.C: Chylous ascites is milky with high triglycerides and is not defined by malignant cells on cytology.
whyNot.D: Hepatic vein obstruction raises sinusoidal pressure and gives a high SAAG.
whyNot.E: Low oncotic pressure gives a low-protein transudate, not a protein-rich exudate with malignant cells.

items.objective: Apply SAAG to the mechanism of malignant ascites.

items.stemHtml: In an experimental model, colon carcinoma cells that are able to metastasise secrete higher amounts of a family of zinc-dependent proteases than nonmetastatic cells. Blocking these enzymes prevents the cells from crossing the epithelial basement membrane. Which of the following extracellular matrix components is the principal target of these enzymes at the basement membrane?
items.explanationHtml:
Matrix metalloproteinases are zinc-dependent endopeptidases. MMP-2 and MMP-9 (gelatinases) degrade type IV collagen, the network-forming collagen of basement membranes, allowing carcinoma cells to invade the stroma and enter vessels.

Loss of E-cadherin, integrin attachment to laminin, and directed migration complete the invasive step.

Takeaway: Invasion requires metalloproteinases that degrade basement membrane type IV collagen.

whyNot.A: Elastin gives recoil to arteries, lung and skin; it is not the basement membrane barrier to invasion.
whyNot.B: Type I collagen is the main collagen of bone, skin and tendon stroma, not the sheet-forming collagen of basement membranes.
whyNot.C: Type II collagen is found in cartilage and the vitreous humour.
whyNot.D: Type III collagen forms reticular fibres in vessels and granulation tissue, not basement membranes.

items.objective: Describe the biochemistry of basement membrane invasion.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with colorectal cancer metastatic to the liver receives combination chemotherapy every 2 weeks. After the second cycle she reports tingling in her fingers and tightness in her throat when she drinks a cold beverage or touches a cold door handle. The symptoms resolve within a few days. Which drug is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Oxaliplatin, part of FOLFOX and CAPOX, causes an acute neurotoxicity triggered by cold, with perioral and pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesias, thought to involve altered voltage-gated sodium channel function. With cumulative doses it causes a persistent sensory neuropathy.

Patients are counselled to avoid cold drinks and cold exposure around infusions.

Takeaway: Cold-triggered dysesthesias are characteristic of oxaliplatin.

whyNot.A: 5-Fluorouracil causes mucositis, diarrhoea, myelosuppression and coronary vasospasm, not cold-triggered dysesthesias.
whyNot.B: Bevacizumab causes hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding and GI perforation.
whyNot.C: Irinotecan causes early cholinergic and late secretory diarrhoea and neutropenia.
whyNot.D: Leucovorin potentiates 5-fluorouracil and has no neurotoxicity of its own.

items.objective: Recognise the characteristic adverse effect of oxaliplatin.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man has metastatic adenocarcinoma of the descending colon. His oncologist considers adding an antibody against the epidermal growth factor receptor to his chemotherapy. Tumour sequencing shows a KRAS codon 12 mutation, and the antibody is withheld. Which of the following best explains why the antibody would be ineffective?

options.label: A
options.html: The mutant protein signals downstream of the receptor independently of ligand binding

options.label: B
options.html: The mutation activates a drug efflux pump

options.label: C
options.html: The mutation downregulates receptor expression on tumour cells

options.label: D
options.html: The mutation increases hepatic clearance of the antibody

options.label: E
options.html: The mutation prevents the antibody from binding the receptor's extracellular domain

items.explanationHtml:
Cetuximab and panitumumab block ligand binding to EGFR. Activating KRAS (or NRAS) mutations lock RAS in the GTP-bound state, so the MAP kinase pathway stays on whatever happens at the receptor.

Extended RAS testing is therefore required before anti-EGFR therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer.

Takeaway: Activating RAS mutations make EGFR antibodies useless because signalling is constitutive downstream.

whyNot.B: Efflux pumps affect small-molecule drugs, not large monoclonal antibodies.
whyNot.C: Response does not depend on receptor quantity; KRAS-mutant tumours fail despite expressing EGFR.
whyNot.D: Tumour mutations do not change the pharmacokinetics of monoclonal antibodies.
whyNot.E: KRAS is an intracellular GTPase; its mutation does not alter the receptor epitope.

items.objective: Explain resistance to anti-EGFR antibodies in RAS-mutant colorectal cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman had a right hemicolectomy for stage III colon cancer 18 months ago, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. Surveillance CT shows two lesions, 2.5 cm and 3 cm, in segments VI and VII of the liver. CT of the chest and pelvis shows no other disease, and liver MRI confirms only these two lesions. She is active and her liver function is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Observation with repeat CT in 3 months

options.label: E
options.html: Referral for evaluation for hepatic resection with perioperative chemotherapy

items.explanationHtml:
Colorectal cancer metastatic only to the liver is potentially curable. When all lesions can be removed with clear margins and an adequate liver remnant, a multidisciplinary team offers resection, usually with perioperative chemotherapy.

Long-term survival after resection is substantial, which is why every patient with liver-only disease should be assessed by a hepatobiliary surgeon.

Takeaway: Resectable liver-only colorectal metastases are treated with curative-intent resection.

whyNot.A: Whole-liver radiation is not curative and risks radiation-induced liver disease.
whyNot.B: Isolated resectable colorectal liver metastases can be cured; hospice would forgo potentially curative treatment.
whyNot.C: Transplant is not standard for colorectal metastases outside selected research protocols; resection is the established curative option.
whyNot.D: Waiting allows progression and may make resectable disease unresectable.

items.objective: Manage isolated colorectal liver metastases.

items.stemHtml:
A 66-year-old man had a sigmoid colectomy for stage IIIA adenocarcinoma 2 years ago and completed adjuvant chemotherapy. He feels well and has no symptoms. Colonoscopy 1 year after surgery was normal. His surveillance carcinoembryonic antigen values are shown.

Time after surgeryCEA (reference below 3.0 ng/mL)
Preoperative14.1 ng/mL
3 months2.1 ng/mL
12 months2.3 ng/mL
18 months5.4 ng/mL
24 months9.8 ng/mL

Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
CEA normalised after resection and has risen on two consecutive measurements, which signals recurrence until proven otherwise. The next step is CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to find it; PET-CT is used if CT is unrevealing.

Recurrence confined to the liver or lung may still be resectable, so finding it early matters.

Takeaway: A rising CEA after colorectal cancer resection calls for CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

whyNot.B: Treatment is chosen only after recurrence is located and its resectability assessed.
whyNot.C: Blind exploration is not used now that cross-sectional imaging can localise recurrence.
whyNot.D: Additional markers do not localise disease and would not change the need for imaging.
whyNot.E: Two consecutive rises after normalisation strongly suggest recurrence; waiting may miss a resectable lesion.

items.objective: Interpret a rising tumour marker during surveillance.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man has had poor appetite, early satiety and a 10-kg weight loss over 4 months. He has smoked for 50 years. Examination shows a hard, fixed, 2-cm lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa and a firm 1-cm nodule at the umbilicus. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (13.5-17.5) with MCV 74 fL (80-100). Which of the following is the most likely primary site of his cancer?
items.explanationHtml:
A left supraclavicular (Virchow) node and a periumbilical (Sister Mary Joseph) nodule both signal intra-abdominal cancer. With early satiety, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia, the stomach is the most likely primary.

Upper endoscopy with biopsy is the next test; these signs usually indicate advanced disease.

Takeaway: Virchow node plus periumbilical nodule with early satiety indicates advanced gastric cancer.

whyNot.A: Laryngeal cancer causes hoarseness and spreads to deep cervical nodes, not to the umbilicus.
whyNot.B: Lung cancer commonly spreads to supraclavicular nodes, but early satiety, iron-deficiency anaemia and an umbilical nodule point to an intra-abdominal primary.
whyNot.C: Prostate cancer spreads mainly to bone and pelvic nodes and does not cause early satiety or iron deficiency.
whyNot.E: Thyroid cancer spreads to central and lateral neck nodes and does not cause early satiety or a periumbilical nodule.

items.objective: Recognise physical signs of metastatic gastric cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is diagnosed by colonoscopic biopsy with adenocarcinoma of the transverse colon. He has no symptoms other than mild fatigue, and liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate study to evaluate for distant metastases?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
Distant staging of colorectal cancer uses contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, which covers the liver, lungs, nodes and peritoneum. A baseline CEA is drawn at the same time.

Rectal cancer adds pelvic MRI for local staging; liver MRI helps characterise indeterminate lesions.

Takeaway: Stage colorectal cancer with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis plus baseline CEA.

whyNot.A: Ultrasound misses small liver lesions and does not evaluate the lungs or nodes adequately.
whyNot.C: Brain imaging is reserved for neurologic symptoms; brain metastases at diagnosis are rare.
whyNot.D: Bone metastases are uncommon in colon cancer, and a bone scan is used only for symptoms.
whyNot.E: PET-CT is not routine at initial staging and is reserved for equivocal findings or before metastasectomy.

items.objective: Choose the staging study for a new colon cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman asks for a blood test for cancer at her annual visit because a colleague was recently diagnosed with colon cancer. She has no symptoms and no family history of cancer. She had a normal colonoscopy 4 years ago. She would like her carcinoembryonic antigen and CA 19-9 levels measured. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain that these markers are inaccurate for screening and continue her current screening schedule

options.label: B
options.html: Order both markers and refer for colonoscopy if either is elevated

options.label: C
options.html: Order CEA only, because it is specific for colorectal cancer

options.label: D
options.html: Order CT of the abdomen and pelvis for reassurance

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat colonoscopy now because of her concern

items.explanationHtml:
Tumour markers such as CEA and CA 19-9 lack the sensitivity and specificity to screen asymptomatic people. They are used as a baseline before treatment and for follow-up after resection.

Her colonoscopy 4 years ago was normal, so the next is due 10 years after it. Explaining this, and addressing her worry, is the best response.

Takeaway: Tumour markers are for follow-up, never for screening asymptomatic people.

whyNot.B: Markers are often raised by benign conditions and normal in early cancer, so they would add false alarms without benefit.
whyNot.C: CEA rises with smoking, inflammation and other cancers and is not specific.
whyNot.D: Imaging without an indication exposes her to radiation and incidental findings with no screening benefit.
whyNot.E: After a normal colonoscopy, the next one is due at 10 years for average risk; anxiety alone does not shorten the interval.

items.objective: Counsel a patient requesting tumour markers for screening.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman with gastric adenocarcinoma treated with gastrectomy 2 years ago has had increasing abdominal girth for 6 weeks. She has no history of liver disease or alcohol use. Examination shows shifting dullness and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. CT shows moderate ascites, omental thickening and no liver lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Diagnostic paracentesis with SAAG, total protein and cytology

items.explanationHtml:
New ascites in a patient with prior gastric cancer and omental thickening suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis. Diagnostic paracentesis comes first: SAAG below 1.1 g/dL, high protein and positive cytology confirm it.

Cytology is usually positive in carcinomatosis because the tumour lines the peritoneum.

Takeaway: New ascites needs diagnostic paracentesis with SAAG, protein and cytology before treatment.

whyNot.A: Diuretics treat portal hypertensive ascites; the cause of this fluid must first be established.
whyNot.C: There are no liver lesions and no evidence of liver disease, so biopsy would not explain the ascites.
whyNot.D: TIPS treats refractory ascites from portal hypertension, not suspected peritoneal carcinomatosis.
whyNot.E: Heart failure is possible in theory, but omental thickening after gastric cancer makes carcinomatosis far more likely and fluid analysis is the direct test.

items.objective: Choose the first test for ascites in a patient with cancer.

items.stemHtml: Paracentesis shows a SAAG of 0.6 g/dL, total protein 4.1 g/dL and adenocarcinoma cells on cytology. She starts palliative chemotherapy. Three weeks later she returns with tense ascites, dyspnoea and early satiety; 5 L was drained 10 days ago with temporary relief. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for symptom control?

options.label: B
options.html: Placement of a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter

items.explanationHtml:
Carcinomatous ascites that reaccumulates quickly after therapeutic paracentesis is best managed with a tunnelled indwelling catheter, which allows drainage at home and avoids repeated hospital visits.

Diuretics help mainly when ascites results from portal hypertension (high SAAG), such as extensive liver metastases.

Takeaway: Rapidly recurrent malignant ascites is palliated with a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter.

whyNot.A: Diuretics are rarely effective in low-SAAG carcinomatous ascites and risk hypotension and renal injury.
whyNot.C: Restriction does not prevent reaccumulation of exudative malignant ascites.
whyNot.D: Parenteral nutrition does not control ascites and adds infection risk without improving symptoms here.
whyNot.E: TIPS lowers portal pressure, which is not the mechanism of her ascites.

items.objective: Palliate recurrent malignant ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with ovarian cancer and extensive peritoneal carcinomatosis has had colicky abdominal pain and vomiting for 5 days. CT shows dilated small-bowel loops with transition points at several levels. She has decided against further surgery or chemotherapy and wishes to remain at home with hospice. A nasogastric tube relieves her vomiting. In addition to opioids for pain, which medication is most appropriate to reduce intestinal secretions and vomiting?
items.explanationHtml:
Inoperable malignant bowel obstruction at multiple levels is palliated pharmacologically. Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, reduces gastrointestinal secretions and increases water and electrolyte absorption, lessening distension and vomiting.

Haloperidol for nausea, opioids for pain, anticholinergics for colic and a venting gastrostomy in place of a long-term nasogastric tube complete the plan.

Takeaway: Octreotide reduces secretions and vomiting in inoperable malignant bowel obstruction; avoid prokinetics.

whyNot.A: Erythromycin is a motilin agonist prokinetic and would worsen cramping in mechanical obstruction.
whyNot.B: Loperamide slows motility but does not reduce the secretions driving distension and vomiting.
whyNot.C: Metoclopramide increases peristalsis and worsens colic in complete mechanical obstruction.
whyNot.E: Stimulant laxatives provoke painful contractions against an obstruction and are avoided.

items.objective: Choose palliative pharmacotherapy for malignant bowel obstruction.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer develops new jaundice and pruritus 4 months after diagnosis. He is still walking daily and wants to continue chemotherapy. Bilirubin, total, is 9.4 mg/dL (0.1-1.0), with alkaline phosphatase 520 U/L (25-100). Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts, with a few small liver lesions that are unchanged from prior imaging. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: ERCP with placement of a self-expanding metal biliary stent

items.explanationHtml:
Dilated intra- and extrahepatic ducts mean the jaundice is from tumour compressing the distal common bile duct, not from liver replacement by metastases, which are small and stable. Endoscopic biliary drainage with a self-expanding metal stent relieves jaundice and itch and allows chemotherapy to continue.

Distinguishing obstructive jaundice from hepatic replacement changes management, because only the first can be relieved.

Takeaway: Jaundice with dilated ducts in metastatic pancreatic cancer is palliated with an endoscopic metal stent.

whyNot.B: His jaundice is from a correctable bile duct obstruction, and he wants further treatment; relieving it improves symptoms and allows chemotherapy.
whyNot.C: Cholestyramine may ease itch but does not relieve the obstruction or permit chemotherapy.
whyNot.D: Resection is not appropriate for metastatic disease.
whyNot.E: Ursodiol does not relieve mechanical obstruction of the bile duct.

items.objective: Manage malignant biliary obstruction in metastatic disease.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman receiving cisplatin for cervical cancer is given an intravenous antiemetic before each infusion. After the third dose an ECG obtained for palpitations shows a QTc of 498 ms, longer than her baseline. The antiemetic most likely blocks which of the following receptors?

options.label: B
options.html: Histamine H1 receptors in the vestibular nuclei

options.label: E
options.html: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the area postrema

items.explanationHtml:
Cisplatin damages enterochromaffin cells, which release serotonin that stimulates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Ondansetron and related drugs block these receptors and are the backbone of chemotherapy antiemetic regimens.

Their notable adverse effects are headache, constipation and dose-related QT prolongation, so electrolytes and other QT-prolonging drugs should be reviewed.

Takeaway: 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron can prolong the QT interval.

whyNot.A: Dronabinol is a cannabinoid agonist, not an antagonist, and is an adjunct rather than standard premedication.
whyNot.B: H1 blockers treat motion sickness and cause sedation; they are not standard premedication for cisplatin.
whyNot.C: Muscarinic antagonists such as scopolamine are for motion sickness and cause anticholinergic effects.
whyNot.D: NK1 antagonists such as aprepitant are added for cisplatin but are known for CYP3A4 interactions rather than QT prolongation.

items.objective: Link a chemotherapy antiemetic to its receptor and adverse effect.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is given intravenous prochlorperazine in the emergency department for nausea from gastroenteritis. Ninety minutes later her neck twists painfully to the right and her eyes deviate upward. Blockade of receptors in which of the following pathways most directly causes this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway

options.label: B
options.html: Dopamine D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway

options.label: C
options.html: Histamine H1 receptors in the hypothalamus

options.label: D
options.html: Muscarinic receptors in the basal ganglia

options.label: E
options.html: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the area postrema

items.explanationHtml:
Prochlorperazine and metoclopramide block D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which is how they relieve nausea. They also block D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway, upsetting the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the striatum and causing acute dystonia within hours to days, most often in young people.

Treatment is an anticholinergic such as benztropine or diphenhydramine.

Takeaway: Acute dystonia from antiemetics reflects nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

whyNot.B: Tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin and causes galactorrhoea, not dystonia.
whyNot.C: H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain; H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine actually treat dystonia.
whyNot.D: Muscarinic blockade in the striatum relieves, rather than causes, drug-induced dystonia.
whyNot.E: 5-HT3 blockade causes headache, constipation and QT prolongation, not movement disorders.

items.objective: Explain extrapyramidal effects of dopamine-blocking antiemetics.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with lung cancer has nausea that begins 2 to 4 days after each cycle of a highly emetogenic regimen, despite ondansetron and dexamethasone. His oncologist adds an oral drug that prevents substance P from activating its receptor in the brainstem. Which of the following drugs was added?
items.explanationHtml:
Substance P acts on neurokinin-1 receptors in the nucleus tractus solitarius and area postrema and is especially important in delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea. Aprepitant (and intravenous fosaprepitant) are NK1 antagonists added to a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone for highly emetogenic regimens.

Aprepitant inhibits and induces CYP3A4, so it interacts with drugs such as dexamethasone and warfarin.

Takeaway: NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) block substance P and target delayed chemotherapy nausea.

whyNot.B: Granisetron is another 5-HT3 antagonist and would duplicate ondansetron.
whyNot.C: Meclizine is an H1 antagonist used for vertigo and motion sickness.
whyNot.D: Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist, not a substance P blocker.
whyNot.E: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist used for motion sickness.

items.objective: Identify the NK1 antagonist antiemetic.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia applies a transdermal patch behind his ear before a cruise. Two days later he is confused, his mouth is dry, his pupils are dilated, and his bladder is palpable to the umbilicus. The drug in the patch most likely acts at which of the following receptors?
items.explanationHtml:
The transdermal motion-sickness patch contains scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist that dampens vestibular input to the vomiting centre. It readily enters the brain.

Anticholinergic effects (confusion, dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, constipation) are most dangerous in older adults, especially those with prostatic enlargement or angle-closure glaucoma.

Takeaway: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist with anticholinergic toxicity in older adults.

whyNot.A: D2 antagonists cause extrapyramidal effects and hyperprolactinaemia, not mydriasis and retention.
whyNot.B: H1 antagonists such as meclizine have some anticholinergic effect, but the transdermal motion-sickness patch contains a muscarinic antagonist.
whyNot.D: Nicotinic blockade at ganglia or the neuromuscular junction is not the mechanism of motion-sickness drugs.
whyNot.E: 5-HT3 antagonists are poorly effective in motion sickness and do not cause anticholinergic toxicity.

items.objective: Recognise anticholinergic adverse effects of motion-sickness therapy.

items.stemHtml: Opioids, cardiac glycosides and uraemic toxins cause nausea partly by acting on a brainstem structure that lies on the floor of the fourth ventricle and samples circulating blood directly. Which of the following features of this structure allows it to detect these substances?

options.label: A
options.html: Dense dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra

options.label: B
options.html: Direct projections from the semicircular canals

options.label: C
options.html: Fenestrated capillaries without a blood-brain barrier

options.label: E
options.html: Tight junctions between choroid plexus epithelial cells

items.explanationHtml:
The area postrema is a circumventricular organ with fenestrated capillaries and no blood-brain barrier. Its chemoreceptor trigger zone therefore detects drugs, toxins and metabolic products in blood and relays to the vomiting centre in the nucleus tractus solitarius.

It carries D2, 5-HT3, NK1 and opioid receptors, which is where many antiemetics act.

Takeaway: The chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema lies outside the blood-brain barrier.

whyNot.A: Nigral projections go to the striatum, not to the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
whyNot.B: Vestibular input reaches the vomiting centre through vestibular nuclei, not by chemical sensing of blood.
whyNot.D: Vagal efferents carry motor output; they do not explain detection of circulating chemicals.
whyNot.E: The choroid plexus forms the blood-CSF barrier and produces CSF; it does not trigger vomiting.

items.objective: Explain how the chemoreceptor trigger zone detects emetogenic chemicals.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has bloating, cramps and loose stools after meals that contain milk products. His symptoms resolve when he fasts. Stool analysis shows sodium 25 mEq/L and potassium 30 mEq/L, and the stool is acidic. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of his diarrhoea?

options.label: A
options.html: Accelerated transit from excess thyroid hormone

options.label: B
options.html: Failure of pancreatic lipase to digest dietary fat

options.label: C
options.html: Mucosal inflammation with exudation of blood and protein

options.label: D
options.html: Toxin-mediated activation of intestinal chloride secretion

options.label: E
options.html: Unabsorbed carbohydrate retaining water in the lumen

items.explanationHtml:
The stool osmotic gap is 290 minus 2 x (25 + 30) = 180 mOsm/kg, well above about 125, indicating an osmotic diarrhoea. Diarrhoea that stops with fasting and follows dairy fits lactase deficiency.

Unabsorbed lactose holds water in the lumen; colonic bacteria ferment it to short-chain acids and hydrogen gas, lowering stool pH and causing bloating.

Takeaway: A high stool osmotic gap that resolves with fasting means osmotic diarrhoea, such as lactase deficiency.

whyNot.A: Hyperthyroid motility diarrhoea is not food-specific and does not produce a high osmotic gap.
whyNot.B: Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhoea after fatty meals generally, not symptoms tied to milk with acidic stool.
whyNot.C: Inflammatory diarrhoea causes blood, fever and faecal leukocytes, none of which are described.
whyNot.D: Secretory diarrhoea persists with fasting and has a low osmotic gap; his gap is high and symptoms stop with fasting.

items.objective: Calculate and interpret the stool osmotic gap.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old aid worker develops profuse, painless, watery diarrhoea that looks like rice water and continues overnight while she is fasting. Stool osmotic gap is 20 mOsm/kg. Culture grows a curved, motile gram-negative rod. The toxin produced by this organism causes diarrhoea by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of guanylate cyclase by a heat-stable peptide

options.label: B
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of Gi that prevents inhibition of adenylate cyclase

options.label: C
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of Gs that keeps adenylate cyclase active

options.label: D
options.html: Cleavage of SNARE proteins at nerve terminals

items.explanationHtml:
A curved, motile gram-negative rod causing rice-water stools is Vibrio cholerae. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs alpha subunit, locking adenylate cyclase on. High cAMP opens CFTR chloride channels, and sodium and water follow.

The low osmotic gap and persistence during fasting identify secretory diarrhoea. Glucose-coupled sodium absorption still works, which is why oral rehydration solution saves lives.

Takeaway: Cholera toxin causes secretory diarrhoea by ADP-ribosylating Gs and raising cAMP.

whyNot.A: Heat-stable toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli raises cGMP; this organism is a curved, motile rod producing a cAMP-raising toxin.
whyNot.B: Inactivation of Gi describes pertussis toxin, not the toxin of this enteric pathogen.
whyNot.D: SNARE cleavage describes botulinum and tetanus toxins, which affect neurotransmission, not chloride secretion.
whyNot.E: Ribosome inactivation describes Shiga toxin, which causes bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of a secretory diarrhoea toxin.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has had 8 hours of dull, poorly localised pain around his umbilicus with nausea. He cannot point to one spot. Over the next few hours the pain becomes sharp, localised to the right lower quadrant, and worse when he coughs. The initial periumbilical location of his pain is best explained by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the ilioinguinal nerve by the swollen appendix

options.label: B
options.html: Inflammation of the parietal peritoneum overlying the appendix

options.label: C
options.html: Irritation of the diaphragm referring pain through the phrenic nerve

options.label: D
options.html: Stimulation of the pudendal nerve by pelvic inflammation

options.label: E
options.html: Visceral afferents from the appendix enter the spinal cord at the T10 level

items.explanationHtml:
The appendix is a midgut structure. Its visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres and enter the cord at about T10, the dermatome of the umbilicus, so distension of the inflamed appendix is felt as dull periumbilical pain with nausea.

When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation, pain becomes sharp and localised to the right lower quadrant.

Takeaway: Early appendicitis pain is periumbilical because midgut visceral afferents enter at T10.

whyNot.A: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the groin and is not the source of periumbilical visceral pain.
whyNot.B: Parietal peritoneal irritation produces the later sharp, localised right lower quadrant pain, not the early vague pain.
whyNot.C: Diaphragmatic irritation refers to the shoulder, not the umbilicus.
whyNot.D: The pudendal nerve supplies the perineum and would not cause periumbilical pain.

items.objective: Distinguish visceral from parietal abdominal pain.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had repeated self-induced vomiting for 3 weeks. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg with orthostatic tachycardia. Serum sodium is 134 mEq/L (136-145), potassium 2.8 mEq/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 84 mEq/L (95-105) and bicarbonate 38 mEq/L (22-28). Her urine pH is 5.5. Which of the following best explains why her kidneys continue to reabsorb bicarbonate despite alkalaemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased chloride delivery to the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretions in the vomitus

options.label: C
options.html: Primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma

options.label: E
options.html: Volume contraction stimulating proximal bicarbonate reabsorption and aldosterone release

items.explanationHtml:
Vomiting removes HCl, generating a metabolic alkalosis. It is maintained by volume and chloride depletion: angiotensin II and low volume increase proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, and aldosterone drives distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions.

The result is hypokalaemia and paradoxically acidic urine. Restoring volume with saline and potassium allows bicarbonate excretion.

Takeaway: Vomiting alkalosis is maintained by volume contraction, chloride depletion and aldosterone.

whyNot.A: Chloride delivery is reduced in vomiting; low chloride limits bicarbonate secretion by the collecting duct.
whyNot.B: Losing bicarbonate would cause acidosis, and gastric vomitus contains mainly HCl.
whyNot.C: Primary aldosteronism causes hypertension and volume expansion, whereas she is hypotensive and orthostatic.
whyNot.D: The primary disorder is metabolic; compensation would be hypoventilation, not hyperventilation.

items.objective: Explain the maintenance of metabolic alkalosis after vomiting.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had crampy lower abdominal pain about twice weekly for 8 months, relieved by defecation and associated with loose, more frequent stools. She has no rectal bleeding, weight loss or nocturnal symptoms, and no family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Examination is normal. A complete blood count is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

options.label: E
options.html: Tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA level

items.explanationHtml:
Her symptoms meet Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea, and she has no alarm features. A positive diagnosis is encouraged, with limited testing: celiac serology (tTG IgA plus total IgA to detect IgA deficiency) and faecal calprotectin or CRP to exclude inflammatory bowel disease.

Celiac disease can mimic IBS with diarrhoea and is treatable.

Takeaway: Suspected IBS with diarrhoea needs celiac serology, not routine colonoscopy or CT.

whyNot.A: Colonoscopy is not routinely needed in a young patient with typical IBS and no alarm features.
whyNot.B: CT exposes her to radiation without benefit when there are no alarm features or signs on examination.
whyNot.C: Breath testing for bacterial overgrowth is not part of the standard initial evaluation of IBS with diarrhoea.
whyNot.D: Routine parasite testing is not recommended in suspected IBS unless travel or exposure history suggests it.

items.objective: Order appropriate testing for suspected IBS.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has had epigastric discomfort and fullness after meals for 2 months, with a 4-kg unintentional weight loss. He takes no NSAIDs. Hemoglobin is 13.9 g/dL (13.5-17.5). Examination shows mild epigastric tenderness without a mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Eight-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor

options.label: E
options.html: Urea breath test, then treat if positive

items.explanationHtml:
Dyspepsia in a patient aged 60 or older should be evaluated with upper endoscopy to exclude gastric or esophageal cancer, peptic ulcer and other structural disease; his weight loss adds urgency.

Younger patients without concerning features are managed with H. pylori test-and-treat, then PPI therapy.

Takeaway: New dyspepsia at age 60 or older, especially with weight loss, needs upper endoscopy.

whyNot.A: An empiric PPI trial may mask a gastric cancer in an older patient with weight loss.
whyNot.B: Gastric emptying studies evaluate gastroparesis after structural disease is excluded.
whyNot.D: Barium studies are less sensitive than endoscopy and do not allow biopsy.
whyNot.E: Test-and-treat suits dyspepsia in patients under 60; his age and weight loss call for direct visualisation.

items.objective: Choose the evaluation of dyspepsia by age and alarm features.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis who has taken naproxen daily for 2 months comes to the emergency department after passing three black, tarry stools. He feels light-headed. Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL (13.5-17.5), urea nitrogen 54 mg/dL (7-18) and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.6-1.2). Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?
items.explanationHtml:
