Melena and a BUN that is high relative to creatinine (blood proteins digested and absorbed in the small intestine, plus volume depletion) point to bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Daily NSAID use makes peptic ulcer, especially duodenal, the most likely source.

NSAIDs inhibit COX-1-dependent prostaglandins that maintain mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow.

Takeaway: Melena with a disproportionately raised BUN in an NSAID user suggests a bleeding peptic ulcer.

whyNot.A: Colonic angiodysplasia usually causes intermittent hematochezia or occult loss, not melena with a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio.
whyNot.B: Diverticular bleeding causes painless hematochezia and would not raise BUN disproportionately.
whyNot.D: Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper or stool surface, not melena or haemodynamic compromise.
whyNot.E: Left-sided colon cancer causes hematochezia or change in bowel habit rather than melena.

items.objective: Localise GI bleeding using clinical and laboratory clues.

items.stemHtml: The patient receives two large-bore intravenous lines and crystalloid, and his pulse falls to 94/min. Naproxen is stopped. A repeat hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL. He has no history of coronary artery disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous proton pump inhibitor and upper endoscopy within 24 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Transfusion of red cells to a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
After resuscitation, suspected upper GI bleeding is managed with an intravenous PPI and upper endoscopy within 24 hours, which both diagnoses and treats (for example, clips or thermal therapy for a visible vessel).

A restrictive transfusion strategy is used. After the event, NSAIDs are avoided and H. pylori is tested and treated.

Takeaway: Resuscitate, give an IV PPI and perform upper endoscopy within 24 hours for upper GI bleeding.

whyNot.A: The clinical picture points to an upper source, so upper endoscopy comes first.
whyNot.B: Surgery is reserved for bleeding that fails endoscopic and angiographic therapy.
whyNot.D: Nuclear scintigraphy is used for obscure lower bleeding, not as first evaluation of a likely upper source.
whyNot.E: Restrictive transfusion (threshold 7 g/dL without cardiac disease) improves outcomes; he is above that threshold.

items.objective: Manage suspected upper GI bleeding after resuscitation.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man with a history of peptic ulcer disease has vomited after every meal for 10 days and has lost 5 kg. A succussion splash is heard over the epigastrium. Blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg and pulse 108/min, with dry mucous membranes. Laboratory results are shown.

TestResultReference range
Sodium133 mEq/L136-145 mEq/L
Potassium2.9 mEq/L3.5-5.0 mEq/L
Chloride82 mEq/L95-105 mEq/L
Bicarbonate37 mEq/L22-28 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen34 mg/dL7-18 mg/dL
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL0.6-1.2 mg/dL
Magnesium1.7 mEq/L1.5-2.0 mEq/L

A nasogastric tube is placed. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous fluid?

options.label: A
options.html: 0.9% sodium chloride with added potassium chloride

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous acetazolamide in place of fluid

items.explanationHtml:
Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic ulcer scarring causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with volume depletion. It is chloride-responsive: isotonic saline restores volume and chloride, and potassium chloride corrects hypokalaemia, letting the kidney excrete the excess bicarbonate.

After stabilisation, upper endoscopy identifies the cause of obstruction (ulcer or malignancy).

Takeaway: Vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis is treated with normal saline plus potassium chloride.

whyNot.B: Free water does not restore extracellular volume or chloride and can worsen hyponatraemia.
whyNot.C: Acetazolamide is for alkalosis with volume overload; he is volume depleted and hypokalaemic.
whyNot.D: Bicarbonate would worsen an existing metabolic alkalosis.
whyNot.E: Lactate is metabolised to bicarbonate, which adds alkali, and its 4 mEq/L of potassium cannot correct his marked potassium deficit.

items.objective: Correct fluid and electrolyte losses from prolonged vomiting.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer to bone takes long-acting oxycodone for pain, which is well controlled. She has had hard stools every 4 to 5 days for 6 weeks despite daily senna and polyethylene glycol at full doses. She has no abdominal pain, vomiting or distension, and an abdominal radiograph shows stool in the colon without obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Add oral naloxone at analgesic-reversing doses

items.explanationHtml:
Opioid-induced constipation that persists despite stimulant and osmotic laxatives is treated with a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist such as naloxegol, methylnaltrexone or naldemedine. These block gut mu receptors but do not cross the blood-brain barrier, so analgesia is preserved.

They are contraindicated when mechanical bowel obstruction is present, which the radiograph has excluded.

Takeaway: Refractory opioid-induced constipation is treated with a peripherally acting mu-opioid antagonist.

whyNot.A: Loperamide is an antidiarrhoeal opioid agonist and would worsen constipation.
whyNot.C: Giving an opioid antagonist that reaches the brain risks reversing analgesia and causing withdrawal.
whyNot.D: Docusate alone is weak and no better than her current regimen.
whyNot.E: Stopping an effective opioid would leave bone pain uncontrolled; constipation can be treated directly.

items.objective: Manage opioid-induced constipation in a patient with cancer pain.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy has had vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 2 days; two children at his day care have similar symptoms. He has fewer wet diapers. He is alert and drinking eagerly. Pulse is 128/min. His mucous membranes are dry and capillary refill is 3 seconds. Estimated dehydration is moderate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent volumes

items.explanationHtml:
Mild to moderate dehydration from acute gastroenteritis in children is treated with oral rehydration solution, given in small, frequent amounts (for example by spoon or syringe) to limit vomiting. Its balanced glucose and sodium use the intact SGLT1 co-transporter to drive water absorption.

A single dose of ondansetron may help a vomiting child tolerate oral fluids. Normal diet should resume once he is rehydrated.

Takeaway: Oral rehydration solution is first line for mild to moderate paediatric dehydration.

whyNot.A: Sports drinks are low in sodium and high in sugar compared with oral rehydration solution.
whyNot.B: Juice has too little sodium and too much sugar to replace losses, though diluted juice can be used in mild dehydration.
whyNot.C: IV fluids are for severe dehydration, shock or failure of oral rehydration; this alert child is drinking.
whyNot.D: Antimotility drugs are not recommended in young children with acute gastroenteritis because of adverse effects.

items.objective: Manage dehydration from acute gastroenteritis in a child.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man with Parkinson disease treated with carbidopa-levodopa has nausea and two episodes of vomiting on the first day after an elective hip replacement. His QTc on a preoperative ECG was 420 ms, and electrolytes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate antiemetic?
items.explanationHtml:
Patients with Parkinson disease should avoid centrally acting dopamine antagonists, which block the effects of levodopa and worsen rigidity and bradykinesia. A 5-HT3 antagonist such as ondansetron is the preferred antiemetic; his normal QTc and electrolytes make it safe.

Anticholinergic and sedating drugs also raise the risk of delirium in older adults after surgery.

Takeaway: In Parkinson disease use ondansetron and avoid dopamine-antagonist antiemetics.

whyNot.A: Haloperidol is a potent D2 antagonist and should be avoided in Parkinson disease.
whyNot.B: Metoclopramide blocks central D2 receptors and can acutely worsen parkinsonism.
whyNot.D: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine D2 antagonist that worsens parkinsonian symptoms.
whyNot.E: Promethazine has D2-blocking and strong anticholinergic and sedative effects that raise the risk of delirium in an older postoperative patient.

items.objective: Select an antiemetic for a patient with Parkinson disease.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to a clinic for his first medical visit in several years. He has a history of injection drug use. Examination shows painless, white, vertically ridged plaques along both lateral borders of the tongue. The plaques cannot be removed with a tongue blade. A biopsy shows hyperkeratosis and ballooned, pale epithelial cells in the upper layers of the epithelium; a PAS stain shows no fungal forms. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
Fixed, corrugated white plaques on the lateral tongue in an immunosuppressed person are oral hairy leukoplakia, caused by productive Epstein-Barr virus replication in the epithelium. It does not scrape off, which separates it from candidiasis, and it is not premalignant. Its presence should prompt HIV testing.

Takeaway: Oral hairy leukoplakia is an EBV lesion of the lateral tongue that signals immunosuppression and is not a precancer.

whyNot.A: Candidiasis forms creamy plaques that wipe off, and PAS staining would show yeast and pseudohyphae.
whyNot.B: CMV causes ulcers in the mouth or esophagus with large cells containing nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions, not hyperkeratotic white plaques.
whyNot.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which appears as violaceous patches or nodules, often on the palate.
whyNot.E: HPV-16 drives oropharyngeal squamous carcinoma of the tonsil and tongue base, not benign bilateral ridged plaques on the lateral tongue.

items.objective: Identify the organism responsible for oral hairy leukoplakia from its clinical and histologic features.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging, painless, mobile mass in front of her left ear that has grown over 3 years. Facial movements are normal. The mass is shelled out through a small incision. Microscopy shows ducts lined by epithelial cells and sheets of spindle-shaped myoepithelial cells set in a myxoid, cartilage-like stroma. Two years later a nodule appears at the same site. Which of the following best explains the recurrence?

options.label: A
options.html: Lymphatic spread to intraparotid lymph nodes

options.label: B
options.html: Malignant change in a dense lymphoid stroma

options.label: C
options.html: New primary tumors from a germline mutation

options.label: D
options.html: Perineural spread along the facial nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Tumor projections through an incomplete capsule

items.explanationHtml:
The biphasic epithelial and myoepithelial tumor in a chondromyxoid stroma is a pleomorphic adenoma, the most common salivary gland tumor. Its capsule is incomplete and the tumor sends finger-like extensions into surrounding gland. Enucleation leaves these behind, so the tumor recurs. It is removed with a cuff of normal tissue, usually by parotidectomy with preservation of the facial nerve.

Takeaway: Pleomorphic adenoma recurs after enucleation because of tumor extensions beyond its incomplete capsule.

whyNot.A: This tumor is benign and does not metastasize to nodes; recurrence comes from tumor left behind at the margin.
whyNot.B: Lymphoid stroma is a feature of Warthin tumor, which does not have myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid matrix.
whyNot.C: A single slow-growing tumor recurring in the operative bed is explained by residual tumor, not by an inherited predisposition.
whyNot.D: Perineural invasion is the hallmark of adenoid cystic carcinoma, which has a cribriform pattern rather than a chondromyxoid stroma.

items.objective: Explain why pleomorphic adenoma recurs after simple enucleation.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history notices painless swelling at the angle of the jaw on both sides. Ultrasonography shows a well-circumscribed, partly cystic mass in the tail of each parotid gland. Fine-needle aspiration of one mass yields brown fluid with sheets of granular eosinophilic epithelial cells and many mature lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral, cystic masses in the parotid tail of an older smoker with oncocytic epithelial cells and lymphocytes on aspiration are typical of Warthin tumor. It is benign, occurs only in the parotid, and is the salivary tumor most likely to be bilateral or multifocal.

Takeaway: Warthin tumor: older smoker, parotid tail, often bilateral, oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid stroma.

whyNot.A: Adenoid cystic carcinoma has a cribriform pattern with perineural invasion and is not linked to smoking or bilateral cystic masses.
whyNot.B: MALT lymphoma usually arises in Sjogren syndrome and shows monotonous atypical B cells rather than oncocytic epithelium with mature lymphocytes.
whyNot.C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma contains mucin-secreting and squamoid cells and is rarely bilateral.
whyNot.D: Pleomorphic adenoma is usually solitary and shows epithelial and myoepithelial cells in chondromyxoid stroma rather than oncocytes and lymphocytes.

items.objective: Recognize Warthin tumor from its epidemiology and cytology.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old woman with urge urinary incontinence began taking oxybutynin 2 months ago. She now has a persistently dry mouth, difficulty swallowing crackers, and two new cavities at the gum line found by her dentist. Blockade of which of the following receptors on salivary acinar cells most directly explains her mouth symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Watery saliva is driven by parasympathetic acetylcholine acting on M3 receptors (Gq, IP3, raised calcium) on acinar cells. Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic, so it reduces salivary flow. Loss of saliva removes buffering and antimicrobial protection, causing root caries and candidiasis. In older adults, anticholinergic drugs are a leading, reversible cause of dry mouth.

Takeaway: Antimuscarinic drugs cause dry mouth by blocking M3 receptors on salivary acinar cells.

whyNot.A: Alpha<sub>1</sub> blockade causes orthostatic hypotension and nasal congestion; it does not cause marked loss of saliva.
whyNot.B: Sympathetic beta input adds only a small volume of protein-rich saliva, so beta blockade does not dry the mouth.
whyNot.C: D<sub>2</sub> antagonists such as antipsychotics dry the mouth through their separate antimuscarinic activity, not through D<sub>2</sub> blockade at the gland.
whyNot.E: N<sub>N</sub> receptors sit on autonomic ganglion cells, not on acinar cells, and oxybutynin does not block them.

items.objective: Relate drug-induced xerostomia to muscarinic M3 blockade.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man who grew up in Turkey has had painful oral ulcers several times a year since adolescence. Over the past year he has had two painful scrotal ulcers that healed with scars and one episode of a painful red eye with blurred vision. A sterile pustule appeared at a venipuncture site 2 days after blood was drawn. Which of the following is most strongly associated with this condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent oral ulcers with genital ulcers, uveitis and a positive pathergy reaction define Behcet disease, a variable-vessel vasculitis most common along the Silk Road. Its strongest genetic association is HLA-B51.

Takeaway: Behcet disease: recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and pathergy, associated with HLA-B51.

whyNot.A: HLA-B27 is linked to spondyloarthritis and acute anterior uveitis, but not to recurrent orogenital ulcers and pathergy.
whyNot.C: HLA-DQ2 is the main celiac disease allele; celiac disease can cause aphthous ulcers but not genital ulcers, uveitis or pathergy.
whyNot.D: HLA-DR3 is associated with type 1 diabetes, celiac disease and Graves disease, not with this vasculitis.
whyNot.E: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.

items.objective: Associate Behcet disease with its HLA type and clinical triad.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl from a rural area is brought for a well-child visit. Her family drinks well water that is low in fluoride, and she sips sweetened juice throughout the day. Examination shows chalky white spots and two brown cavities on her upper front teeth. Her physician applies fluoride varnish and prescribes oral fluoride supplements. Which of the following is the main mechanism by which fluoride protects her teeth?

options.label: A
options.html: Buffering lactic acid in saliva at the tooth surface

options.label: B
options.html: Forming fluorapatite crystals that resist acid dissolution

options.label: C
options.html: Increasing salivary flow through muscarinic stimulation

options.label: D
options.html: Killing Streptococcus mutans by disrupting its cell wall

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulating ameloblasts to lay down new enamel

items.explanationHtml:
Acid from bacterial fermentation of sugar dissolves enamel hydroxyapatite. Fluoride replaces hydroxyl groups to form fluorapatite, which is less soluble in acid, and it promotes remineralization of early white-spot lesions. Reducing frequent sugar exposure and applying fluoride varnish are the main preventive measures in young children.

Takeaway: Fluoride prevents caries mainly by forming acid-resistant fluorapatite and aiding remineralization.

whyNot.A: Salivary bicarbonate, not fluoride, is the main buffer; fluoride acts by changing the enamel crystal.
whyNot.C: That is the action of pilocarpine and cevimeline, not fluoride.
whyNot.D: Fluoride is not a bactericidal cell-wall agent; its main benefit is on the mineral of enamel.
whyNot.E: Ameloblasts are lost once a tooth erupts, so enamel cannot be regenerated by cells.

items.objective: Describe how fluoride prevents dental caries.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has had dry eyes and a dry mouth for 8 years. Serum anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are positive. Over the past 4 months her right parotid gland has become persistently, firmly enlarged. It is nontender, and she has had no fever or pain with meals. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the new parotid enlargement?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic antigen-driven B-cell activation in Sjogren syndrome raises the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, most often extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma arising in the salivary glands. A persistent, unilateral, firm parotid enlargement in a patient with long-standing disease should prompt biopsy.

Takeaway: New persistent parotid enlargement in Sjogren syndrome suggests MALT lymphoma.

whyNot.A: Bacterial parotitis is painful, warm and tender with fever and pus at the duct, none of which is present.
whyNot.C: A benign mixed tumor is possible in anyone, but it is not the specific, expected complication of long-standing Sjogren syndrome.
whyNot.D: Sarcoid parotitis is usually bilateral with lung, eye or skin disease and does not explain this antibody profile.
whyNot.E: Stones cause intermittent swelling and pain with meals and favor the submandibular gland.

items.objective: Recognize the lymphoma risk in Sjogren syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man who has never smoked and drinks rarely has a painless, enlarging lump in the left upper neck. Examination shows a firm 3-cm level II lymph node and an indurated left palatine tonsil. Biopsy of the tonsil shows nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma with strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic immunostaining for p16. Which of the following viral actions most directly explains the p16 staining?

options.label: A
options.html: E6 protein promoting degradation of p53

options.label: B
options.html: E7 protein binding and inactivating retinoblastoma protein

options.label: C
options.html: LANA protein binding and inhibiting p53

options.label: D
options.html: LMP1 protein mimicking an activated CD40 receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Tax protein activating host gene transcription

items.explanationHtml:
High-risk HPV (mainly type 16) drives oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsils and base of tongue, often in younger nonsmokers. E7 binds Rb and releases E2F, pushing cells into S phase. Functional Rb normally represses p16 expression, so loss of Rb leads to marked p16 overexpression, which is used as a surrogate marker of HPV-driven tumors. These tumors respond better to treatment than tobacco-related carcinomas.

Takeaway: p16 overexpression marks HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer because E7 inactivates Rb.

whyNot.A: E6-mediated p53 loss is part of HPV oncogenesis, but p16 overexpression results from loss of Rb function, not p53.
whyNot.C: LANA is an HHV-8 latency protein in Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma.
whyNot.D: LMP1 is an Epstein-Barr virus protein linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not HPV-related tonsil cancer.
whyNot.E: Tax is the HTLV-1 transactivator implicated in adult T-cell leukemia.

items.objective: Explain the molecular basis of p16 positivity in HPV-related oropharyngeal carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is referred by his dentist for a red patch in his mouth that was first noted 4 weeks ago and is unchanged since. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years and drinks 4 to 5 beers daily. Examination shows a 1.5-cm flat, velvety, bright red patch on the floor of the mouth. It is painless and cannot be wiped off. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Clotrimazole troches and reexamination in 2 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: PET-CT of the head and neck

items.explanationHtml:
A persistent, unexplained red patch is erythroplakia, the oral lesion with the highest likelihood of dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. The floor of the mouth is a high-risk site and he has heavy tobacco and alcohol exposure. The next step is biopsy, followed by staging if carcinoma is confirmed, and counselling to stop smoking and drinking.

Takeaway: Persistent erythroplakia needs biopsy; it carries the highest malignant potential of oral lesions.

whyNot.B: Erythematous candidiasis is less likely in a fixed lesion at a high-risk site, and delaying tissue diagnosis of possible carcinoma is not appropriate.
whyNot.C: Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis; it does not replace biopsy.
whyNot.D: Watchful waiting is unsafe for erythroplakia, which most often shows dysplasia or carcinoma.
whyNot.E: Topical corticosteroids treat aphthous ulcers and lichen planus; they could mask, not exclude, a malignancy.

items.objective: Choose biopsy as the next step for a persistent red oral lesion in a high-risk patient.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of worsening pain and swelling under his jaw. He has had a painful lower left molar for 2 weeks. He is sitting upright, leaning forward, and drooling, and his voice is muffled. Temperature is 39.2 C (102.6 F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. There is firm, tender, symmetric swelling of the submandibular and submental regions without fluctuance, and the floor of the mouth is raised, pushing the tongue upward and backward. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Extract the infected molar in the emergency department

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain contrast-enhanced CT of the neck

options.label: C
options.html: Perform needle aspiration of the submandibular space

options.label: D
options.html: Secure the airway with awake fiberoptic intubation

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces after a lower molar infection is Ludwig angina. Drooling, a muffled voice, an upright posture and tachypnea are signs of a threatened airway. The first priority is a controlled airway, usually awake fiberoptic intubation in the operating room with a surgical airway ready, avoiding sedation and the supine position.

Takeaway: In Ludwig angina with airway signs, secure the airway before imaging or anything else.

whyNot.A: Treating the dental source comes later; the immediate threat is to the airway.
whyNot.B: CT is useful once the airway is safe, but lying flat in the scanner can precipitate complete obstruction in a patient already drooling with a muffled voice.
whyNot.C: There is no fluctuant collection, and aspiration does nothing for the threatened airway.
whyNot.E: This is a rapidly spreading deep neck infection with airway compromise that needs admission and IV therapy.

items.objective: Prioritize airway management in Ludwig angina.

items.stemHtml: The patient's airway is secured by awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation in the operating room. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck then shows diffuse cellulitis of the bilateral submandibular and sublingual spaces with no drainable abscess. He has no drug allergies and no other medical conditions. Which of the following is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of oral streptococci and anaerobes from a dental source. Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam covers both and is a standard first choice in an immunocompetent patient. Broader coverage is used in immunocompromised patients, and clindamycin is an option with severe penicillin allergy. Drainage is added if an abscess forms, and the dental source is treated.

Takeaway: Treat Ludwig angina with IV antibiotics covering oral streptococci and anaerobes, such as ampicillin-sulbactam.

whyNot.B: This is a bacterial infection of dental origin; antifungal therapy has no role.
whyNot.C: Aminoglycosides have no anaerobic activity and poor streptococcal activity when used alone.
whyNot.D: Vancomycin covers streptococci and staphylococci but misses the oral anaerobes that are central to this mixed infection.
whyNot.E: Metronidazole covers anaerobes but not oral streptococci, and oral therapy is inadequate for a life-threatening infection.

items.objective: Select empiric antibiotic therapy for Ludwig angina.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old woman is evaluated on postoperative day 4 after repair of a hip fracture because of painful swelling of her right cheek. Oral intake has been poor since surgery. Examination shows a dry mouth and a warm, firm, tender right parotid gland; massage of the gland expresses pus from the duct opening on the buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar. Facial movements are normal. Findings are shown.

MeasureResult
Temperature38.6 C (101.5 F)
Pulse104/min
Blood pressure108/64 mm Hg
Sodium151 mEq/L (136-145)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)38 mg/dL (7-18)
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (0.6-1.2)
Leukocytes15,800/mm3 (4,500-11,000)
Current medicationsOxycodone, diphenhydramine at bedtime, enoxaparin

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Fine-needle aspiration of the gland for cytology

options.label: C
options.html: IV fluids, sialogogues and IV antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus

options.label: D
options.html: Oral acyclovir, warm compresses and analgesia

items.explanationHtml:
Acute suppurative parotitis develops when salivary flow falls, as in older postoperative patients who are dehydrated (high sodium and BUN-to-creatinine ratio) and taking drying drugs such as diphenhydramine and opioids. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism. Treatment is rehydration, sialogogues, gland massage, warm compresses, and IV antibiotics that cover S. aureus (with MRSA coverage if risk factors) and oral anaerobes. Stop the diphenhydramine. Image for abscess if there is no improvement.

Takeaway: Suppurative parotitis in a dehydrated older patient: rehydrate, stimulate saliva, and give IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

whyNot.A: This acute, febrile, purulent process is infection rather than a tumor; cytology adds nothing now.
whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids do not treat bacterial infection and would worsen it.
whyNot.D: This is a bacterial infection with pus at the duct, not a viral sialadenitis.
whyNot.E: Surgery is not indicated for uncomplicated suppurative parotitis; drainage is reserved for an abscess that fails to respond.

items.objective: Manage acute bacterial parotitis and recognize its predisposing factors.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma began using a fluticasone-salmeterol dry-powder inhaler twice daily 3 months ago, and her asthma is now well controlled. She has had a sore mouth for 1 week. Examination shows creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa and soft palate that wipe off with gauze, leaving a red base. She has no difficulty or pain with swallowing, and an HIV test 6 months ago was negative. In addition to clotrimazole troches, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each inhaler dose

options.label: D
options.html: Take oral fluconazole once weekly indefinitely

options.label: E
options.html: Use a chlorhexidine mouthwash before each dose

items.explanationHtml:
Pseudomembranous candidiasis is a common local adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids, which deposit in the oropharynx. Mild disease responds to topical antifungals. Rinsing and spitting after each dose removes residual drug and prevents recurrence; with metered-dose inhalers, a spacer also reduces oropharyngeal deposition.

Takeaway: Prevent inhaled-corticosteroid thrush by rinsing and spitting after each dose (and a spacer for metered-dose inhalers).

whyNot.B: Her asthma needs controller therapy; thrush is prevented and treated without abandoning inhaled corticosteroids.
whyNot.C: Systemic corticosteroids have far more adverse effects and also raise the risk of candidiasis.
whyNot.D: Long-term antifungal suppression is not needed for a preventable, mild, local infection in an immunocompetent patient.
whyNot.E: Rinsing before the dose does not remove the corticosteroid deposited in the mouth by the inhaler.

items.objective: Prevent oral candidiasis in patients using inhaled corticosteroids.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had a painless lump on the right side of his neck for 6 weeks. He has never used tobacco and drinks alcohol rarely. A 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate prescribed at an urgent care center left it unchanged. He has no fever, sore throat or weight loss. Examination shows a 3-cm, firm, nontender, mobile mass deep to the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle at the level of the hyoid bone. The oral cavity appears normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck shows a 3-cm cystic level II lymph node. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Open excisional biopsy of the mass

items.explanationHtml:
An adult with a persistent lateral neck mass, particularly a cystic level II node, must be evaluated for cancer. HPV-related oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma commonly presents this way in nonsmokers in middle age. After imaging, fine-needle aspiration is the preferred diagnostic step, with p16 or HPV testing of the sample, together with examination of the pharynx by flexible laryngoscopy.

Takeaway: Persistent adult neck mass: imaging and FNA, not more antibiotics or open biopsy first; think HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer.

whyNot.A: A persistent neck mass that did not respond to antibiotics should not be treated with more antibiotics; that delays a cancer diagnosis.
whyNot.C: Open biopsy is not the first step because it can spill tumor and complicate definitive treatment; FNA is preferred.
whyNot.D: A neck mass persisting for weeks in an adult is presumed malignant until proven otherwise and needs tissue now.
whyNot.E: EBV serology does not diagnose a cystic metastasis and would delay tissue diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose fine-needle aspiration for a persistent cystic neck mass in an adult.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food at night, and a 5-kg weight loss. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus with an air-fluid level that tapers smoothly to a narrow point at the gastroesophageal junction. Which of the following best explains her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: A thin fibrous mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction

options.label: B
options.html: Dense eosinophilic infiltration of the squamous epithelium

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus of the distal esophagus

options.label: D
options.html: Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the distal esophageal wall

options.label: E
options.html: Uncoordinated premature contractions with normal sphincter relaxation

items.explanationHtml:
Dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation and a bird-beak taper indicate achalasia. Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons that release nitric oxide and VIP leaves the LES unable to relax with swallowing and abolishes peristalsis, so the esophagus dilates above the sphincter.

Takeaway: Achalasia is caused by loss of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus.

whyNot.A: A Schatzki ring causes intermittent dysphagia to solids only, not progressive dysphagia to liquids with a dilated esophagus.
whyNot.B: Eosinophilic esophagitis causes solid-food dysphagia and impaction with rings and furrows, not achalasia physiology.
whyNot.D: This is the lesion of systemic sclerosis, which lowers LES pressure and causes reflux rather than a tight, nonrelaxing sphincter.
whyNot.E: This describes distal esophageal spasm, which causes intermittent chest pain and dysphagia without a dilated esophagus and bird-beak.

items.objective: Explain the neural basis of achalasia.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man who grew up in a rural adobe home in Bolivia and moved to the United States 20 years ago has progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids. An ECG shows right bundle branch block, and echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an apical aneurysm. Esophageal manometry shows absent peristalsis and incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following was the most likely route by which he acquired the causative organism?

options.label: D
options.html: Feces of a triatomine bug contaminating a bite wound

items.explanationHtml:
Achalasia physiology with a dilated cardiomyopathy and apical aneurysm in someone raised in rural Latin America indicates chronic Chagas disease. Trypanosoma cruzi is shed in the feces of triatomine (reduviid, kissing) bugs, which enter the bite wound or mucosa. The parasite destroys myenteric ganglia, causing megaesophagus and megacolon decades later. Congenital and transfusion transmission also occur.

Takeaway: Chagas disease (T. cruzi, triatomine bug feces) causes secondary achalasia, megacolon and cardiomyopathy.

whyNot.A: Sandflies transmit Leishmania, which causes cutaneous or visceral leishmaniasis.
whyNot.B: Tsetse flies transmit Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African sleeping sickness, not cardiomyopathy and megaesophagus.
whyNot.C: Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria, which does not destroy enteric ganglia.
whyNot.E: Undercooked pork transmits Taenia solium and Trichinella, which do not cause this syndrome.

items.objective: Identify the transmission route of Trypanosoma cruzi in Chagas-related achalasia.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman with Raynaud phenomenon, thickened tight skin over her fingers, and telangiectasias on her face has worsening heartburn and dysphagia to solid food. Which of the following manometric findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Incomplete LES relaxation with absent peristalsis

options.label: B
options.html: Low LES resting pressure with weak or absent distal peristalsis

options.label: C
options.html: Normal LES pressure with normal peristalsis

options.label: D
options.html: Premature contractions with normal LES relaxation

options.label: E
options.html: Very high-amplitude distal contractions with normal LES relaxation

items.explanationHtml:
Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly and telangiectasias indicate systemic sclerosis. Atrophy and fibrosis of smooth muscle in the lower two-thirds of the esophagus weaken peristalsis and lower LES pressure, so acid refluxes freely and clears poorly, leading to esophagitis, strictures and Barrett esophagus.

Takeaway: Scleroderma esophagus: hypotensive LES and absent distal peristalsis, causing severe reflux.

whyNot.A: This is achalasia, in which a nonrelaxing sphincter causes obstruction rather than severe reflux.
whyNot.C: Systemic sclerosis characteristically damages the distal smooth muscle, so manometry is abnormal.
whyNot.D: This is distal esophageal spasm, which is unrelated to systemic sclerosis.
whyNot.E: This is hypercontractile (jackhammer) esophagus, a primary motility disorder.

items.objective: Predict manometric findings in systemic sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with 15 years of heartburn undergoes upper endoscopy, which shows salmon-colored mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. Which of the following is most likely seen on biopsy of this area?

options.label: B
options.html: Keratinizing squamous cells forming keratin pearls

options.label: C
options.html: Squamous cells with Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions

options.label: D
options.html: Squamous epithelium with dense intraepithelial eosinophils

options.label: E
options.html: Stratified squamous epithelium with basal cell hyperplasia

items.explanationHtml:
Salmon-colored mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction in a patient with chronic reflux is Barrett esophagus. The diagnostic histology is intestinal metaplasia: columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing the normal squamous lining. It is a precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Takeaway: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia (columnar cells with goblet cells) of the distal esophagus.

whyNot.B: Keratin pearls indicate squamous cell carcinoma, which typically arises in the upper and middle esophagus.
whyNot.C: These are features of herpes simplex esophagitis, which presents with painful punched-out ulcers.
whyNot.D: This is eosinophilic esophagitis, which shows rings and furrows rather than salmon-colored mucosa.
whyNot.E: This is reflux esophagitis without metaplasia; it would look like inflamed pale squamous mucosa, not salmon-colored tongues.

items.objective: Identify the histology of Barrett esophagus.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone has had 5 days of severe pain with swallowing. Endoscopy shows several small, sharply punched-out ulcers with raised edges in the mid-esophagus and no plaques. Biopsy from the edge of an ulcer shows multinucleated squamous cells with molded, ground-glass nuclei and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Small, punched-out ulcers with multinucleated squamous cells, nuclear molding and Cowdry A inclusions at the ulcer edge are the features of HSV esophagitis. HSV infects squamous epithelium, so the edge is the best place to biopsy; CMV infects endothelial and stromal cells, so the base is sampled for CMV. HSV is treated with acyclovir.

Takeaway: HSV esophagitis: small punched-out ulcers, multinucleated squamous cells with Cowdry A inclusions at the ulcer edge.

whyNot.A: Candida causes white plaques with yeast and pseudohyphae, not punched-out ulcers with viral inclusions.
whyNot.B: CMV causes large, shallow, linear ulcers, and its inclusions are in endothelial and stromal cells at the ulcer base, with cytoplasmic as well as nuclear inclusions.
whyNot.D: HPV causes squamous papillomas, not painful ulcers in immunosuppressed patients.
whyNot.E: Esophageal tuberculosis is rare and shows caseating granulomas rather than multinucleated cells with viral inclusions.

items.objective: Distinguish HSV from CMV and Candida esophagitis by endoscopy and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man has had 1 year of bad breath, gurgling in his throat when he swallows, and regurgitation of food he ate the day before. He has had two episodes of pneumonia. A barium swallow shows a contrast-filled pouch projecting posteriorly from the junction of the pharynx and esophagus. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Full-thickness outpouching of the mid-esophagus pulled by scarred nodes

options.label: B
options.html: Herniation of the gastric fundus through the esophageal hiatus

options.label: C
options.html: Mucosal herniation between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal fibers

options.label: D
options.html: Mucosal herniation just above the lower esophageal sphincter

options.label: E
options.html: Persistent remnant of the thyroglossal duct at the tongue base

items.explanationHtml:
Halitosis, gurgling and regurgitation of old food in an older adult with a posterior pouch at the pharyngoesophageal junction is Zenker diverticulum. It is a false (pulsion) diverticulum: mucosa and submucosa herniate through Killian triangle, between the oblique thyropharyngeal and horizontal cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor, driven by high pressure above a poorly relaxing cricopharyngeus.

Takeaway: Zenker diverticulum is a false pulsion diverticulum through Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus.

whyNot.A: This is a traction diverticulum, a true diverticulum of the mid-esophagus, usually asymptomatic.
whyNot.B: A paraesophageal hernia lies at the diaphragm and does not cause a posterior pouch at the pharyngoesophageal junction.
whyNot.D: This is an epiphrenic diverticulum, which sits in the distal esophagus and is linked to motility disorders.
whyNot.E: Thyroglossal duct cysts are anterior midline neck masses that move with swallowing, not posterior pharyngeal pouches.

items.objective: Describe the anatomy and mechanism of Zenker diverticulum.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student is being treated for acne. Three weeks after starting a new medication she develops sharp retrosternal pain with every swallow. She usually takes the pill with a sip of water just before lying down to sleep. Endoscopy shows a single, discrete ulcer in the mid-esophagus with normal surrounding mucosa. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
A discrete mid-esophageal ulcer with normal surrounding mucosa after taking a pill with little water at bedtime is pill esophagitis. Tablets lodge where the aortic arch narrows the esophagus. Doxycycline and other tetracyclines are among the commonest causes, along with bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, iron and NSAIDs. Patients should take them upright with a full glass of water.

Takeaway: Doxycycline taken with little water before lying down is a classic cause of pill esophagitis.

whyNot.A: Oral contraceptives raise thrombosis risk but are not caustic to the esophagus.
whyNot.C: Isotretinoin causes dry lips and skin, teratogenicity and raised lipids, but it is not a typical cause of pill esophagitis.
whyNot.D: Spironolactone causes hyperkalemia and menstrual irregularity, not focal esophageal ulceration.
whyNot.E: Benzoyl peroxide is applied to the skin and does not contact the esophagus.

items.objective: Recognize drugs that cause pill esophagitis.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has 6 months of difficulty swallowing solid food, which she feels sticking high in her throat. Examination shows pale conjunctivae, spoon-shaped nails, cracks at the corners of the mouth, and a smooth, red tongue. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL (12.0-16.0) and MCV is 71 fL (80-100). A barium swallow shows a thin, shelf-like membrane in the postcricoid region. Correction of which of the following deficiencies is most important in her treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Microcytic anemia, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis and an upper esophageal web are Plummer-Vinson syndrome, linked to iron deficiency (here from menorrhagia). Iron replacement corrects the anemia and may improve the dysphagia; dilation treats a persistent web. The syndrome carries an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the hypopharynx and upper esophagus.

Takeaway: Plummer-Vinson syndrome: iron deficiency anemia, postcricoid web, dysphagia; treat the iron deficiency and watch for squamous cancer.

whyNot.A: Folate deficiency also causes macrocytic anemia and is not associated with postcricoid webs.
whyNot.C: Riboflavin deficiency can cause angular cheilitis and glossitis, but not microcytic anemia, koilonychia and webs.
whyNot.D: B<sub>12</sub> deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia and neurologic signs, not a microcytic anemia with esophageal webs.
whyNot.E: Zinc deficiency causes dermatitis, alopecia, poor wound healing and taste changes.

items.objective: Link Plummer-Vinson syndrome to iron deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has endoscopy that shows large distal esophageal varices. These varices form because portal hypertension diverts portal blood into the systemic circulation through which of the following venous connections?

options.label: A
options.html: Left gastric vein to esophageal veins draining to the azygos system

options.label: B
options.html: Paraumbilical veins to superficial epigastric veins

options.label: C
options.html: Retroperitoneal colic veins to lumbar veins

options.label: D
options.html: Splenic vein to left renal vein

options.label: E
options.html: Superior rectal vein to middle and inferior rectal veins

items.explanationHtml:
The lower esophagus drains into both the left gastric (coronary) vein of the portal system and the esophageal tributaries of the azygos system. With portal hypertension, flow reverses in the left gastric vein and the submucosal veins of the distal esophagus dilate into varices.

Takeaway: Esophageal varices form at the left gastric to azygos portosystemic anastomosis.

whyNot.B: This anastomosis produces caput medusae on the abdominal wall, not esophageal varices.
whyNot.C: These retroperitoneal anastomoses do not produce varices in the esophageal submucosa.
whyNot.D: This is a spontaneous splenorenal shunt, which decompresses the portal system into the left renal vein.
whyNot.E: This connection produces rectal varices.

items.objective: Identify the portosystemic anastomosis that forms esophageal varices.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has 2 months of burning retrosternal discomfort after large meals and when lying down, with an occasional sour taste in his mouth. Antacids help briefly. He has no difficulty or pain with swallowing, weight loss, vomiting or black stools. His BMI is 29 kg/m2. Examination is normal, and hemoglobin is 15.1 g/dL (13.5-17.5). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Once-daily proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks, taken before breakfast

items.explanationHtml:
Typical heartburn and regurgitation without alarm features is diagnosed clinically. The next step is an 8-week empiric trial of a once-daily PPI taken 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal, with weight loss and avoiding late meals. If symptoms resolve, taper to the lowest effective dose.

Takeaway: Uncomplicated typical GERD: 8-week once-daily PPI trial before breakfast, plus lifestyle measures.

whyNot.A: pH monitoring is reserved for unclear cases, PPI nonresponders with a normal endoscopy, or before surgery.
whyNot.B: A barium study does not reliably diagnose reflux and would not change initial management.
whyNot.C: Surgery is considered only after reflux is objectively confirmed and medical therapy is unsatisfactory.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy is for alarm features, PPI failure or Barrett screening in higher-risk patients, none of which applies here.

items.objective: Start empiric PPI therapy for typical reflux without alarm features.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has 10 months of gradually worsening difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food when she lies down, and a 4-kg weight loss. She drinks water to help food pass. Upper endoscopy shows a dilated esophagus containing retained food and saliva, and a puckered gastroesophageal junction that the endoscope passes with gentle pressure; there is no mass and the mucosa is normal. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that tapers smoothly at the gastroesophageal junction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the chest and abdomen

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat endoscopy with biopsies of the junction

items.explanationHtml:
Progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation, a dilated esophagus with retained food and a smooth taper suggests achalasia. Endoscopy has excluded an obstructing lesion. High-resolution manometry is the most accurate test: it shows incomplete LES relaxation with absent peristalsis and classifies the subtype, which guides treatment.

Takeaway: After endoscopy excludes obstruction, high-resolution manometry confirms achalasia.

whyNot.A: pH monitoring assesses reflux, which is not her problem.
whyNot.B: CT is added when pseudoachalasia from cancer is suspected, as in an older patient with rapid weight loss; it does not confirm achalasia.
whyNot.C: EUS looks for a submucosal or junctional tumor when malignancy is suspected; it does not measure sphincter function.
whyNot.E: The junction looked normal and was passed easily; manometry, not more biopsies, establishes the diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose manometry to confirm suspected achalasia.

items.stemHtml: High-resolution manometry shows incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, absent peristalsis and pressurization of the whole esophagus with each swallow, consistent with type II achalasia. She is otherwise healthy and wants a durable treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Botulinum toxin injection into the lower esophageal sphincter

options.label: D
options.html: Laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication

items.explanationHtml:
Healthy patients with achalasia should receive a durable treatment that disrupts the LES. Laparoscopic Heller myotomy with a partial fundoplication (to limit reflux) is a standard choice. Pneumatic dilation and peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) are comparably effective alternatives for type II disease, and the choice depends on local expertise and patient preference; POEM causes more reflux.

Takeaway: Fit patients with achalasia get myotomy (Heller or POEM) or pneumatic dilation; botulinum toxin is for poor candidates.

whyNot.A: Botulinum toxin gives only temporary relief and is reserved for patients who cannot undergo dilation or myotomy.
whyNot.B: Esophagectomy is reserved for end-stage megaesophagus that has failed other treatments.
whyNot.C: Achalasia is a failure of sphincter relaxation, not an acid disorder, so acid suppression does not relieve the obstruction.
whyNot.E: Calcium channel blockers lower LES pressure only slightly and are poorly effective.

items.objective: Select definitive therapy for achalasia in a fit patient.

items.stemHtml:
A 57-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis has screening upper endoscopy that shows large esophageal varices with no stigmata of recent bleeding. He has never had GI bleeding, ascites or encephalopathy. Findings are shown.

MeasureResult
Blood pressure132/84 mm Hg
Pulse82/min
Albumin3.6 g/dL (3.5-5.5)
Bilirubin, total1.2 mg/dL (0.1-1.0)
INR1.2 (0.8-1.1)
Platelets92,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000)
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL (0.6-1.2)
Current medicationsMetformin, atorvastatin

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his risk of variceal bleeding?

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat endoscopy in 2 years without treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Patients with compensated cirrhosis and large varices need primary prophylaxis. A nonselective beta blocker is preferred, and carvedilol is favored because its added alpha1 blockade lowers portal pressure more than propranolol; endoscopic band ligation is the alternative when beta blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. His blood pressure and pulse allow beta blockade.

Takeaway: Primary prophylaxis of large varices: nonselective beta blocker (carvedilol preferred) or band ligation if beta blockers cannot be used.

whyNot.B: Nitrates alone do not prevent first variceal bleeding and are not recommended as monotherapy.
whyNot.C: Cardioselective beta blockers lack the beta<sub>2</sub> blockade needed to reduce splanchnic inflow and portal pressure.
whyNot.D: TIPS is used for refractory bleeding, high-risk acute bleeding or refractory ascites, not primary prophylaxis.
whyNot.E: Large varices carry a substantial bleeding risk, so prophylaxis is indicated now.

items.objective: Choose primary prophylaxis for large esophageal varices in compensated cirrhosis.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department after a night of heavy drinking. He vomited forcefully more than ten times, and then twice vomited fluid streaked with bright red blood. He has mild epigastric soreness but no chest pain or shortness of breath. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. There is no crepitus in the neck or chest, the lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft. Hemoglobin is 14.8 g/dL (13.5-17.5). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Blood-streaked vomitus after repeated forceful retching in a stable patient is a Mallory-Weiss tear, a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction. Most stop bleeding spontaneously; endoscopic therapy is needed only for active bleeding. Its absence of chest pain, crepitus and instability separates it from Boerhaave syndrome.

Takeaway: Retching then a small hematemesis in a stable patient suggests Mallory-Weiss; chest pain and crepitus suggest Boerhaave.

whyNot.A: Transmural rupture causes severe chest pain, fever, crepitus or pleural effusion and a toxic patient.
whyNot.B: A Dieulafoy lesion causes sudden, often brisk bleeding unrelated to retching from an abnormal submucosal artery.
whyNot.C: An ulcer is less likely given the clear sequence of repeated retching followed by blood-streaked vomitus in a young, stable patient.
whyNot.D: Variceal bleeding is usually large-volume in a patient with signs of portal hypertension, which he lacks.

items.objective: Distinguish Mallory-Weiss tear from Boerhaave syndrome and variceal bleeding.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 1 year ago has 2 weeks of pain when swallowing both food and liquids. He can still drink. Temperature is 37.4 C (99.3 F). Examination shows white plaques on the soft palate and buccal mucosa that scrape off easily. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 64/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Upper endoscopy with biopsy before any treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Odynophagia with oral thrush in a patient with advanced HIV is presumed Candida esophagitis. The best next step is empiric systemic therapy with oral fluconazole. Endoscopy is reserved for patients who do not improve within several days, to look for CMV, HSV or other causes. Restarting antiretroviral therapy prevents recurrence.

Takeaway: Thrush plus odynophagia in advanced HIV: empiric oral fluconazole; endoscope only if no response.

whyNot.A: Topical agents treat oral thrush only and are inadequate for esophageal candidiasis.
whyNot.C: Ganciclovir treats CMV esophagitis, which should be confirmed by biopsy before therapy.
whyNot.D: Acyclovir treats HSV esophagitis; thrush with odynophagia points to Candida.
whyNot.E: With thrush and odynophagia in advanced HIV, empiric antifungal therapy comes first; endoscopy is for failure to respond within a few days.

items.objective: Manage suspected Candida esophagitis in HIV.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with long-standing reflux has upper endoscopy. A 5-cm segment of flat, salmon-colored mucosa without nodules is seen. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia. He takes omeprazole daily and his symptoms are controlled. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Radiofrequency ablation of the segment now

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat endoscopy with biopsies in 3 years

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat endoscopy with biopsies in 6 months

options.label: E
options.html: Stop omeprazole and repeat endoscopy in 10 years

items.explanationHtml:
Nondysplastic Barrett esophagus is managed with continued PPI therapy and surveillance endoscopy with four-quadrant biopsies. Under the ACG 2022 guideline the interval is 3 years for segments of 3 cm or more and 5 years for shorter segments. Ablation is reserved for confirmed dysplasia.

Takeaway: Nondysplastic Barrett of 3 cm or more: PPI plus surveillance endoscopy every 3 years.

whyNot.A: Fundoplication controls reflux but does not reliably cause regression or replace surveillance.
whyNot.B: Ablation of nondysplastic Barrett is not recommended because its risk of progression is low.
whyNot.D: Six-month intervals are used after treatment of dysplasia, not for nondysplastic Barrett.
whyNot.E: Barrett esophagus needs ongoing acid suppression and surveillance at 3 to 5 years, not a 10-year interval.

items.objective: Choose the surveillance interval for nondysplastic Barrett esophagus.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman has 8 months of difficulty swallowing that she feels in her throat, coughing after meals, bad breath, and occasional regurgitation of pills she swallowed hours earlier. She has been treated twice for aspiration pneumonia. Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
items.explanationHtml:
Oropharyngeal symptoms with halitosis, regurgitation of food or pills taken hours earlier and aspiration in an older adult suggest Zenker diverticulum. A barium swallow (often a videofluoroscopic study) shows the posterior pouch safely. Symptomatic diverticula are treated by cricopharyngeal myotomy, often endoscopically.

Takeaway: Suspected Zenker diverticulum: barium swallow first, not blind endoscopy.

whyNot.A: pH monitoring evaluates reflux, which does not explain regurgitation of undigested pills hours later.
whyNot.C: A chest radiograph may show aspiration but cannot define the cause of her dysphagia.
whyNot.D: Manometry assesses body and LES motility and does not show a pharyngeal pouch.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy can miss the pouch and risks perforating it when the scope enters the diverticulum blindly; it is not the first test here.

items.objective: Choose the initial test for suspected Zenker diverticulum.

items.stemHtml: A researcher studies acid secretion in isolated rabbit gastric glands. Adding histamine sharply increases hydrogen ion secretion, and the response is abolished by famotidine. Which of the following intracellular changes in parietal cells mediates the effect of histamine?

options.label: B
options.html: Decreased cAMP through an inhibitory G protein

options.label: C
options.html: Increased cAMP through a stimulatory G protein

options.label: E
options.html: Increased IP3 and cytosolic calcium through Gq

items.explanationHtml:
Histamine released from ECL cells binds H2 receptors on parietal cells. These couple to Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase, raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, moving H+/K+ ATPase pumps into the canalicular membrane. Famotidine competitively blocks the H2 receptor.

Takeaway: Histamine stimulates acid through H2 receptors, Gs and cAMP; gastrin and ACh act through Gq and calcium.

whyNot.A: JAK-STAT signaling transmits cytokine receptor signals, not H2 receptor signals.
whyNot.B: Gi-coupled lowering of cAMP is how somatostatin and prostaglandin E2 inhibit acid.
whyNot.D: cGMP mediates nitric oxide and natriuretic peptide effects, not parietal cell acid secretion.
whyNot.E: This pathway mediates the actions of acetylcholine (M3) and gastrin (CCK-B), not histamine.

items.objective: Describe the second messenger pathways that control parietal cell acid secretion.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has fatigue and numbness and tingling in both feet. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (12.0-16.0) and MCV is 114 fL (80-100). Upper endoscopy shows thin, flat mucosa in the gastric body and fundus with a normal-appearing antrum. Biopsies of the body show loss of oxyntic glands with a lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate. Which of the following findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Body-predominant atrophic gastritis with macrocytic anemia and neuropathy in a woman with another autoimmune disease is autoimmune gastritis with pernicious anemia. Antibodies and T cells destroy parietal cells and block intrinsic factor. With no acid, antral D cells release less somatostatin, so antral G cells secrete gastrin unchecked. Sustained hypergastrinemia drives ECL-cell hyperplasia and can lead to gastric neuroendocrine tumors. B12 replacement is required lifelong.

Takeaway: Autoimmune gastritis: achlorhydria, high gastrin, low pepsinogen I and B12 deficiency.

whyNot.A: Antral G cells are spared and lose the inhibitory feedback of acid, so gastrin rises rather than falls.
whyNot.B: Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency raises methylmalonic acid because B<sub>12</sub> is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
whyNot.C: Destruction of parietal cells causes very low acid output, not hypersecretion.
whyNot.E: Pepsinogen I comes from chief cells in the body and falls as the oxyntic mucosa atrophies.

items.objective: Predict the gastrin level and related findings in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with severe hip osteoarthritis needs long-term NSAID therapy. He had a bleeding gastric ulcer 2 years ago. He is prescribed a combination tablet of diclofenac and misoprostol. Which of the following best describes how misoprostol protects his gastric mucosa?

options.label: A
options.html: Acts as a prostaglandin E1 analog that increases mucus and bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.html: Blocks the potassium-binding site of the proton pump

options.label: D
options.html: Irreversibly inhibits the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase

options.label: E
options.html: Polymerizes in acid and binds proteins in the ulcer base

items.explanationHtml:
NSAIDs remove protective prostaglandins by inhibiting COX-1. Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analog, restores that protection: it increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion, supports mucosal blood flow and modestly lowers acid through Gi-coupled receptors on parietal cells. Diarrhea and cramps are common, and it can induce uterine contractions, so it is contraindicated in pregnancy for ulcer prevention.

Takeaway: Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog that replaces the mucosal protection NSAIDs remove; avoid in pregnancy.

whyNot.B: This describes potassium-competitive acid blockers such as vonoprazan.
whyNot.C: This describes famotidine and other H2 antagonists.
whyNot.D: This is the mechanism of proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole.
whyNot.E: This is the action of sucralfate.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism and key adverse effects of misoprostol.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has taken omeprazole daily for 6 years for reflux. She comes to the emergency department with muscle cramps and painful spasms of her hands. Tapping anterior to the ear causes twitching of the facial muscles. Serum calcium is 7.4 mg/dL (8.4-10.2) with albumin 4.0 g/dL (3.5-5.5), potassium is 3.2 mEq/L (3.5-5.0), and PTH is inappropriately low-normal. Which additional laboratory abnormality is most likely present?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term PPI therapy can impair intestinal magnesium absorption through TRPM6/7 channels. Severe hypomagnesemia reduces PTH secretion and causes end-organ resistance to PTH, producing hypocalcemia, and increases renal potassium loss. Calcium and potassium correct poorly until magnesium is replaced. This patient also needs her ongoing indication for a PPI reviewed.

Takeaway: Long-term PPIs can cause hypomagnesemia, which leads to hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.

whyNot.A: A raised chloride is not a recognized effect of long-term PPI use and does not explain the tetany.
whyNot.B: Her potassium is low; hypomagnesemia promotes renal potassium wasting.
whyNot.C: High magnesium suppresses neuromuscular excitability and causes weakness and hyporeflexia, not tetany.
whyNot.D: Sodium abnormalities do not explain low calcium with low PTH and tetany.

items.objective: Recognize hypomagnesemia as an adverse effect of long-term PPI therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man has 4 months of epigastric discomfort, early satiety, a 6-kg weight loss and swelling of both legs. Urinalysis shows no protein. Serum albumin is 2.4 g/dL (3.5-5.5). Endoscopy shows massively enlarged rugal folds in the gastric body and fundus with sparing of the antrum. Gastric acid output is low. Which of the following is most likely seen on full-thickness biopsy of the folds?

options.label: A
options.html: Marked foveolar hyperplasia with atrophy of oxyntic glands

options.label: B
options.html: Noncaseating granulomas in the lamina propria

options.label: C
options.html: Parietal cell hyperplasia with thickened oxyntic mucosa

options.label: D
options.html: Sheets of small B cells forming lymphoepithelial lesions

options.label: E
options.html: Signet-ring cells infiltrating a thickened, rigid wall

items.explanationHtml:
Giant rugal folds in the body and fundus, low acid output and hypoalbuminemia without proteinuria point to Menetrier disease. Excess TGF-alpha signaling through the EGF receptor causes massive foveolar (mucous cell) hyperplasia and atrophy of the acid-producing glands. Protein leaks into the lumen, producing edema. Severe disease may be treated with an EGFR-blocking antibody or gastrectomy.

Takeaway: Menetrier disease: giant folds from foveolar hyperplasia, low acid and protein-losing gastropathy.

whyNot.B: Granulomatous gastritis occurs in Crohn disease or sarcoidosis and does not produce giant folds with low acid.
whyNot.C: Parietal cell hyperplasia occurs with gastrinoma, which causes high acid output and ulcers rather than low acid and protein loss.
whyNot.D: This is MALT lymphoma, which is not associated with low albumin from protein-losing gastropathy.
whyNot.E: Diffuse gastric carcinoma (linitis plastica) causes a rigid stomach rather than giant hyperplastic folds with protein loss.

items.objective: Identify the histology of Menetrier disease and contrast it with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man is in the intensive care unit after a severe traumatic brain injury with raised intracranial pressure. On hospital day 3, coffee-ground material appears in his nasogastric tube. Endoscopy shows several ulcers in the proximal duodenum and stomach. He received no NSAIDs. Which of the following mechanisms most likely contributed to these ulcers?

options.label: B
options.html: Autonomous gastrin secretion by a duodenal tumor

options.label: C
options.html: Increased vagal stimulation causing gastric acid hypersecretion

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of mucosal prostaglandins from COX inhibition

options.label: E
options.html: Mucosal ischemia from hypovolemia after loss of plasma

items.explanationHtml:
Ulcers after severe brain injury are Cushing ulcers. Raised intracranial pressure stimulates vagal nuclei, increasing acetylcholine-driven acid secretion. Curling ulcers after burns reflect hypovolemic ischemia. Critically ill patients with risk factors receive stress ulcer prophylaxis with a PPI or H2 blocker.

Takeaway: Cushing ulcer (brain injury) = vagal acid hypersecretion; Curling ulcer (burns) = hypovolemic ischemia.

whyNot.A: Urease-producing H. pylori causes chronic gastritis and ulcers, not ulcers that appear within days of brain injury.
whyNot.B: Gastrinoma causes chronic, recurrent ulcers, not acute ulcers after head injury.
whyNot.D: That is the mechanism of NSAID injury, and he received no NSAIDs.
whyNot.E: Ischemia from plasma loss explains Curling ulcers after severe burns.

items.objective: Distinguish the mechanisms of Cushing and Curling stress ulcers.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man who takes naproxen daily for back pain passes a large amount of black stool and becomes lightheaded. Endoscopy shows an ulcer in the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb with active arterial spurting. Which of the following arteries is most likely bleeding?
items.explanationHtml:
The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer can erode into it and cause massive bleeding. Anterior duodenal ulcers tend to perforate instead, releasing free air.

Takeaway: Posterior duodenal ulcers bleed from the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ones perforate.

whyNot.B: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature and bleeds from lesser curvature gastric ulcers.
whyNot.C: These supply the gastric fundus and can bleed from fundal lesions, not duodenal ulcers.
whyNot.D: The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas, away from the duodenal bulb.
whyNot.E: The SMA supplies the distal duodenum and midgut and is not adjacent to the posterior bulb.

items.objective: Relate ulcer location to the artery at risk of bleeding.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes has early satiety, postprandial fullness and vomiting of food eaten hours earlier. A gastric emptying study confirms delayed emptying, and she starts a medication that improves her symptoms. Ten months later she develops involuntary lip smacking, grimacing and tongue protrusion. Blockade of which of the following receptors most likely caused these movements?

options.label: A
options.html: Dopamine D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway

options.label: B
options.html: Histamine H1 receptors in the vestibular nuclei

options.label: C
options.html: Motilin receptors on gastric smooth muscle

options.label: E
options.html: Serotonin 5-HT3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

items.explanationHtml:
Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist (with 5-HT4 agonist activity) that speeds gastric emptying and suppresses nausea. Because it crosses the blood-brain barrier, chronic nigrostriatal D2 blockade can cause tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. Its labeling carries a boxed warning against use for longer than 12 weeks.

Takeaway: Metoclopramide blocks D2 receptors; long-term use can cause tardive dyskinesia.

whyNot.B: H1 blockers such as meclizine cause sedation and dry mouth, not tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.C: Erythromycin is a motilin agonist rather than a blocker, and motilin effects do not cause tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: Antimuscarinic drugs are used to treat drug-induced parkinsonism and do not produce tardive dyskinesia in this way.
whyNot.E: Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors and causes constipation, headache and QT prolongation, not tardive dyskinesia.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of metoclopramide-induced tardive dyskinesia.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department after passing black, tarry stools twice today and feeling lightheaded on standing. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention and naproxen for knee pain. He has no history of liver disease and drinks no alcohol. Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Two large-bore IV catheters are placed and isotonic crystalloid is given. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL (13.5-17.5). After resuscitation, pulse is 94/min and blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg. An IV proton pump inhibitor is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Melena with orthostatic symptoms in a patient taking aspirin and naproxen suggests a bleeding peptic ulcer. After resuscitation, upper endoscopy within 24 hours allows diagnosis, risk stratification and treatment. Very early endoscopy has not improved outcomes over endoscopy within 24 hours in patients who respond to resuscitation.

Takeaway: Nonvariceal upper GI bleeding: resuscitate, start PPI, and perform endoscopy within 24 hours.

whyNot.A: Melena with hemodynamic changes in an NSAID user points to an upper source; upper endoscopy comes first.
whyNot.B: CT angiography is used for brisk bleeding that cannot be localized or treated endoscopically, not as the first test for a likely ulcer.
whyNot.C: Octreotide is used for suspected variceal bleeding, and he has no evidence of liver disease.
whyNot.D: Tagged red cell scans help localize slow, intermittent lower GI bleeding, not suspected upper bleeding.

items.objective: Choose the timing of endoscopy in acute upper GI bleeding.

items.stemHtml: Endoscopy 10 hours after arrival shows a 1.2-cm ulcer on the lesser curvature of the gastric antrum. At its base is a raised, pigmented protuberance without active bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step during this endoscopy?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoscopic hemostasis with thermal coagulation or clips

options.label: B
options.html: Injection of dilute epinephrine as the only treatment

options.label: C
options.html: No endoscopic treatment and continued PPI only

options.label: D
options.html: Referral for surgical oversewing of the ulcer

items.explanationHtml:
A raised, pigmented protuberance is a nonbleeding visible vessel, a high-risk stigma for rebleeding. It should be treated endoscopically with thermal coagulation or clips (epinephrine may be added but never used alone). Afterward, give high-dose PPI for 3 days, biopsy for H. pylori, and stop naproxen and the primary-prevention aspirin. Because this is a gastric ulcer, biopsy helps exclude malignancy.

Takeaway: Active bleeding or a nonbleeding visible vessel needs endoscopic hemostasis followed by high-dose PPI.

whyNot.B: Epinephrine alone is inferior; it should be combined with a thermal or mechanical method.
whyNot.C: This is the approach for a clean base or flat pigmented spot, which carry a low rebleeding risk.
whyNot.D: Surgery is a rescue option after failed endoscopic and radiologic treatment.
whyNot.E: Embolization is reserved for bleeding that persists or recurs despite endoscopic therapy.

items.objective: Match endoscopic ulcer stigmata to treatment.

items.stemHtml:
A 48-year-old woman was admitted yesterday with melena from a duodenal ulcer, which was treated endoscopically with clips. She has no history of heart disease. She has had no further melena or hematemesis and feels well. Her trend is shown.

MeasureOn admissionToday
Pulse104/min84/min
Blood pressure104/66 mm Hg120/74 mm Hg
Hemoglobin9.1 g/dL8.2 g/dL (12.0-16.0)
Platelets242,000/mm3228,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000)
INR1.01.0 (0.8-1.1)
MedicationsIV pantoprazoleIV pantoprazole

Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding transfusion?

options.label: A
options.html: No transfusion now; transfuse if hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL

options.label: B
options.html: Transfuse 1 unit of red cells now to keep it above 9 g/dL

options.label: C
options.html: Transfuse 2 units of red cells now to reach 10 g/dL

items.explanationHtml:
In acute upper GI bleeding, a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusing at hemoglobin below 7 g/dL) reduces rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal strategy. Guidelines set the threshold at 7 to 8 g/dL in patients without cardiovascular disease; she is above both. A small fall in hemoglobin after resuscitation is expected from hemodilution. She is hemodynamically stable with no ongoing bleeding and no heart disease, so she should not be transfused now. A higher threshold (about 8 g/dL) is used in cardiovascular disease.

Takeaway: Stable upper GI bleeding without heart disease: transfuse only when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL.

whyNot.B: A threshold of 9 g/dL is higher than recommended for a stable patient without cardiovascular disease.
whyNot.C: A liberal target increases the risk of rebleeding and offers no benefit in a stable patient without heart disease.
whyNot.D: Her INR is normal, so plasma would add risk without benefit.
whyNot.E: Her platelet count is normal, and she is not taking antiplatelet drugs.

items.objective: Apply a restrictive transfusion threshold in upper GI bleeding.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with dyspepsia had a positive Helicobacter pylori stool antigen test and completed 14 days of bismuth quadruple therapy with omeprazole, bismuth subcitrate, tetracycline and metronidazole 1 week ago. His symptoms have resolved, and he is still taking omeprazole daily. He asks how to confirm that the infection is gone. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: A
options.html: No testing, because his symptoms have resolved

options.label: B
options.html: Repeat stool antigen test now while taking omeprazole

options.label: C
options.html: Serum H. pylori IgG antibodies measured now

options.label: D
options.html: Upper endoscopy with biopsy for culture now

options.label: E
options.html: Urea breath test 4 or more weeks after therapy, after holding omeprazole for 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Every patient treated for H. pylori should have a test of cure with a urea breath test, stool antigen test or biopsy-based test at least 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics, with PPIs stopped for 2 weeks beforehand to avoid false negatives. Serology stays positive after cure. If the infection persists, choose a regimen that avoids antibiotics likely to be resisted.

Takeaway: Confirm H. pylori eradication in everyone, at least 4 weeks after treatment and 2 weeks off PPI, with a breath or stool test.

whyNot.A: Symptom resolution does not prove eradication; current guidance recommends a test of cure for everyone treated.
whyNot.B: Testing this soon after treatment and while taking a PPI gives false-negative results.
whyNot.C: Antibodies persist long after cure, so serology cannot confirm eradication.
whyNot.D: Endoscopy is unnecessary for an uncomplicated case, and testing now would be falsely reassuring.

items.objective: Plan an appropriate test of cure after H. pylori treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 3 months of epigastric burning and fullness after meals. She has had no weight loss, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, black stools or blood in vomit, and there is no family history of gastric cancer. She takes no NSAIDs. Examination is normal, and hemoglobin is 13.4 g/dL (12.0-16.0). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
