For dyspepsia in a patient younger than 60 without alarm features, guidelines recommend a test-and-treat strategy: noninvasive H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) and eradication if positive. If testing is negative or symptoms persist after eradication, a PPI trial follows.

Takeaway: Dyspepsia under age 60 without alarm features: test and treat for H. pylori.

whyNot.A: CT does not evaluate the gastric mucosa and has no role in uncomplicated dyspepsia.
whyNot.B: Gastrin is measured when Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is suspected, as with refractory or multiple ulcers and diarrhea.
whyNot.C: Emptying studies are for suspected gastroparesis after obstruction has been excluded, not first-line dyspepsia evaluation.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy is recommended for dyspepsia at age 60 or older or with alarm features, which she lacks.

items.objective: Choose the initial evaluation for uncomplicated dyspepsia in a younger adult.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has had 6 months of nausea, early satiety, bloating and vomiting of food eaten several hours earlier. She has retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy, and her hemoglobin A1c is 9.1% (below 5.7%). She takes insulin glargine and insulin lispro and no other medications. Upper endoscopy shows no ulcer, mass or obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the abdomen with contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Gastric emptying scintigraphy with a solid meal over 4 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing diabetes with autonomic and microvascular complications plus postprandial vomiting suggests diabetic gastroparesis. After endoscopy excludes mechanical obstruction, the standard diagnostic test is 4-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy, performed with glucose controlled as well as possible because hyperglycemia itself slows emptying. Initial management is dietary change and better glycemic control, with metoclopramide used for a limited period if needed.

Takeaway: Suspected gastroparesis: exclude obstruction with endoscopy, then confirm with 4-hour solid-meal scintigraphy.

whyNot.A: Ultrasound evaluates the gallbladder and liver; it does not assess gastric emptying.
whyNot.B: Manometry is a specialized test for selected refractory cases, not the standard first diagnostic test.
whyNot.C: Endoscopy has already excluded obstruction, and CT does not measure emptying.
whyNot.E: Barium studies evaluate anatomy and are not a validated measure of gastric emptying.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected diabetic gastroparesis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with chronic back pain treated with ibuprofen developed sudden, severe epigastric pain 3 hours ago that has spread across his abdomen. He lies very still. Temperature is 37.9 C (100.2 F), pulse is 116/min and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. The abdomen is rigid with diffuse rebound tenderness. An upright chest radiograph shows free air under both hemidiaphragms. IV fluids, a nasogastric tube, an IV proton pump inhibitor and broad-spectrum antibiotics are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Barium upper GI series to confirm the site

options.label: B
options.html: Emergency surgical repair of the perforation

options.label: C
options.html: Nonoperative care with serial abdominal examinations

options.label: D
options.html: Upper endoscopy to locate and clip the ulcer

options.label: E
options.html: Urea breath test before deciding on surgery

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden severe pain, a board-like abdomen and free air in an NSAID user indicate a perforated peptic ulcer. After resuscitation, antibiotics and acid suppression, the patient needs emergency surgery, usually laparoscopic or open omental patch repair. H. pylori testing and eradication and stopping NSAIDs follow recovery.

Takeaway: Perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis needs resuscitation, antibiotics and emergency surgical repair.

whyNot.A: Barium is contraindicated with suspected perforation because it causes severe peritonitis.
whyNot.C: Nonoperative management is reserved for selected stable patients with a sealed perforation, not generalized peritonitis and tachycardia.
whyNot.D: Insufflation during endoscopy can enlarge a perforation and worsen peritoneal contamination; it is not the treatment for generalized peritonitis.
whyNot.E: H. pylori testing matters for later care but must not delay treatment of peritonitis.

items.objective: Manage a perforated peptic ulcer.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man who moved from Vietnam to the United States a year ago has bloating, flatulence and watery diarrhea that begin about an hour after he drinks the milk-based protein shakes he started for weight training. The diarrhea stops completely when he fasts. Stools contain no blood or leukocytes. After an oral lactose load, breath hydrogen rises sharply. Which of the following best explains his diarrhea?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial hydroxylation of unabsorbed fatty acids in the colon

options.label: B
options.html: Excess bile acids stimulating colonic chloride secretion

options.label: C
options.html: Immune-mediated villous atrophy reducing the absorptive surface

options.label: D
options.html: Toxin-mediated activation of enterocyte adenylyl cyclase

options.label: E
options.html: Unabsorbed disaccharide retaining water in the intestinal lumen

items.explanationHtml:
Most adults worldwide lose intestinal lactase after weaning. Undigested lactose stays in the lumen and holds water osmotically; colonic bacteria ferment it to gases (the hydrogen detected on breath testing) and short-chain fatty acids. Osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting, as in this patient, and has a large stool osmotic gap.

Takeaway: Diarrhea that stops with fasting and a positive lactose hydrogen breath test indicate osmotic diarrhea from lactase deficiency.

whyNot.A: Hydroxy fatty acids cause diarrhea in fat malabsorption, which would produce steatorrhea, not symptoms tied to milk with a positive lactose breath test.
whyNot.B: Bile acid diarrhea follows ileal disease or resection and is secretory; nothing here suggests ileal loss.
whyNot.C: Villous atrophy (celiac disease) causes broader malabsorption and does not resolve simply with fasting from one food.
whyNot.D: Toxin-induced cAMP secretion (for example cholera) causes secretory diarrhea that continues during fasting.

items.objective: Distinguish osmotic diarrhea due to lactase nonpersistence from secretory causes.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis has had bloating, loose stools and a 5-kg weight loss over 6 months. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL and MCV 109 fL. Serum cobalamin is low and serum folate is above the reference range. A glucose breath test is positive. Which of the following best explains this vitamin pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoantibodies against intrinsic factor block cobalamin uptake

options.label: B
options.html: Fibrosis destroys cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum

options.label: C
options.html: Jejunal villous atrophy impairs folate deconjugation

options.label: D
options.html: Luminal bacteria consume cobalamin and synthesise folate

options.label: E
options.html: Pancreatic insufficiency prevents release of cobalamin from haptocorrin

items.explanationHtml:
Systemic sclerosis impairs small-bowel motility, which allows bacterial overgrowth. Anaerobic bacteria take up cobalamin before it can be absorbed, while synthesising folate that the host absorbs. The result is megaloblastic anemia with low B12 and normal or high folate; deconjugation of bile acids adds fat malabsorption.

Takeaway: Low B12 with high folate in a patient with stasis suggests small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

whyNot.A: Pernicious anemia lowers B12 but does not raise folate and is unrelated to stasis or a positive breath test.
whyNot.B: Systemic sclerosis affects muscle layers rather than ileal receptors, and this would leave folate unexplained.
whyNot.C: Jejunal mucosal injury would lower folate rather than raise it.
whyNot.E: Pancreatic insufficiency can lower B12 but gives no reason for an elevated folate.

items.objective: Explain the cobalamin and folate pattern produced by bacterial overgrowth.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 5 years ago. She has fatigue and brittle nails. Hemoglobin is 9.5 g/dL, MCV 71 fL and ferritin low. She has taken oral ferrous sulfate daily for 6 months with little change. She has no bleeding. Which of the following best explains her poor response to oral iron?

options.label: A
options.html: Accelerated intestinal transit through the colon

options.label: C
options.html: Exclusion of the duodenum, the main site of nonheme iron uptake

options.label: D
options.html: Increased hepatic hepcidin production degrading ferroportin

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of ileal receptors for the intrinsic factor complex

items.explanationHtml:
Nonheme iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum: duodenal cytochrome b reduces it to Fe2+ and DMT1 carries it into the enterocyte. A Roux-en-Y bypass diverts food past the duodenum and also reduces gastric acid, which normally keeps iron soluble. Many patients need IV iron.

Takeaway: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, so bypass operations that exclude it commonly cause refractory iron deficiency.

whyNot.A: Iron is not absorbed in the colon, so colonic transit speed is irrelevant.
whyNot.B: Transferrin synthesis actually increases in iron deficiency; it is not the limiting step.
whyNot.D: Hepcidin rises with inflammation; iron deficiency suppresses hepcidin, so this would not explain her course.
whyNot.E: Loss of ileal cubilin causes cobalamin deficiency with macrocytosis, not microcytic iron deficiency.

items.objective: Relate the duodenal site of iron absorption to iron deficiency after bariatric surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man is 2 days out from coronary artery bypass surgery, during which he had prolonged hypotension requiring norepinephrine. He develops crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by several small bloody stools. CT shows segmental wall thickening of the distal transverse colon and splenic flexure; the rectum appears normal. This colonic segment is most vulnerable because it lies at the junction of the territories of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery

options.label: C
options.html: Inferior mesenteric and internal iliac arteries

options.label: D
options.html: Superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries

options.label: E
options.html: Superior rectal and middle rectal arteries

items.explanationHtml:
The splenic flexure is supplied at the far ends of the middle colic branch of the SMA and the left colic branch of the IMA. With low flow, perfusion fails first at such watershed segments, producing ischemic colitis. The rectum is protected by dual supply from the IMA and internal iliac branches.

Takeaway: Low-flow ischemic colitis targets watershed segments: the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and the rectosigmoid junction (IMA/internal iliac).

whyNot.A: The celiac-SMA boundary lies in the duodenum and pancreatic head, not the colon.
whyNot.B: Both are SMA branches supplying the right colon; their junction is not a major watershed.
whyNot.C: The IMA-internal iliac boundary is the rectosigmoid junction, not the splenic flexure.
whyNot.E: Superior and middle rectal arteries overlap in the rectum, which was spared here.

items.objective: Identify the arterial watershed responsible for splenic flexure ischemia.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man had 40 cm of terminal ileum resected after a gunshot wound 1 year ago. Since then he has had 4 to 6 watery stools daily. Quantitative fecal fat is normal and he has kept his weight. His diarrhea improves markedly with cholestyramine. Which of the following best explains his diarrhea before treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial overgrowth deconjugating bile acids in the jejunum

options.label: B
options.html: Depletion of the bile acid pool preventing micelle formation

options.label: C
options.html: Increased colonic absorption of dietary oxalate

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of the ileal brake causing rapid gastric emptying

options.label: E
options.html: Unabsorbed bile acids stimulating colonic chloride and water secretion

items.explanationHtml:
With limited ileal resection, bile acids that would normally be reabsorbed spill into the colon. There they stimulate chloride and water secretion and speed transit, producing watery (choleretic) diarrhea. The liver increases synthesis enough to maintain micelle formation, so fat absorption stays normal. Cholestyramine binds the bile acids in the lumen and stops the effect.

Takeaway: Short ileal loss causes secretory bile acid diarrhea that responds to sequestrants; long ileal loss causes steatorrhea.

whyNot.A: Overgrowth causes fat malabsorption and B12 deficiency and would not respond selectively to cholestyramine.
whyNot.B: Pool depletion follows long resections and causes steatorrhea; his fecal fat is normal, and sequestrants would worsen it.
whyNot.C: Enteric hyperoxaluria predisposes to kidney stones, not to watery diarrhea.
whyNot.D: The ileal brake may contribute to faster transit but does not explain the striking response to a bile acid binder.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of bile acid diarrhea after limited ileal resection.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman has had three episodes of painless hematochezia over a year and iron-deficiency anemia. A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids. Colonoscopy shows several flat, cherry-red, fern-like vascular lesions in the cecum. Platelet count and PT are normal; plasma testing shows loss of the largest von Willebrand factor multimers. Which of the following best explains her bleeding tendency?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoantibodies directed against coagulation factor VIII

options.label: B
options.html: Consumption of platelets within thrombosed vascular lesions

options.label: C
options.html: Inherited mutation reducing von Willebrand factor synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors

options.label: E
options.html: Shear stress unfolding von Willebrand factor for cleavage by ADAMTS13

items.explanationHtml:
High shear stress across a stenotic aortic valve stretches large von Willebrand factor multimers, exposing the site cleaved by ADAMTS13. Loss of high-molecular-weight multimers (acquired type 2A pattern) impairs platelet adhesion, so angiodysplasias in the right colon bleed. Aortic valve replacement often corrects the multimer defect and reduces bleeding.

Takeaway: Aortic stenosis with bleeding cecal angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome) reflects acquired loss of large vWF multimers from shear stress.

whyNot.A: Acquired hemophilia prolongs the aPTT and causes soft-tissue bleeding; it does not selectively remove large vWF multimers.
whyNot.B: Her platelet count is normal and angiodysplasias are not thrombosed lesions.
whyNot.C: An inherited defect would appear earlier in life and would not be linked to her new valve disease.
whyNot.D: Normal PT argues against a vitamin K-dependent factor deficit.

items.objective: Explain the link between aortic stenosis and bleeding from angiodysplasia.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban 10 days ago because of cost. Three hours ago she developed sudden, severe periumbilical pain and vomited once, then had a loose bowel movement. Pulse is 114/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg and temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F). She is writhing in pain, but the abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness and no guarding. Leukocyte count is 16,800/mm3 and venous lactate 2.9 mmol/L (0.5-2.2 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis

items.explanationHtml:
Sudden pain out of proportion to examination in a patient with atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation suggests embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. CT angiography is fast, widely available and shows the occlusion, bowel wall enhancement and alternative diagnoses. While it is arranged she should receive fluids, heparin and antibiotics, and surgery or interventional radiology should be called; revascularisation and resection of nonviable bowel follow.

Takeaway: Suspected acute mesenteric ischemia calls for immediate CT angiography; normal or mildly raised lactate must never delay it.

whyNot.A: Colonoscopy does not evaluate the SMA or small bowel and risks perforation of ischemic bowel.
whyNot.C: Duplex is useful for chronic stenosis but is limited by bowel gas and is too slow and operator-dependent in the emergency.
whyNot.D: Plain films are usually normal early and cannot show the vessel occlusion.
whyNot.E: Lactate rises late, after transmural infarction; waiting allows bowel to die.

items.objective: Choose the best initial test for suspected acute arterial mesenteric ischemia.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has had 4 days of worsening left lower quadrant pain and fever. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse 104/min and blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg. The left lower quadrant is tender without rigidity; the rest of the abdomen is soft. Leukocyte count is 17,600/mm3. CT with IV contrast shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 6-cm rim-enhancing pericolic fluid collection and no free intraperitoneal air. IV antibiotics are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Barium enema to define the anatomy

options.label: B
options.html: Colonoscopy to examine the sigmoid colon

options.label: C
options.html: CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the collection

options.label: E
options.html: Emergency sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy

items.explanationHtml:
This is complicated diverticulitis with a large pericolic abscess in a hemodynamically stable patient without generalised peritonitis. IV antibiotics plus image-guided percutaneous drainage controls the source and usually avoids emergency surgery, allowing a later elective, often single-stage, operation if needed. Small abscesses often settle with antibiotics alone.

Takeaway: A large diverticular abscess in a stable patient is drained percutaneously alongside IV antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Barium is contraindicated with possible perforation and adds nothing once CT has defined the disease.
whyNot.B: Colonoscopy is avoided during acute diverticulitis because insufflation can cause perforation.
whyNot.D: A 6-cm abscess with fever and leukocytosis is complicated disease that needs admission and source control.
whyNot.E: Emergency resection is for free perforation with peritonitis, uncontrolled sepsis or failed drainage.

items.objective: Manage complicated diverticulitis with a large abscess.

items.stemHtml: The drain is removed after 10 days and the man recovers fully. At a clinic visit 8 weeks later he is asymptomatic and eating normally. He has never had a colonoscopy, and there is no family history of colorectal cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: No further evaluation unless symptoms recur

options.label: E
options.html: Strict avoidance of nuts, seeds and popcorn

items.explanationHtml:
After an episode of complicated diverticulitis, colonoscopy is recommended once inflammation has settled (commonly 6 to 8 weeks) if no recent high-quality examination exists, because a perforated colorectal cancer can look like diverticulitis on CT. He is also of screening age. Any decision about elective sigmoid resection is made afterwards and individualised.

Takeaway: Perform colonoscopy after recovery from complicated diverticulitis when no recent examination exists.

whyNot.B: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for preventing recurrence.
whyNot.C: Mesalamine has not been shown to prevent recurrent diverticulitis.
whyNot.D: Complicated disease carries a meaningful risk of an underlying neoplasm, and he is overdue for screening regardless.
whyNot.E: Nuts, seeds and popcorn are not associated with diverticulitis, so avoiding them is unnecessary.

items.objective: Plan follow-up evaluation after complicated diverticulitis.

items.stemHtml: An 85-year-old nursing home resident with Parkinson disease and chronic constipation has had 2 days of progressive abdominal distension and no passage of stool or flatus. He is afebrile; pulse is 88/min and blood pressure 132/76 mm Hg. The abdomen is massively distended and tympanitic with mild, diffuse tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Leukocyte count and lactate are within the reference ranges. An abdominal radiograph shows a hugely dilated, inverted U-shaped loop of colon arising from the pelvis and extending to the right upper quadrant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion with placement of a rectal tube

items.explanationHtml:
The radiograph shows sigmoid volvulus. Without peritonitis or signs of gangrene, the first step is endoscopic detorsion, which decompresses the loop and lets the mucosa be inspected for ischemia; a rectal tube helps prevent immediate recurrence. Because recurrence is common, elective sigmoid resection is then planned during the same admission if he is fit for surgery. Peritonitis, dusky mucosa or failed detorsion requires emergency sigmoid resection.

Takeaway: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic detorsion first, then elective sigmoid resection before discharge in fit patients.

whyNot.A: Right hemicolectomy is the operation for cecal volvulus, not sigmoid volvulus.
whyNot.C: Neostigmine treats pseudo-obstruction; in a mechanical twist it is contraindicated and can cause perforation.
whyNot.D: An untreated closed loop progresses to ischemia; prompt decompression is needed.
whyNot.E: Oral laxatives into a closed-loop obstruction can worsen distension and risk perforation.

items.objective: Manage sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis.

items.stemHtml:
A 73-year-old man develops progressive abdominal distension 2 days after a right total hip arthroplasty. He was receiving oxycodone for pain. CT on day 3 showed diffuse dilation of the colon down to the rectum with no transition point, no pneumatosis and no free air. He was managed for 48 hours with nothing by mouth, nasogastric and rectal tubes, opioid withdrawal, mobilisation and electrolyte replacement. He has mild discomfort and the abdomen is distended and tympanitic without guarding. Results:

MeasureDay 3Day 5
Pulse (/min)9688
Blood pressure (mm Hg)134/78130/74
Temperature37.3°C (99.1°F)37.1°C (98.8°F)
Potassium (3.5-5.0 mEq/L)3.14.2
Magnesium (1.5-2.0 mEq/L)1.21.9
Leukocytes (4,500-11,000/mm3)9,8009,400
Cecal diameter on radiograph12.5 cm13 cm

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continued conservative care for another week

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome): mechanical obstruction was excluded on CT, and 48 hours of correct conservative care, including normalised potassium and magnesium, has failed while the cecum remains above about 12 cm. IV neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases parasympathetic colonic activity, is the next step, given with cardiac monitoring and atropine at the bedside because of bradycardia. Colonoscopic decompression is used if it fails.

Takeaway: Ogilvie syndrome that persists after 24 to 48 hours of conservative care, with a dilated cecum and no peritonitis, is treated with IV neostigmine.

whyNot.A: A persistently enlarged cecum risks ischemia and perforation; prolonged waiting is unsafe.
whyNot.B: Surgery is reserved for perforation, ischemia or failure of pharmacologic and endoscopic decompression.
whyNot.C: There is no fever, leukocytosis or peritonitis to suggest infection or perforation.
whyNot.E: Osmotic laxatives increase colonic gas and fluid and can worsen dilation.

items.objective: Escalate management of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction after failed conservative care.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation has had 18 hours of pain that began around the umbilicus and has moved to the right side of her abdomen, with nausea and loss of appetite. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). She has tenderness and voluntary guarding in the right lower and mid abdomen. Leukocyte count is 15,200/mm3. Urinalysis is normal. Fetal heart rate is 150/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Graded-compression ultrasonography of the right abdomen

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the abdomen with gadolinium

options.label: E
options.html: Serial examinations at home with return precautions

items.explanationHtml:
Suspected appendicitis in pregnancy is imaged first with ultrasonography, which uses no ionising radiation. If it is inconclusive, MRI without gadolinium is the next test; CT is used only when MRI is unavailable. Prompt diagnosis matters because perforation sharply increases fetal loss. Appendectomy, usually laparoscopic, is safe in any trimester.

Takeaway: In pregnancy, image suspected appendicitis with ultrasound first, then noncontrast MRI if needed.

whyNot.A: CT exposes the fetus to radiation and is reserved for cases where ultrasound and MRI are unavailable or inconclusive.
whyNot.B: Proceeding to surgery without imaging raises the rate of negative operations, which also carry fetal risk.
whyNot.D: MRI is the second-line test, and gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta.
whyNot.E: Fever, localised guarding and leukocytosis need a diagnosis now; delay risks perforation.

items.objective: Select imaging for suspected appendicitis in a pregnant patient.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has noticed bright red blood on the toilet paper after bowel movements for 3 months. Defecation is painless. Anoscopy shows engorged purple vascular cushions proximal to the dentate line that bleed with straining. Which of the following best explains why these lesions are painless?

options.label: A
options.html: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve

options.label: B
options.html: Perineal branches of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Sensory fibres of the ilioinguinal nerve

options.label: D
options.html: Somatic sensory fibres of the inferior rectal nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Visceral afferent fibres travelling with the pelvic autonomic plexus

items.explanationHtml:
Internal hemorrhoids lie above the pectinate line, where the mucosa is supplied by visceral afferents that travel with the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) autonomic plexus. These fibres respond to stretch, not to cutting, pinching or heat, so internal hemorrhoids bleed without pain. Below the line, the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, so fissures and thrombosed external hemorrhoids are very painful.

Takeaway: Lesions above the pectinate line are painless (visceral innervation); lesions below it are painful (somatic pudendal innervation).

whyNot.A: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the scrotum or labia and upper thigh.
whyNot.B: Posterior femoral cutaneous branches supply perineal and thigh skin, not anal mucosa.
whyNot.C: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies skin of the groin and anterior genitalia, not the anal canal.
whyNot.D: The inferior rectal nerve supplies the anoderm below the line, which is why external lesions hurt.

items.objective: Relate the innervation of the anal canal to pain from hemorrhoids.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman has anal bleeding and pain. Examination shows an ulcerated mass in the anal canal that lies entirely below the dentate line and extends to the anal verge. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. To which lymph node group does this tumour drain first?
items.explanationHtml:
Lymph from the anal canal below the pectinate line, like that of the perianal skin, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Above the line, drainage follows the arteries to the internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes. Inguinal examination and imaging are therefore part of staging anal cancer.

Takeaway: Below the pectinate line, lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

whyNot.A: Deep cervical nodes drain the head and neck.
whyNot.B: Inferior mesenteric nodes drain the upper rectum and sigmoid along the superior rectal artery.
whyNot.C: Internal iliac nodes drain the canal above the pectinate line and the lower rectum.
whyNot.D: Para-aortic nodes are reached later or drain the gonads, not the first station for the distal canal.

items.objective: Predict lymphatic spread of a tumour below the pectinate line.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and portal hypertension undergoes flexible sigmoidoscopy for minor bleeding. It shows dilated, tortuous submucosal veins in the distal rectum that are separate from the hemorrhoidal cushions. These vessels form through communication between which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Internal pudendal vein and internal iliac vein

options.label: B
options.html: Left gastric vein and esophageal veins

options.label: C
options.html: Paraumbilical veins and superficial epigastric veins

options.label: D
options.html: Splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein

options.label: E
options.html: Superior rectal vein and middle and inferior rectal veins

items.explanationHtml:
The superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and the portal system, while the middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac veins and the inferior vena cava. When portal pressure rises, blood is shunted through these connections and they dilate into anorectal varices. This is one of the portosystemic anastomoses, alongside esophageal varices and caput medusae.

Takeaway: Anorectal varices form between the portal superior rectal vein and the systemic middle and inferior rectal veins.

whyNot.A: Both are systemic veins; the internal pudendal is a tributary of the internal iliac.
whyNot.B: The left gastric-esophageal connection produces esophageal varices, not rectal ones.
whyNot.C: Paraumbilical-epigastric connections produce caput medusae on the abdominal wall.
whyNot.D: Both the splenic and inferior mesenteric veins are portal tributaries, so their junction is not a portosystemic shunt.

items.objective: Identify the portosystemic anastomosis that forms anorectal varices.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has a rectal mass whose lower edge lies 2 cm above the dentate line. Biopsy shows invasive malignant glands with dirty necrosis. From which embryologic tissue is the epithelium at this site derived?
items.explanationHtml:
The anal canal above the pectinate line and the rectum derive from hindgut endoderm (the dorsal part of the cloaca) and are lined by glandular columnar epithelium, which gives rise to adenocarcinoma. Below the line, the canal comes from the ectoderm of the anal pit (proctodeum) and is lined by squamous epithelium, the source of squamous cell carcinoma.

Takeaway: Above the pectinate line: endoderm, columnar epithelium, adenocarcinoma. Below: ectoderm, squamous epithelium, SCC.

whyNot.A: Proctodeal ectoderm forms the canal below the pectinate line, where squamous epithelium lies.
whyNot.C: Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys and gonads.
whyNot.D: Neural crest forms enteric ganglia and melanocytes, not the glandular lining.
whyNot.E: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, skeletal muscle and vertebrae.

items.objective: Link the embryologic origin of the anorectum to its epithelium and tumour type.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has had severe tearing pain during and for an hour after each bowel movement for 4 weeks, with a streak of blood on the paper. She had constipation after starting an iron supplement. Gentle separation of the buttocks shows a linear tear in the posterior midline of the anoderm; the sphincter is tight. She is prescribed topical nitroglycerin ointment. Which of the following is the mechanism of this drug's benefit?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of guanylate cyclase, relaxing internal sphincter smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Activation of mu-opioid receptors on anal sensory nerves

options.label: C
options.html: Antagonism of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in vascular smooth muscle

options.label: D
options.html: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in internal sphincter muscle

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of acetylcholine release onto external sphincter fibres

items.explanationHtml:
An anal fissure fails to heal because high internal sphincter tone reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm. Nitroglycerin releases nitric oxide, which activates soluble guanylate cyclase, raises cGMP and relaxes the smooth muscle of the internal sphincter. Lower pressure improves perfusion and allows healing. Headache from vasodilation is the main adverse effect and the most common reason patients stop it.

Takeaway: Topical nitrates heal fissures by NO-cGMP relaxation of the internal sphincter; headache is the typical adverse effect.

whyNot.B: Opioids would not lower sphincter pressure and tend to worsen constipation.
whyNot.C: Nitrates act through cGMP, not by blocking adrenergic receptors.
whyNot.D: This is how topical diltiazem or nifedipine works, an alternative with fewer headaches.
whyNot.E: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, and its target for fissures is the internal sphincter.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of topical nitrate therapy for anal fissure.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man has a chronic posterior anal fissure that persists after 10 weeks of topical diltiazem. He chooses an injection of botulinum toxin into the internal anal sphincter. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve axons

options.label: B
options.html: Cleavage of SNARE proteins needed for acetylcholine vesicle release

options.label: C
options.html: Competitive blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of glycine release from spinal interneurons

items.explanationHtml:
Botulinum toxin is a zinc protease taken up by cholinergic nerve terminals, where it cleaves SNARE proteins (such as SNAP-25) that are needed for synaptic vesicle fusion. Acetylcholine release stops, producing a chemical denervation that lowers sphincter tone for about 2 to 3 months while the fissure heals. Function returns as new terminals sprout, so any incontinence is temporary.

Takeaway: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release, giving reversible sphincter relaxation.

whyNot.A: Local anesthetics block sodium channels; their effect lasts hours, not months.
whyNot.C: Nondepolarising neuromuscular blockers such as rocuronium act this way.
whyNot.D: Tetanus toxin blocks glycine and GABA release from inhibitory interneurons, causing spasm.
whyNot.E: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, which increases rather than decreases cholinergic activity.

items.objective: State the mechanism of botulinum toxin.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man who has receptive anal intercourse with male partners has had 2 weeks of rectal pain, tenesmus and bloody mucopurulent discharge, with tender left inguinal lymph nodes. Sigmoidoscopy shows friable, ulcerated rectal mucosa. Rectal nucleic acid amplification testing is positive, and genotyping identifies serovar L2. Which of the following best describes the causative organism?

options.label: A
options.html: Enveloped double-stranded DNA virus that becomes latent in sacral ganglia

options.label: B
options.html: Gram-negative diplococcus grown on selective chocolate agar

options.label: C
options.html: Gram-negative rod that produces Shiga toxin

options.label: D
options.html: Obligate intracellular bacterium with elementary and reticulate bodies

items.explanationHtml:
Serovars L1 to L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis cause lymphogranuloma venereum, which in men who have sex with men commonly presents as hemorrhagic proctitis that can mimic inflammatory bowel disease. Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria: the small elementary body is infectious and enters cells, then converts to the larger reticulate body that replicates within an inclusion. LGV is treated with a longer course of doxycycline than other chlamydial infections.

Takeaway: LGV proctitis is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1 to L3, obligate intracellular bacteria with an elementary and a reticulate body.

whyNot.A: Herpes simplex virus causes painful vesicles and ulcers, and its genome is not typed into serovars.
whyNot.B: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus; it causes purulent proctitis but has no L serovars.
whyNot.C: Shigella causes dysenteric colitis spread by the fecal-oral route, not a serovar L2 infection.
whyNot.E: Treponema pallidum causes syphilitic proctitis or chancres but is identified by serology or darkfield, not chlamydial serovars.

items.objective: Identify the microbiology of lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man living with HIV is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal. The tumour tests positive for HPV type 16 DNA. One viral oncoprotein binds the retinoblastoma protein, releasing E2F transcription factors and pushing cells into S phase. Which viral protein is this?
items.explanationHtml:
High-risk HPV types integrate into the host genome, often disrupting the E2 gene that normally represses E6 and E7 expression. E7 binds and inactivates Rb, releasing E2F so the cell enters S phase. E6 recruits a ubiquitin ligase to degrade p53, removing the apoptotic and cell-cycle checkpoint. Together they drive anal, cervical and oropharyngeal squamous carcinomas.

Takeaway: HPV E7 inactivates Rb; E6 degrades p53.

whyNot.A: E2 represses E6 and E7 transcription; its loss after integration promotes, rather than causes, Rb inactivation.
whyNot.B: E6 targets p53 for degradation rather than binding Rb.
whyNot.D: L1 is the major capsid protein and the antigen used in HPV vaccines.
whyNot.E: L2 is the minor capsid protein with no direct role in transformation.

items.objective: Identify the HPV oncoprotein that inactivates Rb.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had fecal urgency and leakage of loose stool since a vaginal delivery 6 months ago that involved a prolonged second stage and forceps. Endoanal ultrasonography shows intact internal and external sphincter muscles. Anorectal manometry shows normal resting pressure but markedly reduced voluntary squeeze pressure. Injury to which nerve best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Squeeze pressure is generated by the striated external anal sphincter and puborectalis, innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4). Stretch of the nerve during a prolonged second stage or instrumental delivery causes pudendal neuropathy, which weakens voluntary squeeze while resting tone, provided mainly by the internal sphincter smooth muscle, is preserved. Intact sphincters on ultrasound point to nerve injury rather than a tear.

Takeaway: Reduced squeeze pressure with intact sphincters after a difficult delivery suggests pudendal nerve injury.

whyNot.A: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and skin of the genitals and thigh.
whyNot.B: Hypogastric (sympathetic) fibres increase internal sphincter tone, which is normal here.
whyNot.C: The obturator nerve supplies the thigh adductors.
whyNot.D: Pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) nerves govern rectal contraction and internal sphincter relaxation, not voluntary squeeze.

items.objective: Localise the nerve responsible for external anal sphincter weakness.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has had severe, constant perianal pain for 36 hours that began after he helped a friend move furniture. He has had no fever. Examination shows a tense, exquisitely tender, bluish 1.5-cm lump at the anal verge covered by skin, with no fluctuance or surrounding erythema. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia

options.label: B
options.html: Incision and drainage with oral antibiotics

options.label: E
options.html: Stapled hemorrhoidopexy in the operating room

items.explanationHtml:
A tense, bluish, skin-covered lump at the verge with acute severe pain is a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. When the patient presents within about 72 hours of onset, excision of the whole thrombosed hemorrhoid in the office under local anesthesia relieves pain fastest and reduces recurrence compared with incision and clot evacuation. After 72 hours the pain usually settles on its own, so conservative care is preferred.

Takeaway: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid seen within about 72 hours: excise under local anesthesia; later, treat conservatively.

whyNot.B: This is a thrombus, not an abscess; there is no fluctuance, erythema or fever to treat.
whyNot.C: Banding is for internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line; placing a band on sensate anoderm causes severe pain.
whyNot.D: Sclerotherapy is an office option for bleeding internal hemorrhoids, not external thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Stapled hemorrhoidopexy treats prolapsing internal hemorrhoids and does not address an external thrombus.

items.objective: Manage an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman has had painful defecation for 2 months, intermittent nonbloody diarrhea, crampy right lower quadrant pain and an 8-kg weight loss. Perianal examination shows two fissures, both located laterally away from the midline, with edematous bluish skin tags. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Botulinum toxin injection into the internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.html: Colonoscopy with terminal ileal intubation and biopsies

items.explanationHtml:
Typical fissures sit in the posterior (or anterior) midline. Multiple or lateral fissures, especially with diarrhea, right lower quadrant pain, weight loss, anemia and edematous tags, point to a secondary cause, most likely Crohn disease. The priority is diagnosis, with ileocolonoscopy and biopsies; HIV, syphilis and tuberculosis testing may also be needed. Treating the fissure as idiopathic would delay diagnosis, and sphincter surgery in Crohn disease risks incontinence and poor healing.

Takeaway: An off-midline anal fissure demands a search for Crohn disease, HIV, TB, syphilis or cancer before fissure-directed treatment.

whyNot.A: Anal cancer screening targets high-risk groups; her systemic symptoms point first to inflammatory disease.
whyNot.B: Botulinum toxin addresses sphincter spasm but ignores the systemic clues to an underlying cause.
whyNot.D: Sphincterotomy is contraindicated until secondary causes are excluded, and it heals poorly in Crohn disease.
whyNot.E: Topical therapy is the first treatment for a typical midline fissure, but here it would leave the likely underlying disease undiagnosed.

items.objective: Recognise an atypical anal fissure and evaluate for a secondary cause.

items.stemHtml:
A 26-year-old man comes to the clinic with 5 days of anal pain, tenesmus and mucopurulent rectal discharge. He has receptive anal intercourse with several male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Anoscopy shows inflamed, friable rectal mucosa with purulent exudate and no ulcers or vesicles; there is no bloody discharge. Rectal swabs for nucleic acid amplification testing are sent. Results:

MeasureResult
Temperature37.4°C (99.3°F)
Pulse84/min
Blood pressure124/76 mm Hg
Leukocytes8,900/mm3 (4,500-11,000/mm3)
HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody testNonreactive
Rapid plasma reaginNonreactive

Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric treatment while results are pending?

options.label: A
options.html: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once

options.label: B
options.html: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

options.label: D
options.html: Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

options.label: E
options.html: Valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily for 10 days

items.explanationHtml:
Acute proctitis after receptive anal intercourse is most often caused by N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, HSV or syphilis. Without ulcers, CDC guidance is empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for 7 days while NAATs are pending. If he develops bloody discharge or ulcers, or the chlamydia test is positive with tenesmus, doxycycline is extended to 21 days to cover LGV. He should be offered HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, partner treatment and retesting in about 3 months.

Takeaway: Empiric treatment for STI proctitis is ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, extended to 21 days of doxycycline when LGV is suspected.

whyNot.A: Penicillin treats syphilis, but RPR is nonreactive and there is no chancre; it does not cover gonorrhea or chlamydia.
whyNot.C: Mesalamine treats ulcerative proctitis; an infectious cause must be treated first in this setting.
whyNot.D: Metronidazole covers anaerobes, Trichomonas and amebiasis, not the bacterial STIs that cause proctitis.
whyNot.E: Valacyclovir is added for HSV proctitis, which causes vesicles or ulcers and severe pain; none are present.

items.objective: Choose empiric treatment for sexually transmitted proctitis.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had 4 days of throbbing perianal pain that is worse when he sits, and chills. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F); other vital signs are normal. There is a 3-cm fluctuant, erythematous, very tender swelling 2 cm lateral to the anal verge on the left. Digital rectal examination is limited by pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the pelvis before any intervention

options.label: C
options.html: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days without a procedure

options.label: E
options.html: Warm sitz baths with reassessment in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
A fluctuant, tender perianal swelling with fever is a perianal abscess. The treatment is prompt incision and drainage, close to the anal verge to keep any later fistula tract short. Because he has diabetes and systemic signs, antibiotics are added after drainage, but antibiotics alone do not cure an abscess. Imaging is needed only when a deep (intersphincteric or supralevator) abscess is suspected.

Takeaway: Anorectal abscess: drain it; antibiotics are an adjunct for cellulitis, systemic illness, diabetes or immunosuppression.

whyNot.B: A superficial perianal abscess is diagnosed clinically; MRI is for deep or complex disease.
whyNot.C: Antibiotics cannot penetrate an undrained abscess cavity and delay effective treatment.
whyNot.D: Fistulotomy is not done blindly at presentation; inflamed tissue hides the tract and risks sphincter injury.
whyNot.E: Sitz baths ease symptoms but waiting risks spread of infection, particularly with diabetes.

items.objective: Manage an acute perianal abscess.

items.stemHtml: The abscess is drained and the man recovers. Eight weeks later he reports intermittent purulent drainage from a small opening at the site of the incision. Examination under anesthesia shows a tract running from that external opening to an internal opening at the dentate line; the tract crosses only a small part of the distal internal sphincter and none of the external sphincter. His continence is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent drainage after an abscess is a fistula-in-ano from the infected anal crypt. A simple, low intersphincteric fistula involving little sphincter muscle, in a patient with normal continence, is cured by fistulotomy (laying open the tract), with a low risk of incontinence. Complex or high fistulas are instead treated with a seton and sphincter-sparing repair.

Takeaway: Simple low anal fistula: fistulotomy. Complex or high fistula: seton and sphincter-sparing techniques.

whyNot.A: Abdominoperineal resection is an operation for cancer, far beyond what a benign fistula needs.
whyNot.C: Antibiotics may reduce drainage briefly but do not eliminate an epithelialised tract.
whyNot.D: Drainage alone leaves the tract in place and the problem recurs.
whyNot.E: Nitroglycerin treats anal fissures, not fistula tracts.

items.objective: Treat a simple low anal fistula after abscess drainage.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman has had anal bleeding and discomfort for 3 months. Examination shows a firm 3.5-cm mass in the anal canal; biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Staging pelvic MRI and PET-CT show an enlarged, avid right superficial inguinal lymph node with no distant metastases. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Neoadjuvant FOLFOX followed by total mesorectal excision

options.label: E
options.html: Wide local excision with clear margins

items.explanationHtml:
Locoregional anal squamous cell carcinoma, including nodal disease, is treated with definitive chemoradiation using 5-fluorouracil (or capecitabine) plus mitomycin, the Nigro regimen. Most patients achieve complete response while keeping the sphincter. Response is assessed over the following months; abdominoperineal resection is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease.

Takeaway: Anal SCC is treated with chemoradiation (5-FU or capecitabine plus mitomycin); surgery is salvage.

whyNot.A: Abdominoperineal resection was replaced by chemoradiation as first-line therapy and is now salvage treatment.
whyNot.C: FOLFOX and total mesorectal excision are used for rectal adenocarcinoma, not anal SCC.
whyNot.D: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are used for metastatic or refractory anal cancer, not first-line curative treatment.
whyNot.E: Local excision is limited to small, well-differentiated perianal margin tumours, not a 3.5-cm canal tumour with nodal spread.

items.objective: Choose initial therapy for locoregional anal squamous cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has had intermittent rectal bleeding and a change in stool calibre. Colonoscopy shows a circumferential mass whose lower edge is 7 cm from the anal verge; biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases, and CEA has been drawn. Which of the following studies best determines the depth of tumour invasion, nodal involvement and the distance to the mesorectal fascia to guide neoadjuvant treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Rectal cancer is staged locally with high-resolution pelvic MRI. It shows T stage, mesorectal nodes, extramural venous invasion and the distance between the tumour and the mesorectal fascia, which predicts whether total mesorectal excision will achieve a clear circumferential margin. These findings decide between upfront surgery and neoadjuvant therapy, increasingly given as total neoadjuvant therapy.

Takeaway: Use pelvic MRI for local staging of rectal cancer; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis and CEA complete staging.

whyNot.A: Barium enema shows the luminal outline but cannot assess wall depth, nodes or the mesorectal fascia.
whyNot.C: PET-CT is not routine for rectal cancer staging and has poor spatial resolution for local tumour extent.
whyNot.D: Tattooing marks the lesion for surgery but gives no staging information.
whyNot.E: Transabdominal ultrasound cannot resolve the rectal wall layers deep in the pelvis.

items.objective: Select local staging imaging for rectal adenocarcinoma.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with long-standing constipation and straining has noticed a mass that protrudes from her anus with bowel movements for a year; she pushes it back in. She has mucus soiling and occasional leakage of stool. When she strains while squatting, a 7-cm reddish protrusion appears; it consists of full-thickness bowel wall with concentric circular mucosal folds. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A large protrusion of the full thickness of the rectal wall with concentric rings is full-thickness rectal prolapse (procidentia). It is commonest in older women with chronic straining and a weak pelvic floor and causes mucus discharge, bleeding and incontinence. Treatment is surgical: abdominal rectopexy for fit patients or a perineal procedure for frail patients. Colonoscopy is advised beforehand to exclude a lead point.

Takeaway: Concentric folds mean full-thickness rectal prolapse; radial folds mean hemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse.

whyNot.A: Anal carcinoma presents as a fixed, often ulcerated mass that does not prolapse and reduce.
whyNot.C: Mucosal prolapse involves only the mucosa, is smaller and shows radial folds.
whyNot.D: Prolapsed hemorrhoids form discrete cushions with radial grooves, not a concentric full-thickness ring.
whyNot.E: A polyp is a discrete lesion on a stalk, not a circumferential protrusion of the bowel wall.

items.objective: Distinguish full-thickness rectal prolapse from other protruding anal lesions.

items.stemHtml: A 4-day-old boy born at term to consanguineous parents has jaundice that has deepened steadily since day 2. He is breastfeeding well. Total bilirubin is 24 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL. Direct antiglobulin test is negative, and hemoglobin, reticulocyte count and the blood smear are normal. Intensive phototherapy is started, and a trial of phenobarbital produces no decrease in bilirubin. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Complete absence of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 activity

options.label: B
options.html: Defective canalicular secretion of conjugated bilirubin by MRP2

options.label: C
options.html: Deficiency of red cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

options.label: D
options.html: Deficient hepatic uptake through OATP1B1 and OATP1B3

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced UGT1A1 promoter activity with partial enzyme function

items.explanationHtml:
Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in the first days of life without hemolysis, unresponsive to phenobarbital, indicates Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I: autosomal recessive absence of UGT1A1 activity. Without conjugation, unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier and causes kernicterus. Treatment is daily phototherapy, with liver transplantation as definitive therapy. In type II, residual enzyme can be induced by phenobarbital and bilirubin falls.

Takeaway: Crigler-Najjar type I is absent UGT1A1 activity: severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that phenobarbital cannot lower.

whyNot.B: MRP2 defects (Dubin-Johnson) raise conjugated bilirubin, whereas his is almost entirely unconjugated.
whyNot.C: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis, but his smear, reticulocyte count and hemoglobin are normal.
whyNot.D: OATP1B1/1B3 deficiency (Rotor) causes mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
whyNot.E: Partial enzyme function describes Gilbert syndrome, which causes only mild, intermittent jaundice.

items.objective: Distinguish Crigler-Najjar type I from other inherited hyperbilirubinemias.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman develops mild jaundice 2 months after starting a combined oral contraceptive. She feels well. Total bilirubin is 4.0 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL; AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase and GGT are normal, and ultrasonography shows normal bile ducts. During a laparoscopy for an ovarian cyst a year earlier, the surgeon noted that her liver was strikingly dark, and a biopsy showed coarse dark pigment in centrilobular hepatocytes with normal architecture. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: D
options.html: Deficient sinusoidal uptake by OATP1B1 and OATP1B3

items.explanationHtml:
Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in MRP2 (ABCC2), the canalicular pump that exports conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions into bile. Conjugated bilirubin refluxes into blood, giving benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with otherwise normal liver tests. A dark pigment, probably from retained metabolites, makes the liver look black. Estrogen and pregnancy reduce canalicular excretion further and unmask jaundice.

Takeaway: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal enzymes and a black liver is Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect).

whyNot.A: Absent UGT1A1 causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from birth.
whyNot.B: Bile salt export pump defects cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis in children, with severe pruritus and liver injury.
whyNot.D: Rotor syndrome also causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, but the liver is normal in colour.
whyNot.E: Wilson disease causes hepatitis, hemolysis and neurologic disease, with abnormal aminotransferases.

items.objective: Identify the transporter defect in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has had declining school performance, irritability and a coarse hand tremor for 6 months, and his speech has become slurred. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the periphery of each cornea. ALT is 88 U/L. Serum ceruloplasmin is low and 24-hour urinary copper is high. The disorder is caused by a mutation in the gene encoding which of the following proteins?

options.label: A
options.html: Enterocyte copper-transporting ATPase that exports dietary copper into the blood

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase that moves copper into bile and onto ceruloplasmin

options.label: D
options.html: HFE protein that regulates hepatic hepcidin expression

items.explanationHtml:
Wilson disease results from autosomal recessive mutations in ATP7B on chromosome 13. In hepatocytes this ATPase loads copper onto apoceruloplasmin and exports excess copper into bile. When it fails, copper accumulates in the liver and spills into the blood, brain (basal ganglia), cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings) and red cells. Copper-free apoceruloplasmin is quickly degraded, so serum ceruloplasmin is low, while urinary copper excretion rises.

Takeaway: Wilson disease is an ATP7B defect: impaired biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading.

whyNot.A: This describes ATP7A, mutated in X-linked Menkes disease, which causes copper deficiency in infant boys.
whyNot.B: Ferroportin mutations cause a dominant form of iron overload.
whyNot.D: HFE mutations cause iron overload, not copper accumulation.
whyNot.E: Metallothionein is induced by zinc therapy for Wilson disease; it is not the mutated protein.

items.objective: Identify the gene product defective in Wilson disease.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man who has never smoked has had progressive exertional dyspnea for a year. CT of the chest shows panacinar emphysema predominantly in the lower lobes, and ALT is persistently 70 U/L. A liver biopsy shows round eosinophilic cytoplasmic globules in periportal hepatocytes that stain with periodic acid-Schiff after diastase digestion. Which of the following best explains his liver injury?

options.label: B
options.html: Glycogen storage from a deficient debranching enzyme

options.label: D
options.html: Misfolded protein polymerising within the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: E
options.html: Unopposed neutrophil elastase digesting hepatic matrix

items.explanationHtml:
In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (commonly PiZZ), the mutant protein misfolds and polymerises in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes instead of being secreted. The retained polymers appear as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules and injure the cell, leading to hepatitis, cirrhosis and HCC: a toxic gain of function. Low circulating levels leave lung elastin unprotected from neutrophil elastase, causing early, basal panacinar emphysema: a loss of function.

Takeaway: In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, liver disease comes from retained misfolded protein; lung disease comes from lack of circulating inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Copper accumulation is the mechanism of Wilson disease.
whyNot.B: Glycogen is removed by diastase, so diastase-resistant globules exclude glycogen.
whyNot.C: Iron-driven oxidative injury is the mechanism of hemochromatosis, shown by Prussian blue staining.
whyNot.E: Unopposed elastase explains the emphysema, not the liver injury.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of liver injury in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department because she has been confused and sleepy for 2 days. She has asterixis. A urinary tract infection is found and treated, and she is also started on oral lactulose. Which of the following best describes how lactulose improves her mental status?

options.label: A
options.html: Antagonism at the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors

options.label: B
options.html: Bacterial fermentation to acids that trap ammonia as ammonium in the colon

options.label: C
options.html: Increased dopaminergic signalling in the basal ganglia

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase

options.label: E
options.html: Provision of ornithine to drive the hepatic urea cycle

items.explanationHtml:
Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide that is not absorbed in the small intestine. Colonic bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids, acidifying the lumen. Ammonia (NH3), which diffuses freely, is protonated to ammonium (NH4+), which cannot cross membranes and is excreted. Its osmotic laxative effect also shortens transit time. The dose is titrated to two or three soft stools a day.

Takeaway: Lactulose lowers blood ammonia by colonic acidification (NH3 trapped as NH4+) and catharsis.

whyNot.A: Flumazenil acts here and may transiently improve encephalopathy but is not a standard therapy.
whyNot.C: Dopaminergic drugs are not part of encephalopathy treatment, and lactulose has no central action.
whyNot.D: This is the mechanism of rifaximin, which is added for recurrent encephalopathy.
whyNot.E: L-ornithine L-aspartate works this way; it is not lactulose's mechanism.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man who has drunk about a litre of vodka daily for years is admitted with 3 weeks of jaundice, fever and right upper quadrant pain. The liver is enlarged and tender. AST is 186 U/L and ALT 72 U/L. A transjugular liver biopsy shows swollen, ballooned hepatocytes containing ropy, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions, surrounded by neutrophils, with perivenular fibrosis. The inclusions are composed mainly of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Aggregated keratin intermediate filaments bound to ubiquitin

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatitis B surface antigen in smooth endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: E
options.html: Retained polymers of misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin

items.explanationHtml:
The biopsy shows alcohol-associated hepatitis. Mallory-Denk bodies are tangled aggregates of misfolded keratin 8 and 18 intermediate filaments complexed with ubiquitin and p62, found in ballooned hepatocytes and often surrounded by neutrophils. The AST:ALT ratio above 2 with modest absolute values is typical of alcohol-associated injury. Mallory-Denk bodies are characteristic but also occur in MASH, Wilson disease and chronic cholestasis.

Takeaway: Mallory-Denk bodies are ubiquitinated keratin intermediate filament aggregates, typical of alcohol-associated hepatitis.

whyNot.B: Hemosiderin is golden-brown and stains with Prussian blue.
whyNot.C: HBsAg produces finely granular ground-glass cytoplasm in chronic hepatitis B.
whyNot.D: Lipofuscin is a fine brown wear-and-tear pigment, not an eosinophilic aggregate in ballooned cells.
whyNot.E: Alpha-1 antitrypsin forms round PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules, not ropy inclusions with neutrophils.

items.objective: Recognise the composition of Mallory-Denk bodies in alcohol-associated hepatitis.

items.stemHtml:
A 44-year-old woman who drank about 10 standard drinks daily until 10 days ago has 3 weeks of progressive jaundice, anorexia and abdominal discomfort. She is alert and oriented without asterixis. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F). The liver is enlarged and tender, and there is a small amount of ascites. Blood and urine cultures, chest radiograph and diagnostic paracentesis show no infection, and she has had no GI bleeding. Results:

TestResult
AST212 U/L (12-38 U/L)
ALT84 U/L (10-40 U/L)
Alkaline phosphatase164 U/L (25-100 U/L)
Bilirubin, total14.2 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL)
Bilirubin, direct9.6 mg/dL (0.0-0.3 mg/dL)
Albumin2.7 g/dL (3.5-5.5 g/dL)
PT23 s (control 12 s)
INR2.0 (0.8-1.1)
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mg/dL)
Leukocytes14,600/mm3 (4,500-11,000/mm3)
Platelets124,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000/mm3)

In addition to abstinence support and nutrition, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
This is severe alcohol-associated hepatitis: Maddrey discriminant function = 4.6 × (23 − 12) + 14.2, about 65, well above 32, and her MELD is above 20. Infection, GI bleeding and kidney injury have been excluded, so prednisolone 40 mg daily is indicated, with the Lille score on day 7 deciding whether to continue for 28 days. Steroids improve short-term survival in this group.

Takeaway: Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (Maddrey 32 or more, or MELD above 20) without infection or bleeding is treated with prednisolone, reassessed by the Lille score at day 7.

whyNot.A: TNF inhibitors increased infections and mortality in alcohol-associated hepatitis.
whyNot.B: Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy, which she does not have.
whyNot.C: Pentoxifylline did not improve survival in large trials and is no longer recommended.
whyNot.E: Ursodiol treats primary biliary cholangitis and has no role in alcohol-associated hepatitis.

items.objective: Calculate severity and choose therapy for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with obesity (BMI 34 kg/m2), type 2 diabetes and hypertension has an ALT of 62 U/L and AST of 41 U/L on routine testing. He drinks two beers a week. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody are negative, and ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal. Platelet count is 212,000/mm3. Ultrasonography shows diffuse hepatic steatosis with a smooth liver surface and normal spleen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat liver enzymes in 1 year with no other testing

items.explanationHtml:
He has MASLD: steatosis with cardiometabolic risk factors and no other cause. The prognosis depends on fibrosis stage, so the next step is noninvasive risk stratification, starting with FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets). A low value supports primary-care management with repeat assessment; an indeterminate or high value leads to transient elastography or an enhanced liver fibrosis test and hepatology referral. Lifestyle change and cardiometabolic treatment proceed in parallel.

Takeaway: In MASLD, risk-stratify fibrosis with FIB-4 first, then elastography if FIB-4 is not low.

whyNot.B: CT adds radiation and contrast but does not stage fibrosis better than ultrasound.
whyNot.C: Biopsy is reserved for indeterminate noninvasive results or diagnostic doubt.
whyNot.D: Ignoring fibrosis risk misses patients with advanced fibrosis, who often have only mildly raised enzymes.
whyNot.E: Ceruloplasmin screens for Wilson disease, which is very unlikely at 52 with an obvious metabolic cause.

items.objective: Risk-stratify fibrosis in a patient with MASLD.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the clinic because her 36-year-old brother has just been diagnosed with hemochromatosis and is homozygous for the HFE C282Y mutation. She feels well, takes no medications and has regular menstrual periods. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Liver biopsy with hepatic iron quantification

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the liver to quantify iron

options.label: D
options.html: Reassurance and testing only if symptoms develop

options.label: E
options.html: Transferrin saturation, ferritin and HFE genotyping

items.explanationHtml:
First-degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote should be screened with iron studies and HFE genotyping. A sibling has about a one-in-four chance of also being homozygous. Premenopausal women often have normal iron indices because of menstrual losses, which is why genotyping matters. If she is homozygous with raised ferritin, phlebotomy is started; homozygotes with normal ferritin are monitored.

Takeaway: Screen first-degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote with transferrin saturation, ferritin and HFE genotyping.

whyNot.A: Phlebotomy is started only when iron overload is confirmed.
whyNot.B: Biopsy is invasive and is used to stage fibrosis in patients with very high ferritin or abnormal enzymes, not for screening.
whyNot.C: MRI quantifies established iron overload but does not identify carriers or at-risk homozygotes.
whyNot.D: Waiting for symptoms allows irreversible organ damage, such as cirrhosis, that early phlebotomy prevents.

items.objective: Screen first-degree relatives for HFE hemochromatosis.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of right upper quadrant pain and increasing abdominal girth. She has had pruritus after hot showers for a year. The liver is enlarged and tender, and there is shifting dullness. Jugular venous pressure is normal and there is no peripheral edema. Hemoglobin is 17.9 g/dL and platelet count 640,000/mm3. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL and ascitic total protein of 3.2 g/dL, with a low neutrophil count. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Doppler ultrasonography of the liver and hepatic veins

items.explanationHtml:
Tender hepatomegaly and ascites with a high SAAG and high ascitic protein indicate postsinusoidal outflow obstruction. With erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis and aquagenic pruritus suggesting polycythemia vera (likely JAK2 V617F), Budd-Chiari syndrome is the leading diagnosis. Doppler ultrasonography is the best initial test, showing absent or reversed hepatic venous flow; CT or MRI venography confirms. Treatment begins with anticoagulation and management of the myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Takeaway: Suspected Budd-Chiari syndrome is evaluated first with Doppler ultrasonography of the hepatic veins.

whyNot.B: Wilson disease does not explain polycythemia and a high-protein, high-SAAG ascites.
whyNot.C: Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when imaging can show hepatic venous obstruction.
whyNot.D: Cardiac ascites shares the SAAG and protein pattern, but normal jugular venous pressure and no edema make it unlikely.
whyNot.E: Endoscopy screens for varices later but does not make the diagnosis.

items.objective: Choose the initial imaging study for suspected Budd-Chiari syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of 10 days of jaundice and fatigue; today she has become drowsy and confused. She has no known liver disease, takes no medications or supplements, and denies acetaminophen use; her serum acetaminophen level is undetectable. She has asterixis and scleral icterus. Hemoglobin is 8.7 g/dL with an elevated reticulocyte count and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Total bilirubin is 23 mg/dL (direct 9.4 mg/dL), AST 196 U/L, ALT 84 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 18 U/L and INR 3.0. Tests for hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and core IgM, and hepatitis C RNA are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
She has acute liver failure (INR at least 1.5 with encephalopathy and no prior liver disease). Clues to Wilson disease: young age, Coombs-negative hemolysis from copper released by dying hepatocytes, an unusually low alkaline phosphatase, and AST greater than ALT with only modest aminotransferase levels. These features help separate fulminant Wilson disease from other causes before copper studies return.

Takeaway: Acute liver failure in a young patient with Coombs-negative hemolysis and a very low alkaline phosphatase suggests Wilson disease.

whyNot.A: Acetaminophen injury produces aminotransferases in the thousands; her level is undetectable and she denies use.
whyNot.B: Hepatitis E causes marked aminotransferase elevation and is not associated with hemolysis and a low alkaline phosphatase.
whyNot.C: Autoimmune hepatitis can cause liver failure but does not explain Coombs-negative hemolysis and a very low alkaline phosphatase.
whyNot.D: Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver function.

items.objective: Recognise Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure.

items.stemHtml: Slit-lamp examination shows Kayser-Fleischer rings, and serum ceruloplasmin is low, confirming Wilson disease. Over the next 12 hours she becomes more somnolent and her INR rises to 3.6. She is transferred to the intensive care unit. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure with worsening encephalopathy and coagulopathy is almost uniformly fatal without transplantation, and chelation acts too slowly to rescue the liver. She should be listed urgently at a transplant centre; measures such as plasma exchange or dialysis-based copper removal are only bridges. A new liver corrects the underlying ATP7B defect, so the disease does not recur.

Takeaway: Fulminant Wilson disease requires urgent liver transplantation; chelation is for chronic disease.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids have no role in Wilson disease and increase infection risk.
whyNot.B: N-acetylcysteine is used in acetaminophen-induced failure and sometimes in other early-stage causes, but it does not replace transplantation here.
whyNot.D: Penicillamine takes weeks to lower copper stores and cannot reverse acute liver failure.
whyNot.E: Zinc blocks intestinal absorption and is used for maintenance or presymptomatic disease.

items.objective: Manage Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has lost 38 kg (84 lb) in the 7 months since a sleeve gastrectomy. She now has episodes of steady right upper quadrant pain lasting about 2 hours after large meals. Her hemoglobin and liver tests are normal. Ultrasound shows several mobile, shadowing stones in the gallbladder and a normal-caliber bile duct. Which of the following best explains the formation of her stones?

options.label: B
options.html: Bile supersaturated with cholesterol plus gallbladder stasis

options.label: C
options.html: Calcium carbonate precipitating from alkaline gallbladder bile

options.label: D
options.html: Increased unconjugated bilirubin load from chronic hemolysis

options.label: E
options.html: Parasite ova acting as a nidus for stones within the ducts

items.explanationHtml:
Rapid weight loss mobilizes cholesterol from adipose tissue and increases hepatic cholesterol secretion into bile, while reduced food intake lowers CCK-driven gallbladder emptying. Bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol relative to bile acids and phosphatidylcholine, and stasis gives crystals time to nucleate and grow into cholesterol stones. Prophylactic ursodiol is sometimes used after bariatric surgery for this reason.

Takeaway: Rapid weight loss causes cholesterol stones through cholesterol supersaturation and gallbladder hypomotility.

whyNot.A: Bacterial deconjugation of bilirubin produces brown pigment stones in infected, stagnant ducts, not gallbladder stones after weight loss.
whyNot.C: Calcium carbonate stones are rare and are not the mechanism linked to rapid weight loss.
whyNot.D: Hemolysis causes black pigment stones; her hemoglobin is normal and there is no hemolytic history.
whyNot.E: Parasites such as liver flukes favour brown pigment stones in the bile ducts, mostly in endemic regions.

items.objective: Explain why rapid weight loss predisposes to cholesterol gallstones.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain. Abdominal radiograph shows several small radiopaque densities in the right upper quadrant, and ultrasound confirms multiple small gallstones. Which of the following is the main constituent of these stones?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic hemolysis delivers a large load of bilirubin to the liver. Unconjugated bilirubin in bile precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate, forming small, dark, often radiopaque black pigment stones in the gallbladder. Children with hemolytic anemias such as sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis develop gallstones at an unusually young age.

Takeaway: Chronic hemolysis causes black pigment (calcium bilirubinate) gallstones, often radiopaque.

whyNot.B: Calcium oxalate is a kidney stone constituent, increased in fat malabsorption, not a gallstone component.
whyNot.C: Cholesterol stones are typical of adults with metabolic or hormonal risk factors and are usually radiolucent.
whyNot.D: Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones form in the urinary tract with urease-producing infection.
whyNot.E: Uric acid stones form in the urinary tract and are radiolucent.

items.objective: Identify the gallstone type produced by chronic hemolysis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who grew up in a rural river region of southern China has had three episodes of fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain over 2 years. MRCP shows strictured and dilated intrahepatic ducts containing filling defects. At ERCP, soft, brown, crumbly stones are removed, and stool microscopy shows small operculated ova. Which of the following processes most directly produced these stones?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial hydrolysis of conjugated bilirubin in bile

options.label: B
options.html: Chronic hemolysis with excess bilirubin production

options.label: C
options.html: Gallbladder hypomotility from reduced CCK release

items.explanationHtml:
Brown pigment stones form in the bile ducts when bile is stagnant and infected. Bacteria (and some parasites) release β-glucuronidase, which hydrolyzes bilirubin glucuronide back to unconjugated bilirubin; this precipitates with calcium and fatty acid soaps. Liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis, acquired from raw freshwater fish, cause chronic duct inflammation, strictures and recurrent cholangitis, and raise the risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Takeaway: Brown pigment stones form in infected ducts when bacterial β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin.
