whyNot.B: Hemolysis produces black pigment stones in sterile gallbladder bile.
whyNot.C: Gallbladder hypomotility contributes to cholesterol stones and sludge in the gallbladder, not intrahepatic brown stones.
whyNot.D: Reduced UGT activity (as in Gilbert or Crigler-Najjar syndrome) causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not duct stones with infection.
whyNot.E: Cholesterol supersaturation produces cholesterol stones in the gallbladder, not soft brown duct stones.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of brown pigment stone formation.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman has had generalized itching and fatigue for 8 months. She also reports dry eyes and a dry mouth. Serum alkaline phosphatase is 412 U/L (25-100), GGT 290 U/L (8-38), ALT 52 U/L (10-40) and total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (0.1-1.0). Ultrasound shows a normal liver and nondilated bile ducts. A serum antibody characteristic of her most likely liver disease is directed against which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Cholestatic liver tests with normal large ducts in a middle-aged woman with sicca symptoms suggests primary biliary cholangitis. Its hallmark antimitochondrial antibody recognizes the E2 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The disease destroys small interlobular bile ducts through lymphocytic and often granulomatous inflammation.

Takeaway: Antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC target the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

whyNot.B: Anti-smooth muscle (anti-actin) antibodies support type 1 autoimmune hepatitis, which gives a hepatocellular pattern.
whyNot.C: Anti-LKM1 antibodies against CYP2D6 characterize type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, mostly in children.
whyNot.D: Atypical p-ANCA is found in many patients with PSC and ulcerative colitis but is not specific.
whyNot.E: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies indicate celiac disease, which can cause mild transaminase elevation but not this pattern.

items.objective: Identify the target antigen of the antimitochondrial antibody in PBC.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with a 7-year history of ulcerative colitis has a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase. MRCP shows multifocal short strictures alternating with mildly dilated segments in both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. A liver biopsy is obtained during evaluation. Which of the following histologic findings is most characteristic of his condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Concentric periductal fibrosis around bile ducts

options.label: B
options.html: Granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts

options.label: D
options.html: Interface hepatitis with a dense plasma cell infiltrate

items.explanationHtml:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis produces inflammation and concentric, layered (onion-skin) fibrosis around medium and large bile ducts, eventually replacing ducts with fibrous cords. The resulting strictures and dilations give the beaded cholangiogram. The strong link with ulcerative colitis, male predominance and cholangiocarcinoma risk are classic.

Takeaway: PSC shows onion-skin periductal fibrosis and is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis.

whyNot.B: Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular ducts is the florid duct lesion of primary biliary cholangitis.
whyNot.C: Ground-glass hepatocytes reflect HBsAg accumulation in chronic hepatitis B.
whyNot.D: Interface hepatitis with plasma cells is typical of autoimmune hepatitis.
whyNot.E: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules are the hallmark of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

items.objective: Recognize the histology of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with severe hypertriglyceridemia has taken gemfibrozil for 4 years. He now has recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain, and ultrasound shows multiple radiolucent gallstones. Inhibition of which of the following by his medication most likely contributed to stone formation?
items.explanationHtml:
Fibrates activate PPAR-α, which increases lipoprotein lipase activity and lowers triglycerides. They also inhibit cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts cholesterol to bile acids, and increase biliary cholesterol secretion. Less bile acid and more cholesterol in bile favours cholesterol supersaturation and stone formation.

Takeaway: Fibrates cause cholesterol gallstones by inhibiting 7α-hydroxylase and raising biliary cholesterol.

whyNot.B: HMG-CoA reductase is inhibited by statins, which are not associated with gallstones.
whyNot.C: Fibrates increase, rather than inhibit, lipoprotein lipase activity.
whyNot.D: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein is inhibited by lomitapide, which causes hepatic steatosis, not the fibrate effect.
whyNot.E: Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 is blocked by ezetimibe to reduce intestinal cholesterol absorption; gallstones are not its classic effect.

items.objective: Explain how fibrates predispose to cholesterol gallstones.

items.stemHtml: In a study of postprandial physiology, healthy volunteers eat a high-fat meal. Within 30 minutes, ultrasound shows the gallbladder contracting, and manometry shows relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. The hormone mainly responsible for both responses is secreted by which of the following cells?

options.label: A
options.html: D cells of the pancreatic islets

options.label: B
options.html: G cells of the gastric antrum

options.label: C
options.html: I cells of the duodenum and jejunum

options.label: D
options.html: K cells of the duodenum and jejunum

items.explanationHtml:
Fatty acids and amino acids in the proximal small bowel stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin. CCK contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and stimulates acinar enzyme secretion, delivering bile and enzymes together to digest fat. Patients on prolonged parenteral nutrition lack this stimulus and develop sludge.

Takeaway: CCK from duodenal and jejunal I cells contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

whyNot.A: D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits gallbladder contraction and many GI secretions.
whyNot.B: G cells release gastrin, which stimulates gastric acid secretion.
whyNot.D: K cells release glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide, which enhances insulin release.
whyNot.E: S cells release secretin, which mainly drives pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion.

items.objective: Identify the source and actions of cholecystokinin.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has had several episodes of epigastric pain, two of them with mild jaundice and one with a raised serum lipase. Examination between episodes shows a vague right upper quadrant fullness. MRCP shows fusiform dilation of the extrahepatic common bile duct; the pancreatic duct joins the bile duct well above the duodenal wall, forming a long common channel. Which of the following mechanisms is thought to underlie her duct abnormality?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoimmune destruction of the interlobular ducts

options.label: B
options.html: Ductal plate malformation of the intrahepatic ducts

options.label: C
options.html: Extrinsic duct compression by an annular pancreas

options.label: D
options.html: Inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic ducts

options.label: E
options.html: Reflux of pancreatic secretions into the bile duct

items.explanationHtml:
This is a choledochal cyst. An anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction lets pancreatic juice reflux into the bile duct, where activated enzymes injure and weaken the duct wall, leading to dilation. The cyst predisposes to stasis, stones, cholangitis, pancreatitis and cholangiocarcinoma, so it is treated by excision with a hepaticojejunostomy.

Takeaway: Choledochal cysts are linked to an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction that lets pancreatic juice reflux into the bile duct.

whyNot.A: Autoimmune destruction of interlobular ducts describes primary biliary cholangitis in adults.
whyNot.B: Ductal plate malformation causes Caroli disease, which affects the intrahepatic ducts rather than the extrahepatic duct.
whyNot.C: Annular pancreas causes duodenal obstruction in infancy and does not produce fusiform bile duct dilation with a long common channel.
whyNot.D: Inflammatory obliteration of extrahepatic ducts is biliary atresia, which presents in early infancy with persistent jaundice and acholic stools.

items.objective: Describe the proposed pathogenesis of choledochal cysts.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old woman has had 3 days of intermittent cramping abdominal pain, then persistent vomiting and distension. She had several untreated episodes of right upper quadrant pain over the past year. Abdominal radiograph shows dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels, branching air over the liver, and a 3-cm laminated density in the right lower quadrant. By which route did the obstructing object most likely enter the bowel?

options.label: A
options.html: A fistula between gallbladder and duodenum

options.label: B
options.html: Erosion from the cystic duct into the stomach

options.label: C
options.html: Erosion into the hepatic flexure of the colon

options.label: D
options.html: Through a sphincterotomy made at prior ERCP

options.label: E
options.html: Through the ampulla of Vater after duct passage

items.explanationHtml:
This is gallstone ileus. Repeated inflammation adheres the gallbladder to the duodenum, and a large stone erodes through both walls to form a cholecystoduodenal fistula. Air then enters the biliary tree (pneumobilia), and the stone passes down the small bowel until it impacts at the narrowest point, usually the terminal ileum near the ileocecal valve. Stones small enough to pass through the ampulla rarely obstruct the bowel.

Takeaway: Gallstone ileus: a large stone enters the duodenum through a cholecystoenteric fistula and impacts at the terminal ileum.

whyNot.B: Cholecystogastric fistulas are uncommon and would not explain a stone impacted in the right lower quadrant small bowel as well as a duodenal fistula.
whyNot.C: A cholecystocolonic fistula delivers the stone to the colon, which is wide enough that small-bowel obstruction would not result.
whyNot.D: She has no history of ERCP, and a stone passing through a sphincterotomy is usually small.
whyNot.E: Stones that pass through the ampulla are small enough to traverse the bowel and seldom cause obstruction.

items.objective: Explain the pathogenesis of gallstone ileus.

items.stemHtml:
A 47-year-old woman has had 2 days of right upper quadrant pain, nausea and dark urine. She has no chills. Examination shows scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness without guarding. Results are shown.

TestResult
Temperature37.2°C (99.0°F)
Pulse; blood pressure84/min; 128/78 mm Hg
Leukocytes9,800/mm3 (4,500-11,000)
Bilirubin, total4.6 mg/dL (0.1-1.0)
Bilirubin, direct3.5 mg/dL (0.0-0.3)
Alkaline phosphatase340 U/L (25-100)
ALT210 U/L (10-40)
Lipase90 U/L (0-160)
UltrasoundMultiple gallstones; gallbladder wall normal; common bile duct 11 mm with a shadowing echogenic focus in its distal segment

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone removal

items.explanationHtml:
A stone seen in a dilated common bile duct with cholestatic liver tests places her at high likelihood of choledocholithiasis. Confirmatory imaging adds nothing; she needs a therapeutic procedure. ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction clears the duct, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy should follow during the same admission. She has no fever or hypotension, so this is uncomplicated choledocholithiasis rather than cholangitis.

Takeaway: When ultrasound shows a common bile duct stone, go straight to ERCP for removal, then cholecystectomy.

whyNot.B: A HIDA scan evaluates cystic duct patency in suspected cholecystitis and would delay treatment of a visible duct stone.
whyNot.C: Cholecystectomy alone would leave the obstructing common duct stone in place.
whyNot.D: MRCP is used when the likelihood of a duct stone is intermediate; here the stone has already been seen.
whyNot.E: Percutaneous transhepatic access is a fallback when ERCP fails or anatomy prevents it, not the first choice.

items.objective: Choose ERCP for a high-likelihood common bile duct stone.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is in the intensive care unit on day 12 after 45% total body surface area burns. He is mechanically ventilated, sedated and receiving parenteral nutrition. He develops a new fever of 39.0°C (102.2°F), and the leukocyte count rises to 18,000/mm3. The abdomen is mildly distended, with apparent discomfort on palpation of the right upper quadrant. Chest radiograph and urinalysis are unchanged. Bedside ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a 6-mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and layering sludge, without stones or bile duct dilation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Critical illness, burns, ventilation and parenteral nutrition cause gallbladder stasis and ischemia. Fever, leukocytosis and an ultrasound showing a distended, thick-walled gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid but no stones indicate acute acalculous cholecystitis, which progresses to gangrene and perforation more often than calculous disease.

Takeaway: A febrile ICU patient with a thick-walled, distended gallbladder and no stones has acalculous cholecystitis until proven otherwise.

whyNot.B: Cholangitis requires an obstructed, infected duct; the duct is not dilated and there is no cholestatic picture described.
whyNot.C: Choledocholithiasis produces a duct stone or dilated duct with cholestasis, neither of which is present.
whyNot.D: Emphysematous cholecystitis shows gas in the gallbladder wall or lumen, which is not described.
whyNot.E: A liver abscess would appear as a hepatic collection rather than an inflamed gallbladder.

items.objective: Diagnose acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item is diagnosed with acute acalculous cholecystitis. Blood cultures are drawn and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam is started. Over the next 6 hours his mean arterial pressure falls and he now requires norepinephrine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibiotics alone with ultrasound in 1 week

options.label: D
options.html: Oral ursodiol to dissolve the sludge

items.explanationHtml:
Acalculous cholecystitis needs source control in addition to antibiotics. In a patient in septic shock on vasopressors, operative risk is prohibitive, so the gallbladder is decompressed with an image-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy at the bedside. Cholecystectomy can be considered later if he recovers and remains a candidate.

Takeaway: Unstable patients with acute cholecystitis, especially acalculous disease in the ICU, are treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics alone fail to control an inflamed, ischemic gallbladder that is likely to become gangrenous.
whyNot.B: Emergency surgery in a vasopressor-dependent burn patient carries very high risk when percutaneous drainage can control the source.
whyNot.C: ERCP drains the common bile duct, not the gallbladder, and there is no duct obstruction.
whyNot.D: Ursodiol acts over months and plays no role in acute infection.

items.objective: Select percutaneous cholecystostomy for an unstable patient with cholecystitis.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man with ulcerative colitis diagnosed 8 years ago has a raised alkaline phosphatase on routine monitoring, confirmed on repeat testing at 285 U/L (25-100). GGT is 240 U/L (8-38), ALT 64 U/L (10-40) and total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL (0.1-1.0). He has no symptoms. Antimitochondrial antibodies are negative. Ultrasound shows a normal liver without bile duct dilation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A persistent cholestatic pattern in a patient with ulcerative colitis strongly suggests primary sclerosing cholangitis. MRCP is the noninvasive test of choice and shows multifocal strictures with intervening dilations. Ultrasound is often normal in early PSC because the ducts are not uniformly dilated.

Takeaway: Suspected PSC is diagnosed with MRCP; ERCP is reserved for treatment or tissue sampling.

whyNot.A: CT does not define subtle duct strictures as well as MRCP.
whyNot.B: ERCP can show the same findings but risks pancreatitis and cholangitis, so it is not used for diagnosis alone.
whyNot.C: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assesses gallbladder function and cannot define duct strictures.
whyNot.E: Biopsy is used when small-duct PSC or an overlap syndrome is suspected after a normal MRCP, not as the first test.

items.objective: Choose MRCP to diagnose primary sclerosing cholangitis.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman has had fatigue and itching for a year. Alkaline phosphatase is 330 U/L (25-100), GGT is raised, transaminases are slightly increased and bilirubin is normal. Antimitochondrial antibodies are positive at a high titer, and ultrasound shows normal bile ducts. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy to slow progression of her liver disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Cholestatic liver tests with a positive antimitochondrial antibody establish primary biliary cholangitis without a biopsy. Ursodeoxycholic acid, taken lifelong, improves liver biochemistry, delays progression and improves transplant-free survival in patients who respond. Response is reassessed after about a year; incomplete responders are referred for second-line therapy.

Takeaway: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line, lifelong therapy for primary biliary cholangitis.

whyNot.A: Azathioprine is a maintenance drug for autoimmune hepatitis, not PBC.
whyNot.B: Cholestyramine relieves cholestatic pruritus but does not slow the disease.
whyNot.C: Methotrexate has not been shown to improve outcomes in PBC and is not standard therapy.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids treat autoimmune hepatitis but do not improve outcomes in PBC and worsen bone loss.

items.objective: Select first-line therapy for primary biliary cholangitis.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 19 weeks' gestation has had 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F) and pulse 104/min. She has right upper quadrant tenderness with inspiratory arrest on palpation. Leukocyte count is 15,500/mm3; bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are within the normal range for pregnancy. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid with a normal common bile duct. Fetal heart tones are normal. Intravenous fluids and antibiotics are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibiotics, with surgery deferred until after delivery

options.label: B
options.html: ERCP with sphincterotomy and duct clearance

options.label: D
options.html: Oral ursodiol for the remainder of the pregnancy

options.label: E
options.html: Percutaneous cholecystostomy tube for the pregnancy

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute calculous cholecystitis in the second trimester. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is safe in pregnancy and is recommended over nonoperative management, because conservative treatment often fails and recurrent attacks increase the risk of preterm labor and fetal loss. Surgery is performed with obstetric involvement and fetal monitoring.

Takeaway: Acute cholecystitis in pregnancy is treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the admission, in any trimester.

whyNot.A: Deferring surgery until after delivery carries a high rate of recurrent attacks and complications during the pregnancy.
whyNot.B: ERCP treats common duct stones; her duct and liver tests are normal.
whyNot.D: Ursodiol works slowly, dissolves only some stones and does not treat acute inflammation.
whyNot.E: Cholecystostomy is reserved for patients too unstable or comorbid for surgery, which she is not.

items.objective: Manage acute cholecystitis during pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: In a physiology study, a 30-year-old volunteer has dilute hydrochloric acid infused into the duodenum through a tube. Within minutes, the volume and bicarbonate concentration of pancreatic juice collected from the duodenum rise sharply while its enzyme content changes little. The hormone mediating this response acts mainly on which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Acinar cells, to release zymogen granules

options.label: B
options.html: Ductal epithelial cells, to secrete bicarbonate

options.label: C
options.html: Gallbladder smooth muscle, to cause contraction

options.label: D
options.html: Gastric parietal cells, to raise acid output

options.label: E
options.html: Islet beta cells, to increase insulin release

items.explanationHtml:
Acid in the duodenum releases secretin from S cells. Secretin acts on pancreatic ductal cells, raising cAMP and driving bicarbonate secretion through CFTR and apical chloride-bicarbonate exchange. The result is a large volume of alkaline juice that neutralizes gastric acid and lets pancreatic enzymes work. Enzyme output is driven mainly by CCK, not secretin.

Takeaway: Secretin, released by duodenal acid, stimulates bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreatic ductal cells.

whyNot.A: Acinar enzyme release is mainly driven by CCK and vagal acetylcholine.
whyNot.C: Gallbladder contraction is caused by CCK in response to fat and protein.
whyNot.D: Secretin inhibits, rather than stimulates, gastric acid secretion.
whyNot.E: Insulin release is stimulated by glucose and incretins, not by duodenal acid.

items.objective: Describe the action of secretin on the exocrine pancreas.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy has chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain and generalized edema. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL (3.5-5.5). Sweat chloride is normal. Duodenal fluid collected after stimulation contains normal amounts of trypsinogen but almost no trypsin activity; adding a protease normally found on the duodenal brush border restores the activity of all pancreatic proteases in the sample. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient?
items.explanationHtml:
Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidases and procolipase. Without it, protein digestion fails despite normal pancreatic output, causing malabsorption, hypoproteinemia and edema in infancy. A normal sweat test makes cystic fibrosis unlikely.

Takeaway: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen, which then activates the other pancreatic zymogens.

whyNot.A: Carboxypeptidase A is itself a zymogen product activated by trypsin and does not activate trypsinogen.
whyNot.B: Colipase anchors lipase to fat droplets; its lack would cause steatorrhea but not loss of protease activity.
whyNot.C: Elastase is a downstream protease activated by trypsin.
whyNot.E: Lactase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhea after milk sugar but not failure of protease activation or hypoproteinemia.

items.objective: Explain the role of enteropeptidase in protease activation.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl has had four attacks of acute pancreatitis since age 9. She abstains from alcohol, and serum calcium and triglycerides are normal. Her father and a paternal aunt had similar attacks starting in childhood. CT shows small pancreatic calcifications. Genetic testing shows a heterozygous gain-of-function variant in PRSS1. Which of the following best explains how this variant causes her disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Activated trypsin resists inactivation in acinar cells

options.label: C
options.html: Defective ductal chloride and bicarbonate secretion

options.label: D
options.html: Deficient lipoprotein lipase activity in plasma

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of the main intracellular trypsin inhibitor

items.explanationHtml:
PRSS1 encodes cationic trypsinogen. Gain-of-function variants make trypsinogen activate more readily or make trypsin resistant to autolysis, so once activation begins inside the acinar cell it cannot be shut off. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. Recurrent attacks progress to chronic pancreatitis, and the lifetime risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma is markedly increased.

Takeaway: PRSS1 gain-of-function variants cause autosomal dominant hereditary pancreatitis by leaving activated trypsin uncontrolled.

whyNot.B: Autoantibody-mediated injury suggests autoimmune pancreatitis, not a dominantly inherited trypsinogen variant.
whyNot.C: Defective ductal chloride and bicarbonate secretion is the mechanism of CFTR-related disease.
whyNot.D: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes pancreatitis through extreme hypertriglyceridemia, and her triglycerides are normal.
whyNot.E: Loss of the intracellular trypsin inhibitor describes SPINK1 variants, which mostly modify risk rather than cause dominant disease.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of PRSS1-related hereditary pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old boy is admitted for the third time with acute pancreatitis. He has crops of small yellow papules with red halos on his buttocks and elbows. Funduscopy shows creamy white retinal vessels. A fasting blood sample is milky, and serum triglycerides are 3,800 mg/dL; LDL cholesterol is 96 mg/dL (below 130). A deficiency of which of the following is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome results from deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or its activator apolipoprotein C-II. Chylomicrons cannot be cleared, producing extreme hypertriglyceridemia with milky plasma, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis and recurrent pancreatitis from childhood. It is managed with a very-low-fat diet; it does not cause premature atherosclerosis as LDL-driven disorders do.

Takeaway: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes chylomicronemia, eruptive xanthomas and recurrent pancreatitis in childhood.

whyNot.A: Defective apolipoprotein B-100 impairs LDL clearance and raises LDL cholesterol.
whyNot.B: Apolipoprotein E variants cause dysbetalipoproteinemia with raised remnants and palmar xanthomas.
whyNot.C: CETP deficiency raises HDL cholesterol and does not cause chylomicronemia.
whyNot.D: LDL receptor defects cause familial hypercholesterolemia with very high LDL and tendon xanthomas.

items.objective: Recognize familial chylomicronemia as a cause of pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has 6 weeks of painless jaundice and mild weight loss. CT shows a diffusely enlarged, featureless pancreas surrounded by a thin low-density rim, without a discrete mass. He also has painless enlargement of both submandibular glands. Serum IgG4 is markedly raised. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the pancreas is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Acinar atrophy with calcified intraductal plugs

options.label: C
options.html: Infiltrating malignant glands in desmoplastic stroma

options.label: E
options.html: Papillary mucinous epithelium lining a dilated duct

items.explanationHtml:
Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is part of IgG4-related disease. Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with many IgG4-positive plasma cells, cartwheel (storiform) fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Involvement of other organs, such as the salivary glands, is common. It mimics pancreatic cancer clinically but responds to glucocorticoids.

Takeaway: IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis shows IgG4-rich lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis.

whyNot.A: Acinar atrophy with calcified plugs is the picture of alcohol-associated chronic calcific pancreatitis.
whyNot.B: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis, which rarely involves the pancreas and would not explain raised IgG4.
whyNot.C: Malignant glands in desmoplastic stroma describe pancreatic adenocarcinoma, which usually forms a discrete mass.
whyNot.E: Papillary mucinous epithelium in a dilated duct describes an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.

items.objective: Recognize the histology of IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man had alcohol-associated acute pancreatitis 7 weeks ago. He now has early satiety and epigastric fullness. CT shows a 7-cm round, homogeneous fluid collection with a well-defined enhancing wall next to the stomach, with no solid debris. It is drained endoscopically, and a biopsy of the wall is taken. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in the biopsy?

options.label: A
options.html: Columnar mucinous epithelium over ovarian-type stroma

options.label: B
options.html: Fibrous and granulation tissue without an epithelial lining

options.label: C
options.html: Glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium in many small cysts

options.label: D
options.html: Papillary mucinous epithelium lining a dilated duct

options.label: E
options.html: Stratified squamous epithelium with keratin debris

items.explanationHtml:
A homogeneous fluid collection with a mature wall more than 4 weeks after interstitial pancreatitis is a pseudocyst. Its wall forms from inflamed fibrous and granulation tissue of surrounding structures; it has no epithelial lining, which is why it is called a pseudocyst. Fluid is rich in pancreatic enzymes because the collection often communicates with a disrupted duct.

Takeaway: Pancreatic pseudocysts are walled by fibrous and granulation tissue and lack an epithelial lining.

whyNot.A: Mucinous epithelium over ovarian-type stroma defines a mucinous cystic neoplasm, typically in the body or tail of middle-aged women.
whyNot.C: Glycogen-rich cuboidal cells in many small cysts describe serous cystadenoma.
whyNot.D: Papillary mucinous epithelium in a dilated duct describes an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm.
whyNot.E: Squamous-lined keratin-filled cysts are rare lymphoepithelial or epidermoid cysts, not a sequel of pancreatitis.

items.objective: Describe the histology of a pancreatic pseudocyst.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man with chronic calcific pancreatitis from long-standing alcohol use has had greasy, foul-smelling stools for 2 years and has never taken an enzyme supplement. He now has numbness of the feet. Serum vitamin B12 is low; intrinsic factor antibodies are negative and upper endoscopy shows normal gastric mucosa. Which of the following best explains his low vitamin B12?

options.label: B
options.html: Bacterial overgrowth consuming B12 in the jejunum

options.label: C
options.html: Failure to degrade haptocorrin, so B12 cannot bind intrinsic factor

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced acid-mediated release of B12 from dietary protein

items.explanationHtml:
In the stomach, B12 binds haptocorrin (R-binder). In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin, freeing B12 to bind intrinsic factor for uptake in the terminal ileum. When protease output is very low, B12 stays bound to haptocorrin and is lost. Clinically significant deficiency is uncommon but can occur in long-standing untreated insufficiency, and alcohol-related neuropathy should be considered alongside it.

Takeaway: Pancreatic proteases free B12 from haptocorrin; exocrine insufficiency can therefore impair B12 absorption.

whyNot.A: Parietal cell autoimmunity causes pernicious anemia, which is unlikely with negative antibodies and normal mucosa.
whyNot.B: Bacterial overgrowth can consume B12 but there is no blind loop or motility disorder to suggest it.
whyNot.D: Cubilin loss or ileal disease impairs uptake of the B12-intrinsic factor complex, but his ileum is not affected.
whyNot.E: Acid-mediated release from food fails with atrophic gastritis or long-term acid suppression, which are not present.

items.objective: Explain why exocrine pancreatic insufficiency can cause B12 deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl has had recurrent pneumonia and bulky, greasy stools since infancy, and she is below the 5th percentile for weight. Sweat chloride is elevated on two occasions. Which of the following best explains her stool pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Amyloid deposition within the pancreatic islets

options.label: C
options.html: Deficient enteropeptidase at the duodenal brush border

options.label: D
options.html: Dehydrated ductal secretions that obstruct the ducts

items.explanationHtml:
In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR reduces chloride and bicarbonate secretion by ductal cells, so pancreatic secretions are scant, acidic and viscous. They plug the small ducts, enzymes are retained and destroy acinar tissue, and the gland becomes fibrotic and fatty. Exocrine insufficiency causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and is treated with enzyme replacement with every meal.

Takeaway: Cystic fibrosis causes pancreatic insufficiency because thick ductal secretions obstruct the ducts and destroy acini.

whyNot.A: Islet amyloid is a feature of type 2 diabetes and does not cause steatorrhea.
whyNot.B: Autoimmune acinar destruction is not a feature of cystic fibrosis.
whyNot.C: Enteropeptidase deficiency would not explain recurrent pneumonia or a raised sweat chloride.
whyNot.E: Premature trypsinogen activation describes PRSS1-type hereditary pancreatitis.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis.

items.stemHtml:
A 39-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 12 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back that began after a weekend of heavy drinking. He has vomited several times. Examination shows epigastric tenderness without rigidity. Results are shown.

ParameterResult
Pulse; blood pressure112/min; 118/74 mm Hg
Respirations; SpO220/min; 97% on room air
Temperature37.6°C (99.7°F)
Lipase2,650 U/L (0-160)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)24 mg/dL (7-18)
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL (0.6-1.2)
Calcium, total8.9 mg/dL (8.4-10.2)
Triglycerides210 mg/dL (below 150)
ALT; bilirubin, total48 U/L (10-40); 0.9 mg/dL (0.1-1.0)
UltrasoundNo gallstones; common bile duct normal

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen today

options.label: C
options.html: Nothing by mouth with parenteral nutrition

items.explanationHtml:
Typical pain plus lipase more than three times normal establishes acute pancreatitis, most likely alcohol-associated. Tachycardia and a raised BUN suggest volume depletion. Early management is moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer solution, reassessed frequently against heart rate, urine output and BUN, with analgesia and early oral feeding as tolerated. Aggressive fluid regimens increase fluid overload without improving outcomes.

Takeaway: Initial treatment of acute pancreatitis is moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer solution with frequent reassessment.

whyNot.A: CT is unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear and adds little in the first 72 hours, before necrosis is visible.
whyNot.C: Prolonged fasting and parenteral nutrition increase infection; enteral or oral feeding is preferred.
whyNot.D: Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infected necrosis and are not recommended.
whyNot.E: ERCP is for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; he has no gallstones and normal liver tests.

items.objective: Choose initial fluid therapy for acute pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has 10 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. She has type 2 diabetes with a hemoglobin A1c of 10.8% (below 5.7%) and takes metformin. She abstains from alcohol. Lipase is 1,900 U/L (0-160), calcium 8.6 mg/dL (8.4-10.2), and ALT and bilirubin are normal. The laboratory reports that the serum sample is grossly lipemic. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows no gallstones and a normal bile duct. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her pancreatitis?
items.explanationHtml:
Lipemic serum in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes and no gallstones or alcohol use points to hypertriglyceridemia, which typically causes pancreatitis when triglycerides exceed about 1,000 mg/dL. Measuring triglycerides early in the admission confirms it, because levels fall quickly with fasting. Lipemia can also interfere with some laboratory assays.

Takeaway: Lipemic serum with acute pancreatitis suggests hypertriglyceridemia; measure triglycerides early.

whyNot.A: Autoimmune pancreatitis usually presents with painless jaundice in older patients rather than an acute painful attack with lipemic serum.
whyNot.B: Microlithiasis usually raises ALT early, and the lipemic sample offers a better explanation.
whyNot.C: Metformin is not a classic cause of pancreatitis, and the lipemia points elsewhere.
whyNot.D: Her calcium is normal.

items.objective: Identify hypertriglyceridemia as a cause of acute pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item has serum triglycerides of 2,350 mg/dL. She is treated with fluids, analgesia and an intravenous insulin infusion, and she recovers over 5 days. At discharge she is eating, and her triglycerides are 820 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term plan to prevent another attack?

options.label: A
options.html: Bile acid sequestrant plus fat restriction

options.label: C
options.html: Fibrate plus strict dietary fat restriction

options.label: D
options.html: High-intensity statin as sole lipid therapy

items.explanationHtml:
After hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis, the goal is to keep triglycerides well below the range that triggers attacks. A fibrate is the drug of choice for severe hypertriglyceridemia, combined with strict dietary fat restriction, weight loss, alcohol avoidance and better glycemic control; omega-3 fatty acids can be added. A statin may be added for cardiovascular risk but does not lower triglycerides enough on its own.

Takeaway: Prevent recurrent hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis with a fibrate, dietary fat restriction and glucose control.

whyNot.A: Bile acid sequestrants raise triglycerides and can worsen severe hypertriglyceridemia.
whyNot.B: Ezetimibe has little effect on triglycerides.
whyNot.D: Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and are not sufficient alone at these levels.
whyNot.E: A single attack of acute pancreatitis does not cause exocrine insufficiency requiring enzymes.

items.objective: Plan secondary prevention after hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man had acute gallstone pancreatitis 8 weeks ago and underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy during that admission. At a follow-up visit he is eating normally, has no pain, nausea or weight loss, and has normal liver tests. Follow-up CT shows a 6-cm homogeneous fluid collection with a thin, enhancing wall in the lesser sac, without solid components, compressing nothing. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
A homogeneous, encapsulated collection more than 4 weeks after interstitial pancreatitis is a pseudocyst. Asymptomatic pseudocysts do not need drainage regardless of size, because many resolve and complications are uncommon. Intervention, usually endoscopic, is reserved for pain, gastric outlet or biliary obstruction, infection, bleeding or growth with symptoms.

Takeaway: Asymptomatic pancreatic pseudocysts are observed; size alone is not an indication to drain.

whyNot.A: Endoscopic drainage is the preferred route when drainage is needed, but he has no indication.
whyNot.C: Octreotide has no established role in resolving pseudocysts.
whyNot.D: Percutaneous drainage risks a persistent external fistula and is not indicated without symptoms.
whyNot.E: Surgery is reserved for failed endoscopic treatment or other complex disease.

items.objective: Manage an asymptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman is on hospital day 16 with necrotizing pancreatitis. She had been improving but now has a temperature of 38.9°C (102.0°F) and a leukocyte count of 21,000/mm3. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg; she is breathing comfortably on room air and needs no vasopressors. Blood and urine cultures are pending, and chest radiograph is clear. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a heterogeneous peripancreatic collection containing gas bubbles, with an incompletely formed wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Carbapenem now, delaying drainage until encapsulated

options.label: B
options.html: Empiric fluconazole, then repeat CT in one week

options.label: C
options.html: Observation alone, without antibiotics or drainage

options.label: D
options.html: Open surgical necrosectomy within the next 24 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent ERCP with pancreatic duct stent placement

items.explanationHtml:
Gas within a necrotic collection with new fever in the second week or later indicates infected necrosis. In a stable patient, start antibiotics that penetrate necrotic tissue, such as a carbapenem, and postpone drainage until the collection is walled off, about 4 weeks after onset. If she fails to improve, a step-up approach begins with endoscopic or percutaneous drainage, followed by minimally invasive necrosectomy if needed. Fine-needle aspiration is not routinely required when the clinical and CT picture is this clear.

Takeaway: Infected pancreatic necrosis in a stable patient: carbapenem first, then delayed, step-up drainage of walled-off necrosis.

whyNot.B: Fungal infection is not the likely cause, and antifungals do not treat bacterial infected necrosis.
whyNot.C: Infected necrosis without antibiotics leads to sepsis; observation alone is inadequate.
whyNot.D: Early open necrosectomy carries higher mortality and morbidity than delayed, minimally invasive step-up treatment.
whyNot.E: ERCP does not drain a necrotic collection and adds procedural risk without a biliary indication.

items.objective: Manage infected pancreatic necrosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with 25 years of heavy alcohol use and a 30-pack-year smoking history has recurrent epigastric pain, an 8-kg (18-lb) weight loss over a year and three to four pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools daily. He was recently started on insulin for new diabetes. CT shows scattered pancreatic calcifications and a dilated, irregular main pancreatic duct without a mass. Fecal elastase is 45 μg/g (normal above 200). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his diarrhea?
items.explanationHtml:
Calcifications, steatorrhea and diabetes indicate chronic pancreatitis with exocrine and endocrine insufficiency. Steatorrhea is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals and snacks, along with fat-soluble vitamin replacement, bone density screening, and alcohol and smoking cessation. Adding acid suppression can help when response is incomplete.

Takeaway: Steatorrhea from chronic pancreatitis is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals.

whyNot.A: Cholestyramine treats bile acid diarrhea and can worsen fat malabsorption.
whyNot.B: Loperamide slows transit but does not correct fat malabsorption.
whyNot.C: Metronidazole treats bacterial overgrowth or infection, which is not the primary problem here.
whyNot.D: Octreotide reduces pancreatic secretion and would worsen exocrine insufficiency.

items.objective: Treat exocrine insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has a common bile duct stone confirmed on MRCP 3 months after cholecystectomy, and ERCP is planned. Two years ago she developed acute pancreatitis after a previous ERCP. She has no allergies, and renal function is normal. Which of the following measures given at the time of the procedure is most likely to reduce her risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis?
items.explanationHtml:
A prior episode of post-ERCP pancreatitis and female sex increase her risk. A single dose of rectal indomethacin or diclofenac given around the time of ERCP reduces the incidence of post-ERCP pancreatitis and is recommended for most patients without contraindications. Periprocedural lactated Ringer hydration and, in selected high-risk cases, a temporary pancreatic duct stent add further protection.

Takeaway: Rectal NSAIDs (indomethacin or diclofenac) at the time of ERCP reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics are given at ERCP for specific indications such as incomplete drainage, but they do not prevent pancreatitis.
whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids have not been shown to prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis.
whyNot.C: Octreotide has not reliably prevented post-ERCP pancreatitis and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Oral enzymes do not affect pancreatic injury from instrumentation.

items.objective: Select prophylaxis against post-ERCP pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has increasing abdominal girth. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.8 g/dL and an ascitic total protein of 1.0 g/dL. Ascitic neutrophil count is 40/mm3. Which of the following is the primary force driving fluid into his peritoneal cavity?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased capillary permeability from peritoneal inflammation

options.label: B
options.html: Increased hydrostatic pressure in the hepatic sinusoids

options.label: C
options.html: Increased oncotic pressure of the peritoneal fluid

options.label: D
options.html: Obstruction of peritoneal lymphatic drainage by tumour

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced lymph production by the cirrhotic liver

items.explanationHtml:
A high gradient means the difference between serum and ascitic albumin is large, which reflects a high hydrostatic pressure in the portal and sinusoidal bed. In cirrhosis, increased intrahepatic resistance raises sinusoidal pressure, forcing fluid out of the liver surface and splanchnic capillaries faster than lymphatics can return it. Low ascitic protein fits sinusoidal (rather than cardiac) portal hypertension.

Takeaway: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more reflects raised portal (sinusoidal) hydrostatic pressure as the cause of ascites.

whyNot.A: Inflammatory permeability increases ascitic protein and gives a low gradient, as in peritoneal infection or carcinomatosis.
whyNot.C: The ascitic oncotic pressure is low in cirrhosis, as shown by the low protein.
whyNot.D: Lymphatic obstruction by tumour causes chylous or malignant ascites with a low gradient.
whyNot.E: Hepatic lymph production is increased, not reduced, in cirrhosis because of the high sinusoidal pressure.

items.objective: Relate SAAG to Starling forces in cirrhotic ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has a blood pressure of 96/58 mm Hg, a serum sodium of 129 mEq/L (136-145) and a urine sodium of 8 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are markedly elevated. Overproduction of which of the following in the splanchnic circulation is the main initiating cause of her neurohormonal activation?
items.explanationHtml:
Portal hypertension and bacterial products from the gut increase endothelial nitric oxide synthase activity in splanchnic arteries. The resulting vasodilation lowers effective arterial blood volume, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system and ADH release. These compensations retain sodium and water, producing ascites and dilutional hyponatremia.

Takeaway: Splanchnic vasodilation from nitric oxide underlies the RAAS activation and sodium retention of cirrhosis.

whyNot.A: Angiotensin II is raised as a consequence of underfilling; it is a vasoconstrictor, not the initiating vasodilator.
whyNot.B: Antidiuretic hormone is released in response to underfilling and causes the hyponatremia.
whyNot.C: Endothelin-1 contributes to intrahepatic vasoconstriction, not splanchnic vasodilation.
whyNot.E: Norepinephrine rises with sympathetic activation and constricts, rather than dilates, vessels.

items.objective: Explain the role of splanchnic vasodilation in cirrhotic ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has taken spironolactone and furosemide for 4 months. He now reports tender enlargement of both breasts that began after the medicines were started. Which of the following mechanisms of his medication regimen most likely explains this symptom?
items.explanationHtml:
Spironolactone is a nonselective steroid antagonist: besides blocking mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct, it blocks androgen receptors and alters sex steroid metabolism, causing gynecomastia and reduced libido. Cirrhosis itself shifts the estrogen to androgen balance, so the effect is common. Eplerenone (more selective) or amiloride can replace spironolactone if gynecomastia is troublesome.

Takeaway: Spironolactone causes gynecomastia through androgen receptor antagonism; switch to eplerenone or amiloride if needed.

whyNot.B: ENaC blockade is the action of amiloride and triamterene, which lack antiandrogen effects.
whyNot.C: 5α-reductase inhibition is the action of finasteride; it can cause gynecomastia but is not how spironolactone works.
whyNot.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is the action of acetazolamide, which is not part of his regimen.
whyNot.E: Na-K-2Cl inhibition is the action of furosemide, which does not cause gynecomastia.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of spironolactone-induced gynecomastia.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has 2 days of low-grade fever and mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. Ascitic fluid shows 640 neutrophils/mm3, total protein 0.7 g/dL and glucose 96 mg/dL. CT shows no free air or abscess. Culture grows a single organism. Which of the following organisms is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is usually monomicrobial and most often caused by gut-derived gram-negative rods such as E. coli and Klebsiella, which translocate across the intestinal wall into lymph and blood. Low-protein ascites has little complement and opsonic activity, so the bacteria are not cleared.

Takeaway: SBP is typically a single enteric gram-negative organism, most often E. coli.

whyNot.A: Anaerobes such as Bacteroides point to secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus, often with several organisms.
whyNot.B: Fungal peritonitis is uncommon and usually follows perforation or prolonged antibiotics.
whyNot.D: Tuberculous peritonitis causes a lymphocyte-predominant fluid with a low SAAG, not a neutrophilic one.
whyNot.E: S. aureus is unusual in SBP and suggests an indwelling device or skin source.

items.objective: Identify the usual organisms in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis is treated for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Over 5 days her serum creatinine rises from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL despite stopping diuretics and receiving intravenous albumin for 2 days. Urine sodium is below 10 mEq/L, urinalysis shows no protein or blood and the sediment is bland, and renal ultrasound is normal. She has received no nephrotoxic drugs, and her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains her kidney dysfunction?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug-induced inflammation of the renal interstitium

options.label: B
options.html: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli

options.label: C
options.html: Ischemic necrosis of the proximal tubular epithelium

options.label: D
options.html: Renal arterial vasoconstriction with intact kidneys

options.label: E
options.html: Thrombotic obstruction of both renal veins

items.explanationHtml:
This is hepatorenal syndrome. Severe splanchnic vasodilation and falling effective arterial volume trigger intense renal vasoconstriction through the renin-angiotensin, sympathetic and endothelin systems. Glomerular filtration falls while the kidney remains structurally normal, so the tubules conserve sodium avidly and the sediment is bland. Function returns after liver transplantation.

Takeaway: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal vasoconstriction in structurally normal kidneys, with very low urine sodium.

whyNot.A: Interstitial nephritis causes white cells and casts in the urine and needs an offending drug.
whyNot.B: Glomerulonephritis causes proteinuria and hematuria, which are absent.
whyNot.C: Acute tubular necrosis causes granular casts and a higher urine sodium because damaged tubules cannot conserve sodium.
whyNot.E: Renal vein thrombosis typically causes flank pain, hematuria and proteinuria, often with nephrotic syndrome.

items.objective: Describe the pathophysiology of hepatorenal syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman has 3 months of increasing abdominal girth, drenching night sweats and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. CT shows bulky retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy and moderate ascites with a normal-appearing liver. Paracentesis yields milky white fluid with a triglyceride concentration of 640 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Milky fluid with triglycerides above 200 mg/dL is chylous ascites, caused by leakage of chylomicron-rich lymph from disrupted or obstructed lymphatics. In adults the most common cause is malignancy, especially lymphoma, which obstructs retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphatics. B symptoms and bulky nodes make lymphoma the best answer; tissue biopsy confirms it.

Takeaway: Chylous ascites (triglycerides above 200 mg/dL) in an adult with bulky nodes suggests lymphoma.

whyNot.A: Cirrhosis can rarely cause chylous ascites, but the liver is normal and she has bulky nodes and B symptoms.
whyNot.B: Constrictive pericarditis causes clear, high-gradient ascites with raised jugular venous pressure.
whyNot.C: Nephrotic syndrome causes clear, low-protein ascites with a low gradient.
whyNot.E: Heart failure causes clear, protein-rich, high-gradient ascites, not chylous fluid.

items.objective: Recognize the causes of chylous ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old retired shipyard pipe insulator has abdominal distension and weight loss. CT shows ascites with diffuse, sheet-like thickening and nodularity of the peritoneum and omentum, and no primary tumour elsewhere. Laparoscopic peritoneal biopsy shows malignant epithelioid cells that are positive for calretinin and cytokeratin. Exposure to which of the following is most strongly associated with this tumour?
items.explanationHtml:
Diffuse peritoneal thickening with calretinin-positive malignant epithelioid cells indicates malignant peritoneal mesothelioma. Like pleural mesothelioma, it is strongly associated with occupational asbestos exposure, often decades earlier, in trades such as shipbuilding, insulation and construction. Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies may be found in lung tissue.

Takeaway: Malignant mesothelioma, pleural or peritoneal, is strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

whyNot.A: Aromatic amines, as in dye and rubber work, are linked to urothelial carcinoma.
whyNot.C: Silica causes silicosis and increases risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer, not mesothelioma.
whyNot.D: Arsenic is linked to skin cancer, lung cancer and hepatic angiosarcoma.
whyNot.E: Vinyl chloride is linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.

items.objective: Associate peritoneal mesothelioma with asbestos.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man who moved from a high-prevalence country 2 years ago has 3 months of fever, night sweats, abdominal swelling and weight loss. Ascitic fluid shows 1,100 leukocytes/mm3 with 85% lymphocytes, total protein 4.6 g/dL, a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 0.6 g/dL and raised adenosine deaminase. Acid-fast smear of the fluid is negative. Laparoscopy shows many small white nodules on the peritoneum. A biopsy of a nodule is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: E
options.html: Signet-ring cells in a desmoplastic stroma

items.explanationHtml:
A lymphocyte-predominant, protein-rich ascites with a low gradient and raised adenosine deaminase in someone from an endemic area suggests tuberculous peritonitis. Fluid smears and cultures are often negative because organisms are few, so peritoneal biopsy is the most sensitive test. It shows caseating granulomas, sometimes with acid-fast bacilli on staining and positive mycobacterial culture.

Takeaway: Tuberculous peritonitis: lymphocytic, high-protein, low-SAAG ascites; peritoneal biopsy shows caseating granulomas.

whyNot.B: A neutrophilic process with gram-negative rods fits bacterial peritonitis, not lymphocytic ascites.
whyNot.C: Noncaseating granulomas with asteroid bodies suggest sarcoidosis, which rarely causes ascites.
whyNot.D: Psammoma bodies in papillary clusters suggest serous ovarian carcinoma spread to the peritoneum.
whyNot.E: Signet-ring cells suggest metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma, which would not fit fever and raised adenosine deaminase as well.

items.objective: Recognize the pathology of tuberculous peritonitis.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis due to alcohol use is admitted with confusion and asterixis. He has mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed on admission. Results are shown.

TestResult
Temperature37.9°C (100.2°F)
Blood pressure104/64 mm Hg
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL (0.6-1.2)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)32 mg/dL (7-18)
Bilirubin, total3.8 mg/dL (0.1-1.0)
Albumin, serum2.6 g/dL (3.5-5.5)
INR1.9 (0.8-1.1)
Ascitic neutrophils520/mm3
Ascitic albumin; total protein0.5 g/dL; 0.9 g/dL
Ascitic glucose98 mg/dL
Ascitic Gram stainNo organisms seen

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Abdominal CT and urgent surgical consultation

options.label: D
options.html: Oral ciprofloxacin, then repeat tap in 48 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Withhold antibiotics until culture results return

items.explanationHtml:
An ascitic neutrophil count of 250/mm3 or more establishes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; a negative Gram stain is typical. With encephalopathy and kidney injury, he needs an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin. Intravenous albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3) reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death, especially when creatinine, BUN or bilirubin is raised, as here. The SAAG of 2.1 g/dL and normal glucose fit cirrhotic ascites without a surgical source.

Takeaway: SBP (ascitic PMN of 250/mm3 or more): give an IV third-generation cephalosporin plus IV albumin.

whyNot.A: Nothing suggests secondary peritonitis: one or no organisms, normal glucose and very low protein.
whyNot.C: Large-volume paracentesis during untreated SBP risks circulatory dysfunction and does not treat the infection.
whyNot.D: Oral therapy is reserved for selected uncomplicated cases without encephalopathy or kidney injury.
whyNot.E: Antibiotics should start as soon as the neutrophil count is known; waiting for culture increases mortality.

items.objective: Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with antibiotics and albumin.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has 2 days of worsening diffuse abdominal pain. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse 110/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. The abdomen is distended and diffusely tender. Paracentesis shows an ascitic neutrophil count of 6,200/mm3, total protein 2.4 g/dL, glucose 22 mg/dL and LDH 480 U/L (serum upper limit of normal 225 U/L). Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci, gram-negative rods and gram-positive bacilli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover and CT

options.label: B
options.html: Cefotaxime alone and a repeat tap in 48 hours

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous albumin and diuretic withdrawal only

items.explanationHtml:
Several organism types on Gram stain, a very high neutrophil count, low glucose, high LDH and relatively high protein for cirrhotic ascites indicate secondary bacterial peritonitis from a perforation or abscess rather than SBP. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics that include anaerobic cover and obtain urgent CT of the abdomen to find a surgically treatable source.

Takeaway: Polymicrobial ascites with low glucose and high LDH means secondary peritonitis: broad antibiotics and urgent CT for a source.

whyNot.B: Cefotaxime alone does not reliably cover anaerobes, and waiting 48 hours delays source control.
whyNot.C: Albumin and diuretic withdrawal support the kidneys but do not treat a perforation.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic paracentesis does not address the infection and may worsen hemodynamics.
whyNot.E: TIPS treats refractory ascites or variceal bleeding, not peritoneal infection.

items.objective: Recognize secondary bacterial peritonitis in a patient with ascites.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item is started on piperacillin-tazobactam. CT of the abdomen shows free intraperitoneal air and a thickened sigmoid colon with adjacent extraluminal gas, consistent with a perforated diverticulum. Her blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg after fluids. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Free perforation of the colon with generalized peritonitis requires prompt surgical source control in addition to antibiotics, even though cirrhosis raises operative risk. Delay increases mortality. Surgical risk should be discussed with the patient and family, and the liver team should help with perioperative management.

Takeaway: Secondary peritonitis from a free perforation needs surgical source control along with antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics alone will not control a free colonic perforation.
whyNot.B: Colonoscopy is contraindicated with an acute perforation.
whyNot.C: Repeated paracentesis does not control the source.
whyNot.E: Percutaneous drainage suits a contained abscess, not free perforation with generalized peritonitis.

items.objective: Manage secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25% has 2 months of increasing dyspnea, leg swelling and abdominal distension. Jugular venous pressure is raised to the angle of the jaw, and there is shifting dullness. Liver tests are mildly abnormal and the INR is normal. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL, total protein 3.4 g/dL and 60 neutrophils/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ascites?
items.explanationHtml:
A high gradient means portal hypertension, and a high ascitic protein in that setting points to a postsinusoidal or cardiac cause, where hepatic sinusoids are structurally normal and leak protein-rich lymph. Raised jugular venous pressure and severe cardiomyopathy make heart failure the cause; management is aimed at the heart.

Takeaway: High SAAG with high ascitic protein (2.5 g/dL or more) suggests cardiac ascites or hepatic vein obstruction.

whyNot.A: Cirrhotic ascites has a high gradient but low protein.
whyNot.C: Nephrotic syndrome gives a low gradient with low protein.
whyNot.D: Carcinomatosis gives a low gradient, often with positive cytology.
whyNot.E: Tuberculous peritonitis gives a low gradient with a lymphocyte-predominant fluid.

items.objective: Use SAAG and ascitic protein to identify cardiac ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 53-year-old woman with cirrhosis has tense ascites causing abdominal discomfort and shortness of breath. Ascitic neutrophil count on a diagnostic sample is 30/mm3. A therapeutic paracentesis removes 8 L of fluid. Which of the following should be given to reduce the risk of circulatory dysfunction and kidney injury after the procedure?

options.label: A
options.html: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous albumin, 6 to 8 g per liter removed

options.label: D
options.html: Intravenous furosemide, 40 mg after the tap

options.label: E
options.html: Packed red cells to raise the hemoglobin

items.explanationHtml:
Removing more than 5 L of ascites can cause post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction: further arterial vasodilation, activation of the renin-angiotensin system, hyponatremia, kidney injury and reaccumulation. Intravenous albumin at about 6 to 8 g per liter removed prevents it more effectively than other plasma expanders.

Takeaway: After large-volume paracentesis (more than 5 L), give IV albumin, about 6 to 8 g per liter removed.

whyNot.A: INR does not predict bleeding from paracentesis, and routine plasma is not recommended.
whyNot.B: Saline is less effective than albumin and adds sodium that reaccumulates as ascites.
whyNot.D: Furosemide immediately after a large tap worsens intravascular depletion.
whyNot.E: Red cells are not indicated without bleeding or significant anemia.

items.objective: Prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction with albumin.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man is diagnosed with alcohol-associated cirrhosis after presenting with moderate ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.7 g/dL, total protein 1.1 g/dL and 40 neutrophils/mm3. Serum sodium is 134 mEq/L (136-145), potassium 4.1 mEq/L (3.5-5.0) and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (0.6-1.2). He has stopped drinking. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of his ascites?

options.label: A
options.html: Fluid restriction to 1 L per day as the main treatment

options.label: B
options.html: Furosemide monotherapy with a liberal salt intake

options.label: D
options.html: Sodium restriction with spironolactone and furosemide

items.explanationHtml:
First-line treatment of cirrhotic ascites is dietary sodium restriction to about 2 g per day plus diuretics, usually spironolactone and furosemide started together in a 100:40 mg ratio and titrated to weight loss, with monitoring of electrolytes and creatinine. Abstinence from alcohol may substantially improve ascites over time.

Takeaway: Initial treatment of cirrhotic ascites is about 2 g/day sodium restriction plus spironolactone and furosemide.

whyNot.A: Fluid restriction is reserved for severe hyponatremia; his sodium is only mildly low.
whyNot.B: Loop diuretics alone work poorly in cirrhosis, where aldosterone drives sodium retention, and salt intake must be limited.
whyNot.C: Serial paracentesis is for tense or refractory ascites, not a first-line strategy for moderate ascites.
whyNot.E: TIPS is for refractory ascites, which he does not have.

items.objective: Start first-line treatment for cirrhotic ascites.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and treated with ceftriaxone and intravenous albumin. His creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL over 4 days despite stopping diuretics and receiving albumin for 2 days. Blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, SpO2 is 97% on room air and lungs are clear. Urine sodium is 6 mEq/L, urinalysis is bland and renal ultrasound is normal. He has received no nephrotoxic drugs. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Rising creatinine despite diuretic withdrawal and albumin, with a bland sediment, normal ultrasound and very low urine sodium, meets criteria for hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury, triggered here by SBP. Treatment is a vasoconstrictor plus albumin: terlipressin is preferred and he has no hypoxemia or fluid overload to contraindicate it. Norepinephrine is an alternative in an intensive care setting. He should be evaluated for liver transplantation.

Takeaway: Treat hepatorenal syndrome with a vasoconstrictor (terlipressin, or norepinephrine in the ICU) plus albumin.

whyNot.A: Large saline boluses do not correct the problem and worsen ascites and fluid overload.
whyNot.B: Dialysis bridges selected patients to transplant but does not reverse hepatorenal syndrome and is not first-line.
whyNot.C: Furosemide worsens renal hypoperfusion in hepatorenal syndrome.
whyNot.D: The kidneys are structurally normal, so biopsy adds risk without benefit.

items.objective: Treat hepatorenal syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis due to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis recovers from her first episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which was caused by Escherichia coli. She is ready for discharge, still has moderate ascites and is listed for transplant evaluation. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce her risk of another episode?

options.label: B
options.html: Monthly intravenous albumin infusions at home

options.label: C
options.html: No prophylaxis after a fully treated first episode

options.label: D
options.html: Oral lactulose titrated to three soft stools a day

items.explanationHtml:
After an episode of SBP, the risk of recurrence within a year is high, so long-term secondary prophylaxis with a daily oral antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin (or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is recommended until transplant or until ascites resolves. Survival after SBP is poor, which is why transplant evaluation is also appropriate.

Takeaway: After a first episode of SBP, give long-term daily oral antibiotic prophylaxis and refer for transplant evaluation.

whyNot.B: Long-term albumin infusion is not the standard way to prevent recurrent SBP.
whyNot.C: Without prophylaxis, recurrence is common and often fatal.
whyNot.D: Lactulose treats and prevents hepatic encephalopathy, not SBP.
whyNot.E: Oral vancomycin is used for Clostridioides difficile and does not cover the gram-negative organisms that cause SBP.

items.objective: Provide secondary prophylaxis after spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man has a soft groin bulge on the right that enlarges when he coughs and, on standing, extends into the upper scrotum. At elective laparoscopic repair, the hernia sac is seen entering the abdominal wall lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and travelling within the coverings of the spermatic cord. Failure of which developmental process best explains this hernia?

options.label: B
options.html: Formation of transversalis fascia in the inguinal triangle

items.explanationHtml:
An indirect inguinal hernia leaves through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follows the spermatic cord. Its sac is a patent processus vaginalis, the peritoneal extension that accompanies the testis through the canal and normally obliterates after descent. Because the sac lies within the cord coverings it can reach the scrotum.

Takeaway: Indirect inguinal hernia equals a patent processus vaginalis entering lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

whyNot.A: Incomplete umbilical ring closure causes a midline umbilical hernia, not a groin hernia.
whyNot.B: Weak transversalis fascia medial to the inferior epigastric vessels causes an acquired direct hernia, which does not travel with the cord into the scrotum.
whyNot.C: Persistence of the vitelline duct causes Meckel diverticulum or an umbilical fistula, not an inguinal hernia.
whyNot.E: A persistent urachus causes a urachal fistula, cyst or sinus between bladder and umbilicus.

items.objective: Relate an indirect inguinal hernia to failed obliteration of the processus vaginalis.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man who strains to urinate because of benign prostatic hyperplasia has a reducible, broad-based bulge in the left groin that stays above the scrotum. During laparoscopic repair, the surgeon finds the defect in a weak area of transversalis fascia. Medially the defect is bounded by the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. Which structure forms its lateral boundary?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a direct inguinal hernia through Hesselbach triangle, whose borders are the lateral edge of rectus abdominis (medial), the inferior epigastric vessels (lateral) and the inguinal ligament (inferior). Chronic straining weakens the transversalis fascia of the posterior canal wall.

Takeaway: Direct hernias bulge medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach triangle.

whyNot.A: The femoral vein is the lateral boundary of the femoral ring, which lies below the inguinal ligament.
whyNot.B: The ilioinguinal nerve runs within the inguinal canal and is a structure to protect at repair, not a triangle boundary.
whyNot.D: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring and the medial floor of the inguinal canal.
whyNot.E: The spermatic cord passes through the inguinal canal; it is not a boundary of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle.

items.objective: Identify the boundaries of Hesselbach triangle.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has a painful, tense lump in the right upper thigh that appeared after a bout of coughing. The lump lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. At surgery, the hernia sac passes through the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the hernia sac?
items.explanationHtml:
A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, which also carries lymphatics. Order from lateral to medial is nerve (outside the sheath), artery, vein, canal. The femoral ring is bounded by the inguinal ligament anteriorly, pectineal ligament posteriorly, lacunar ligament medially and femoral vein laterally. The narrow rigid ring explains why femoral hernias strangulate more often than inguinal hernias.

Takeaway: A femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament, immediately medial to the femoral vein.

whyNot.A: The femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein, so the vein, not the artery, is immediately adjacent to the canal.
whyNot.B: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath, well away from the canal.
whyNot.D: The inferior epigastric artery runs above the inguinal ligament and separates direct from indirect inguinal hernias.
whyNot.E: The lacunar ligament is the medial boundary of the femoral ring; its sharp edge contributes to strangulation.

items.objective: Locate the femoral canal and its relations.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 8 months ago. About two hours after meals rich in refined carbohydrate she has episodes of sweating, tremor, hunger and difficulty concentrating. A fingerstick glucose during an episode is 46 mg/dL, and symptoms resolve with juice. Fasting glucose is normal. Which mechanism best explains these episodes?

options.label: A
options.html: Autonomous insulin secretion by a pancreatic islet tumor

options.label: B
options.html: Bacterial consumption of carbohydrate in a stagnant limb

options.label: C
options.html: Excess insulin release after rapid delivery and absorption of glucose

options.label: D
options.html: Fluid shift into the bowel lumen from hyperosmolar chyme

items.explanationHtml:
Late dumping follows rapid emptying of carbohydrate into the small bowel. Glucose is absorbed quickly, and the brisk rise in glucose plus exaggerated incretin (GLP-1) release triggers a large insulin surge that overshoots, producing hypoglycemia one to three hours after eating. Dietary change (less refined carbohydrate, more protein and fiber, small meals) is the first step.

Takeaway: Postprandial hypoglycemia hours after gastric surgery is late dumping from an insulin overshoot.

whyNot.A: An insulinoma typically causes fasting hypoglycemia; this patient's episodes are strictly postprandial and fasting glucose is normal.
whyNot.B: Bacterial overgrowth causes bloating, diarrhea and B12 deficiency, not reactive hypoglycemia.
whyNot.D: Osmotic fluid shift causes early dumping within about 30 minutes, with cramps, diarrhea and palpitations, not hypoglycemia two hours later.
whyNot.E: Biliopancreatic limb obstruction causes pain and possible pancreatitis, not glucose-responsive neuroglycopenic episodes.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of late dumping syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man had a partial gastrectomy with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy many years ago. For several months he has had bloating, bulky foul-smelling stools, weight loss and tingling in his feet. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (13.5-17.5 g/dL), MCV is 112 fL (80-100 fL), serum cobalamin is low and serum folate is elevated. A glucose hydrogen breath test is positive. Which mechanism best explains his anemia?

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of ileal receptors after resection

options.label: E
options.html: Uptake of cobalamin by bacteria in the intestinal lumen

items.explanationHtml:
A stagnant afferent limb allows small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (blind loop syndrome). Anaerobes bind and consume cobalamin before it reaches the terminal ileum, causing megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy, while bacterial folate production raises serum folate. Deconjugation of bile acids impairs micelle formation and causes steatorrhea.

Takeaway: Low B12 with high folate after a blind loop suggests bacterial overgrowth.

whyNot.A: Autoimmune pernicious anemia would not explain steatorrhea, the positive breath test or the high folate.
whyNot.B: Deconjugation explains his fat malabsorption and steatorrhea, but not the cobalamin deficiency causing macrocytic anemia.
whyNot.C: Serum folate is elevated, because overgrowing bacteria synthesize folate.
whyNot.D: He had a gastric operation, not an ileal resection, and the breath test points to overgrowth.

items.objective: Explain B12 deficiency in blind loop syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman reports fatigue and exertional dyspnea three years after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. She stopped her supplements a year ago. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (12.0-16.0 g/dL), MCV is 71 fL (80-100 fL) and ferritin is low. Which change in her anatomy or physiology best explains this anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Bypass of the duodenum and proximal jejunum

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of intrinsic factor from the gastric remnant

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced bile salt delivery to the ileum

items.explanationHtml:
Non-heme iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, helped by gastric acid that keeps iron in the ferrous form. Roux-en-Y bypass routes food past these segments and leaves a small acid-poor pouch, so iron deficiency is common and lifelong supplementation is required.

Takeaway: Iron deficiency after gastric bypass reflects duodenal bypass and reduced acid.

whyNot.B: The terminal ileum is not bypassed in Roux-en-Y surgery and absorbs B12 and bile acids, not iron.
whyNot.C: Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea and fat malabsorption, not iron deficiency.
whyNot.D: Loss of intrinsic factor causes B12 deficiency with macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.
whyNot.E: Bile salt problems impair fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, not iron.

items.objective: Link nutrient deficiency after bariatric surgery to its absorption site.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old man has several episodes of forceful vomiting after an evening of heavy drinking, followed by sudden severe lower retrosternal pain and dyspnea. He has crepitus over the supraclavicular areas. Chest radiograph shows pneumomediastinum and a left pleural effusion. Which lesion is most likely present?

options.label: A
options.html: Full-thickness tear of the distal esophageal wall

options.label: B
options.html: Linear mucosal laceration at the gastresophageal junction

options.label: C
options.html: Mucosal outpouching through the cricopharyngeal muscle
