options.label: D
options.html: Rupture of dilated submucosal esophageal veins

options.label: E
options.html: Thin mucosal ring at the squamocolumnar junction

items.explanationHtml:
Boerhaave syndrome is a transmural esophageal rupture from abrupt pressure rise during vomiting against a closed upper sphincter. The tear is usually in the left posterolateral distal esophagus, so air tracks into the mediastinum and neck (crepitus) and fluid into the left pleural space. Mediastinitis develops rapidly.

Takeaway: Vomiting followed by chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema means transmural rupture, not a Mallory-Weiss tear.

whyNot.B: A Mallory-Weiss tear is mucosal and causes hematemesis; it does not leak air into the mediastinum.
whyNot.C: A Zenker diverticulum causes dysphagia, regurgitation and halitosis in older adults.
whyNot.D: Variceal rupture causes massive hematemesis in portal hypertension, without pneumomediastinum.
whyNot.E: A Schatzki ring causes intermittent solid-food dysphagia and food impaction.

items.objective: Distinguish Boerhaave rupture from other esophageal lesions.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy fell onto the end of his bicycle handlebar, striking his upper abdomen. He seemed well that evening, but 36 hours later he has epigastric fullness and repeated bilious vomiting. CT shows an intramural hematoma narrowing the lumen of a hollow organ that is fixed in the retroperitoneum and lies directly over the vertebral column. Which organ is most likely injured?
items.explanationHtml:
The second to fourth parts of the duodenum are retroperitoneal and fixed across the vertebral column, so a focused epigastric blow such as a handlebar crushes it against the spine. A submucosal hematoma narrows the lumen and gives delayed obstructive symptoms; bilious vomiting reflects obstruction distal to the ampulla.

Takeaway: A handlebar injury with delayed bilious vomiting suggests a duodenal hematoma.

whyNot.B: The gallbladder lies under the liver and is not a retroperitoneal organ crossing the spine.
whyNot.C: The stomach is intraperitoneal and mobile, and obstruction there would cause nonbilious vomiting.
whyNot.D: The jejunum is intraperitoneal on a mesentery and less likely to be crushed against the spine.
whyNot.E: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal on its mesocolon and its obstruction would not cause early bilious vomiting.

items.objective: Relate duodenal retroperitoneal anatomy to its injury mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man comes to the emergency department 3 hours after vomiting forcefully several times following a large meal with alcohol. He then developed severe lower chest and upper abdominal pain and shortness of breath. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 24/min and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. There is crepitus at the suprasternal notch. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest radiograph shows air outlining the mediastinum and a small left pleural effusion. Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Barium esophagography as the first study

items.explanationHtml:
Forceful vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum indicate esophageal rupture. A contrast study with a water-soluble agent (or CT with oral contrast) confirms and localizes the leak while avoiding barium mediastinitis.

Takeaway: Suspected esophageal perforation is confirmed with water-soluble contrast esophagography or CT with oral contrast.

whyNot.A: Barium that leaks into the mediastinum causes severe inflammation; it is reserved for a negative water-soluble study when suspicion remains.
whyNot.B: Bronchoscopy evaluates airway injury, which does not fit a vomiting-induced presentation with a left effusion.
whyNot.C: The ECG shows only sinus tachycardia, and pneumomediastinum with crepitus after vomiting points to the esophagus, not the heart.
whyNot.E: Endoscopic insufflation can enlarge a perforation and worsen mediastinal contamination; contrast imaging is preferred first.

items.objective: Choose the confirmatory study for suspected esophageal perforation.

items.stemHtml: The study shows contrast leaking from the left side of the distal esophagus into the mediastinum and left pleural space. He has received intravenous fluids, a proton pump inhibitor and broad-spectrum antibiotics with antifungal coverage, and he is kept on nothing by mouth. Pulse is now 112/min and blood pressure 108/68 mm Hg. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Emergent surgical repair of the esophagus with drainage

options.label: C
options.html: Endoscopic band ligation of the tear

options.label: D
options.html: Nasogastric suction and observation for 72 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Oral sucralfate with a clear-liquid diet

items.explanationHtml:
Spontaneous rupture with free leakage into the mediastinum and pleura requires early operative repair with drainage of the pleural space and mediastinum, along with antibiotics, nutrition and acid suppression. Small contained iatrogenic leaks in stable patients can sometimes be managed nonoperatively or endoscopically, but this is a free leak.

Takeaway: Boerhaave rupture with free contamination needs emergent surgical repair plus drainage.

whyNot.A: Balloon tamponade is a temporizing measure for variceal bleeding and would worsen a perforation.
whyNot.C: Band ligation treats varices and has no role in closing a transmural rupture.
whyNot.D: A free, uncontained leak with pleural contamination will not seal with observation, and delay greatly raises mortality.
whyNot.E: Oral intake is contraindicated with an active leak, and sucralfate cannot close a full-thickness tear.

items.objective: Manage confirmed spontaneous esophageal rupture.

items.stemHtml:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which she was the restrained driver. She has a seat-belt bruise across the lower abdomen and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Airway is patent and breath sounds are equal. Two large-bore IV lines are placed, and 1 L of crystalloid followed by 2 units of packed red cells are given.

ParameterArrivalAfter transfusion
Pulse128/min134/min
Blood pressure84/52 mm Hg80/50 mm Hg
Respirations26/min28/min
Glasgow Coma Scale1414
Hemoglobin10.2 g/dL (12.0-16.0 g/dL)pending
Lactate, venous37 mg/dL (4.5-20 mg/dL); 4.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2 mmol/L)pending

Pelvic radiograph shows no fracture. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) shows free fluid in the hepatorenal and splenorenal spaces. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

items.explanationHtml:
A blunt trauma patient who remains hypotensive despite initial resuscitation and has intraperitoneal fluid on FAST has intra-abdominal hemorrhage and needs immediate laparotomy, with ongoing balanced blood product resuscitation. Imaging and observation are reserved for stable patients.

Takeaway: Unstable plus positive FAST after blunt trauma means laparotomy.

whyNot.A: Nonoperative observation is only for stable patients; she has not responded to resuscitation.
whyNot.B: CT is for hemodynamically stable patients; moving an unstable patient to the scanner delays hemorrhage control.
whyNot.C: Intraperitoneal blood is already shown by FAST, so lavage adds nothing and delays surgery.
whyNot.E: She has persistent shock despite blood, and a positive FAST already answers the question.

items.objective: Apply the FAST and stability algorithm in blunt abdominal trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is brought in 30 minutes after being stabbed once in the left upper abdomen. He is alert. Pulse is 94/min and blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg. There is a 2-cm wound below the left costal margin through which a tongue of omentum protrudes. The abdomen is mildly tender around the wound without rigidity or rebound. Chest radiograph is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Local wound exploration under local anesthesia

options.label: E
options.html: Replacement of the omentum and wound closure

items.explanationHtml:
For abdominal stab wounds, hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, evisceration, an impaled object and GI bleeding are indications for laparotomy. Stable patients without these can be managed selectively. This patient has evisceration, so he goes to the operating room; tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics are also given.

Takeaway: Evisceration after an abdominal stab wound is an indication for laparotomy even when the patient is stable.

whyNot.A: Selective observation applies to stable stab wounds without evisceration, peritonitis or bleeding.
whyNot.B: Evisceration is an indication for laparotomy regardless of imaging findings.
whyNot.D: Local exploration decides whether the fascia is breached; protruding omentum already proves peritoneal penetration.
whyNot.E: Pushing back eviscerated tissue and closing the skin risks missed visceral injury and contamination.

items.objective: Recognize indications for laparotomy after penetrating abdominal trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her grandfather saw her put something from a remote control in her mouth. She is drooling and refuses to drink but is breathing comfortably. Vital signs are normal. Radiograph shows a 20-mm round radiopaque object at the level of the clavicles; on the frontal view its edge has a double contour, and on the lateral view there is a step-off. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
The double-ring halo on frontal view and step-off on lateral view identify a button battery rather than a coin. A battery lodged in the esophagus generates hydroxide at the mucosa and causes liquefactive necrosis, perforation, fistula or vascular erosion within hours, so removal is emergent even if the child looks well.

Takeaway: An esophageal button battery requires emergent endoscopic removal.

whyNot.A: Contrast studies delay removal and the radiograph has already identified the object.
whyNot.C: Emesis does not reliably dislodge the battery and risks aspiration and further mucosal injury.
whyNot.D: Glucagon is sometimes tried for food bolus impaction at the lower sphincter; it does not treat a battery in the upper esophagus.
whyNot.E: Watchful waiting is acceptable for some coins, but a lodged battery causes deep burns within hours.

items.objective: Manage ingestion of a button battery lodged in the esophagus.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman returns 2 months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. About 15 to 20 minutes after most meals she has crampy abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, palpitations, flushing and light-headedness, worst after sweet foods and drinks taken with meals. Fingerstick glucose during an episode is 104 mg/dL. Examination is normal and she is losing weight as expected. Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: C
options.html: Small frequent meals low in simple sugars, with fluids taken apart from meals

items.explanationHtml:
Symptoms within half an hour of eating with normal glucose are early dumping, caused by rapid delivery of hyperosmolar chyme into the small bowel. First-line therapy is diet: small frequent meals, fewer simple sugars, more protein, fat and fiber, and liquids separated from solids. Acarbose and octreotide are used if symptoms persist.

Takeaway: Early dumping is treated first with dietary modification.

whyNot.A: Rifaximin treats bacterial overgrowth, which presents with bloating, steatorrhea and B12 deficiency rather than immediate vasomotor symptoms.
whyNot.B: Liquid, sugar-rich supplements empty fastest and would worsen osmotic dumping.
whyNot.D: Octreotide is reserved for dumping that persists despite dietary change.
whyNot.E: Revision is a last resort for refractory dumping after diet and medication have failed.

items.objective: Manage early dumping syndrome after bariatric surgery.

items.stemHtml: A routine ultrasound at 20 weeks' gestation in a 37-year-old woman shows a midline anterior abdominal wall defect. Loops of bowel and part of the liver are contained in a thin membranous sac, and the umbilical cord inserts into the apex of the sac. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. Failure of which embryologic process best explains this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells

options.label: E
options.html: Return of the herniated midgut into the abdominal cavity

items.explanationHtml:
The midgut normally herniates into the umbilical cord around week 6 and returns around week 10. Persistence of herniated viscera in a sac of amnion and peritoneum at the cord insertion is an omphalocele. Because it often accompanies aneuploidy (trisomies 13 and 18) and cardiac defects, it prompts genetic testing and fetal echocardiography.

Takeaway: Omphalocele is a membrane-covered midline defect from failure of the physiologically herniated gut to return.

whyNot.A: Incomplete neural crest migration causes Hirschsprung disease.
whyNot.B: A persistent vitelline duct forms a Meckel diverticulum or umbilical fistula, not a membrane-covered herniation.
whyNot.C: A patent processus vaginalis causes indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele.
whyNot.D: Failed recanalization causes duodenal atresia, with polyhydramnios and a double bubble but an intact abdominal wall.

items.objective: Explain the embryologic basis of omphalocele.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl born at 37 weeks after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios has copious frothy oral secretions. During her first feed she coughs, chokes and becomes cyanotic. A soft feeding tube cannot be advanced, and a radiograph shows the tube coiled in the upper chest. The stomach and intestines contain air. Which anatomic configuration is most likely present?

options.label: A
options.html: Blind upper esophageal pouch with the lower esophagus joined to the trachea

options.label: B
options.html: Congenital esophageal web with normal tracheal anatomy

options.label: C
options.html: Esophageal atresia with no tracheal connection

options.label: D
options.html: Tracheesophageal fistula with a fully patent esophagus

options.label: E
options.html: Upper pouch joined to the trachea with a blind lower segment

items.explanationHtml:
The coiled tube proves atresia of the upper esophagus. Air in the stomach means air reaches the gut by another route: a fistula between the trachea and the distal esophagus. This is the most common form of esophageal atresia with tracheesophageal fistula, caused by abnormal partitioning of the foregut by the tracheesophageal septum. Polyhydramnios reflects impaired fetal swallowing.

Takeaway: Coiled tube plus gas in the abdomen means proximal atresia with a distal tracheesophageal fistula.

whyNot.B: A web causes partial obstruction, usually with later solid-food dysphagia, and would not prevent passing a soft tube.
whyNot.C: Pure atresia without a fistula gives a gasless abdomen, because air cannot reach the stomach.
whyNot.D: An H-type fistula allows a tube to pass into the stomach and usually presents later with recurrent aspiration.
whyNot.E: A fistula only from the upper pouch leaves the lower esophagus isolated, so the abdomen would be gasless.

items.objective: Identify the type of esophageal atresia from radiographic findings.

items.stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy with trisomy 21 has feeding intolerance and green emesis. Abdominal radiograph shows a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with a small amount of gas distally. At laparotomy, the bowel is normally rotated, and a band of pancreatic tissue completely encircles and narrows the second part of the duodenum. Abnormal development of which structure best explains this finding?

options.label: D
options.html: Midgut loop rotating around the superior mesenteric artery

items.explanationHtml:
The ventral pancreatic bud normally rotates behind the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud. A bifid ventral bud that migrates around both sides of the second part of the duodenum creates an annular pancreas, which can cause duodenal obstruction in newborns. Like duodenal atresia it is associated with trisomy 21.

Takeaway: Annular pancreas comes from abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum.

whyNot.A: Failure of the dorsal and ventral ducts to fuse is pancreas divisum, which does not encircle the duodenum.
whyNot.B: Failed recanalization causes duodenal atresia or stenosis without a ring of pancreatic tissue.
whyNot.C: The hepatic diverticulum forms the liver and biliary tree, not an obstructing pancreatic ring.
whyNot.D: Malrotation produces Ladd bands and volvulus risk, and rotation was normal here.

items.objective: Explain the embryologic origin of annular pancreas.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy has passed two large, painless, maroon stools. He is pale but comfortable, and his abdomen is soft and nontender. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant. The resected lesion is an outpouching on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum that contains all layers of the bowel wall. Persistence of which embryologic structure caused this lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
A Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum formed by incomplete involution of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac. Heterotopic gastric mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates nearby ileal mucosa, causing painless bleeding, and takes up pertechnetate, which is the basis of the scan.

Takeaway: Meckel diverticulum is a vitelline duct remnant; ectopic gastric mucosa causes bleeding and a positive pertechnetate scan.

whyNot.A: The ductus venosus shunts umbilical venous blood past the liver and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
whyNot.B: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver.
whyNot.C: A patent processus vaginalis causes indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele.
whyNot.D: A persistent urachus connects the bladder to the umbilicus and drains urine; it does not involve the ileum.

items.objective: Relate Meckel diverticulum to its embryologic origin.

items.stemHtml: A newborn boy has a unilateral cleft of the upper lip located just lateral to the philtrum and extending into the floor of the nostril. The secondary palate is intact. Failure of fusion between which embryologic structures best explains this defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Lateral nasal prominence and the frontonasal process

options.label: C
options.html: Maxillary prominence and the merged medial nasal prominences

items.explanationHtml:
The two medial nasal prominences merge to form the intermaxillary segment (philtrum, premaxilla and primary palate). Each maxillary prominence must fuse with this segment to complete the upper lip. Failure produces a cleft lip lateral to the philtrum, which can extend through the alveolus. Cleft palate is a separate failure of the palatine shelves.

Takeaway: Cleft lip is failed fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominences.

whyNot.A: The lateral nasal prominence forms the nasal alae and does not form the upper lip.
whyNot.B: Incomplete fusion at the corner of the mouth widens the oral opening (macrostomia), not a cleft beside the philtrum.
whyNot.D: Failure of the palatine shelves to fuse causes a cleft of the secondary palate, which is intact here.
whyNot.E: Failed mandibular fusion causes a rare midline cleft of the lower lip and jaw.

items.objective: Identify the embryologic basis of cleft lip.

items.stemHtml: A 5-week-old boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed for 5 days and appears dehydrated. Serum studies show sodium 132 mEq/L (136-145 mEq/L), potassium 2.9 mEq/L (3.5-5.0 mEq/L), chloride 83 mEq/L (95-105 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 35 mEq/L (22-28 mEq/L). Despite the systemic alkalosis, his urine is acidic. Which mechanism best explains the acidic urine?

options.label: A
options.html: Aldosterone-driven distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for hydrogen and potassium ions

options.label: B
options.html: Compensatory hypoventilation raising arterial carbon dioxide

options.label: C
options.html: Excess antidiuretic hormone retaining free water

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice in vomitus

options.label: E
options.html: Proximal tubular wasting of filtered bicarbonate

items.explanationHtml:
Pyloric obstruction causes loss of gastric HCl and volume. Hypovolemia activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct in exchange for K+ and H+. Chloride depletion also limits bicarbonate secretion by intercalated cells. The result is hypokalemia and paradoxical aciduria that persist until volume and chloride are restored.

Takeaway: Paradoxical aciduria in pyloric stenosis reflects volume-driven aldosterone action plus chloride depletion.

whyNot.B: Hypoventilation is the respiratory compensation for alkalosis; it does not explain why the kidney excretes acid.
whyNot.C: ADH release with volume depletion helps explain the mild hyponatremia but does not acidify the urine.
whyNot.D: The obstruction is proximal to the ampulla, so the emesis is gastric acid, which is why the infant becomes alkalotic.
whyNot.E: Proximal bicarbonate wasting would make the urine alkaline and is the mechanism of proximal renal tubular acidosis.

items.objective: Explain the acid-base and renal response in pyloric stenosis.

items.stemHtml: A 4-week-old first-born boy is brought to the clinic because of vomiting after nearly every feed for 3 days. The vomitus is milky, without green or blood, and shoots across the room. He seems hungry immediately afterward. He was born at term and was given azithromycin for pertussis exposure in his second week. He has fewer wet diapers than usual. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F) and pulse 168/min; mucous membranes are dry. Examination of the abdomen is limited because he is crying. Which is the most appropriate initial imaging study?
items.explanationHtml:
Projectile nonbilious vomiting in a hungry first-born male a few weeks old, especially after early macrolide exposure, suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Ultrasound is the imaging test of choice: it shows a thickened, elongated pyloric muscle without radiation exposure.

Takeaway: Suspected pyloric stenosis is confirmed by abdominal ultrasound.

whyNot.A: A contrast enema evaluates distal obstruction such as Hirschsprung disease, not gastric outlet obstruction.
whyNot.B: CT exposes the infant to radiation and is not needed when ultrasound is diagnostic.
whyNot.C: A radiograph may show a large gastric bubble but cannot confirm or exclude pyloric stenosis.
whyNot.E: An upper GI series is reserved for equivocal ultrasound or when malrotation is suspected because of bilious vomiting.

items.objective: Choose the best imaging test for suspected pyloric stenosis.

items.stemHtml: Ultrasound shows a thickened, elongated pyloric channel. Serum studies show sodium 133 mEq/L (136-145 mEq/L), potassium 3.1 mEq/L (3.5-5.0 mEq/L), chloride 86 mEq/L (95-105 mEq/L) and bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (22-28 mEq/L). His last wet diaper was 6 hours ago. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous fluid and electrolyte correction, then pyloromyotomy

options.label: C
options.html: Oral erythromycin to speed gastric emptying

options.label: D
options.html: Pyloromyotomy today before any fluid is given

items.explanationHtml:
The infant has hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with dehydration. Restore volume with isotonic IV fluid, then give maintenance fluid with dextrose, adding potassium once he urinates. When electrolytes and bicarbonate have normalized, pyloromyotomy is performed. The operation is urgent but never an emergency.

Takeaway: In pyloric stenosis, correct fluids and electrolytes first; pyloromyotomy follows.

whyNot.A: Balloon dilation is not standard care for infantile pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy is curative.
whyNot.C: Macrolides are a risk factor for pyloric stenosis and do not relieve hypertrophied muscle.
whyNot.D: Operating on a dehydrated, alkalotic infant raises anesthetic risk, including postoperative apnea; surgery waits until correction.
whyNot.E: These measures treat reflux, not a fixed gastric outlet obstruction.

items.objective: Sequence management of pyloric stenosis.

items.stemHtml:
A 6-week-old girl is brought to the clinic because her eyes and skin have been yellow since about 2 weeks of age. She is exclusively breastfed and gaining weight. Her stools have become pale and putty-colored, and her diapers are stained dark yellow. The liver is firm and palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin.

TestResult
Bilirubin, total7.6 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL)
Bilirubin, direct5.8 mg/dL (0.0-0.3 mg/dL)
AST142 U/L (12-38 U/L)
ALT118 U/L (10-40 U/L)
Albumin3.8 g/dL (3.5-5.5 g/dL)
INR1.1 (0.8-1.1)

Ultrasound shows a small, irregular gallbladder and echogenic tissue at the porta hepatis. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy shows no tracer in the bowel at 24 hours, and intraoperative cholangiography fails to fill the extrahepatic ducts. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Liver transplantation as the first operation

options.label: E
options.html: Ursodeoxycholic acid alone with reassessment at 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acholic stools and dark urine in a young infant, an abnormal gallbladder, no excretion on scintigraphy and nonfilling ducts on cholangiography establish biliary atresia. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy, which joins a jejunal Roux limb to the porta hepatis, works best when done early, ideally before about 2 months. Many children later need liver transplantation.

Takeaway: Biliary atresia is treated with an early Kasai procedure; delay worsens outcomes.

whyNot.B: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and does not cause pale stools or dark urine.
whyNot.C: Transplant is reserved for failed Kasai or late presentation with established cirrhosis; a 6-week-old should have a Kasai first.
whyNot.D: Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and does nothing for obstructed bile ducts.
whyNot.E: Medical therapy cannot restore bile flow, and delay lets biliary cirrhosis develop and lowers Kasai success.

items.objective: Manage biliary atresia.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl has bilious vomiting 4 hours after birth. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios, and the infant has upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat nasal bridge and a single palmar crease. Pulse is 150/min and blood pressure is normal for age. The abdomen is soft and nondistended. Radiograph shows two large air bubbles in the upper abdomen and no gas beyond them. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Orogastric decompression and IV fluids, then duodenoduodenostomy

items.explanationHtml:
Bilious vomiting on the first day, polyhydramnios, trisomy 21 and a double bubble without distal gas indicate duodenal atresia. The infant needs gastric decompression, IV fluid and electrolyte correction, and evaluation for associated anomalies (especially echocardiography), followed by surgical bypass of the atresia. Distal gas would raise concern for malrotation and need urgent evaluation.

Takeaway: Duodenal atresia is managed with decompression, fluids and duodenoduodenostomy.

whyNot.A: Feeding a complete proximal obstruction causes more vomiting and aspiration.
whyNot.B: A contrast enema assesses distal bowel obstruction; the obstruction here is proximal.
whyNot.D: Pyloric stenosis develops weeks after birth with nonbilious vomiting and is not present on day 1.
whyNot.E: Rectal biopsy diagnoses Hirschsprung disease, which causes delayed meconium and distension rather than a double bubble.

items.objective: Manage duodenal atresia in a newborn.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 38 weeks by cesarean delivery. He has a 5-cm defect at the umbilicus through which loops of bowel and part of the liver protrude into a translucent sac, and the umbilical cord inserts onto the sac. He is breathing comfortably and his glucose is normal. The sac is covered with sterile moist dressings, an orogastric tube is placed and IV fluids are started. Which is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
An omphalocele is a membrane-covered midline defect that is frequently associated with cardiac defects, chromosomal anomalies (notably trisomies 13 and 18) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. After stabilization, echocardiography and genetic evaluation are needed before planning repair, because associated anomalies largely determine prognosis.

Takeaway: Omphalocele demands a search for associated anomalies, starting with echocardiography.

whyNot.A: Head imaging is not routine; the important associated anomalies to seek first are cardiac.
whyNot.C: Rectal biopsy evaluates Hirschsprung disease, which is not associated with this defect.
whyNot.D: Sweat testing evaluates cystic fibrosis, which is linked to meconium ileus, not omphalocele.
whyNot.E: Hip ultrasound screens for developmental dysplasia and does not address the anomalies linked to omphalocele.

items.objective: Evaluate a newborn with omphalocele for associated anomalies.

items.stemHtml: A 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after passing a large amount of painless, dark red stool. He has been well and has had no vomiting. Pulse is 150/min and he is pale. The abdomen is soft, nontender and without masses. Hemoglobin is low for age. After a fluid bolus and transfusion his vital signs normalize. Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?
items.explanationHtml:
Painless, large-volume rectal bleeding in a toddler suggests a Meckel diverticulum with heterotopic gastric mucosa. Pertechnetate is taken up by gastric mucosa and highlights the diverticulum. Treatment is surgical resection.

Takeaway: Painless lower GI bleeding in a toddler calls for a Meckel (pertechnetate) scan.

whyNot.A: Ultrasound is the test for intussusception or pyloric stenosis and rarely identifies a Meckel diverticulum.
whyNot.B: An enema diagnoses and reduces intussusception, which usually causes episodic pain and vomiting.
whyNot.C: A barium swallow evaluates the esophagus and has no role in lower GI bleeding.
whyNot.D: Infectious colitis causes bloody diarrhea with fever and cramps, not a single painless large bleed.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected Meckel diverticulum.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen several times daily for a year. He now has epigastric pain, and endoscopy shows a clean-based gastric antral ulcer. Biopsies show no Helicobacter pylori. Reduced synthesis of which mediator most directly explains loss of mucosal protection in this patient?
items.explanationHtml:
COX-1 in gastric mucosa produces prostaglandins, chiefly PGE2 and PGI2, that stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintain mucosal blood flow and restrain acid secretion. Systemic COX-1 inhibition removes this protection, which is why even non-oral NSAIDs cause ulcers.

Takeaway: NSAID ulcers result mainly from loss of COX-1-derived mucosal prostaglandins.

whyNot.A: Gastrin stimulates acid secretion and is not reduced by COX inhibition.
whyNot.B: Histamine stimulates acid secretion; NSAIDs do not decrease it, and less histamine would protect the mucosa.
whyNot.C: NSAIDs do not reduce leukotriene synthesis; shunting toward the lipoxygenase pathway may even increase it.
whyNot.E: Reduced platelet thromboxane increases bleeding risk from an ulcer but does not cause the mucosal defect.

items.objective: Explain how NSAIDs cause peptic ulcers.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 days after ingesting a large quantity of acetaminophen. She is jaundiced and confused. AST is 6,800 U/L (12-38 U/L) and INR is 4.2 (0.8-1.1). She dies despite treatment. Which hepatic region would show the most severe necrosis at autopsy, and why?

options.label: A
options.html: Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes, which have the highest CYP2E1 activity

options.label: B
options.html: Interlobular bile duct epithelium within portal tracts

options.label: C
options.html: Midzonal (zone 2) hepatocytes, typical of yellow fever

options.label: D
options.html: Periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes, which receive the most oxygenated blood

options.label: E
options.html: Sinusoidal endothelium around terminal hepatic venules

items.explanationHtml:
Acetaminophen is converted by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione. In overdose glutathione is exhausted and NAPQI binds hepatocellular proteins. Zone 3 hepatocytes around the central vein have the greatest CYP2E1 content and the lowest oxygen tension, so necrosis is centrilobular.

Takeaway: Acetaminophen causes zone 3 necrosis because CYP2E1 is concentrated there.

whyNot.B: Bile duct injury causes cholestatic patterns such as vanishing bile duct syndrome, not massive aminotransferase release.
whyNot.C: Midzonal necrosis is characteristic of yellow fever, not acetaminophen.
whyNot.D: Zone 1 is the first to be injured by directly toxic substances that arrive in portal blood, but acetaminophen toxicity depends on CYP2E1-generated NAPQI.
whyNot.E: Sinusoidal endothelial injury causes sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, seen after some chemotherapy and pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

items.objective: Explain the zonal pattern of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and a previous NSAID-associated gastric ulcer must continue diclofenac. Her physician adds a drug that binds prostaglandin E receptors on parietal cells, lowering cAMP and acid secretion, and also increases gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion. Which adverse effect is she most likely to experience from this added drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Black discoloration of the tongue and stool

items.explanationHtml:
Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog that replaces mucosal prostaglandins. Its prostaglandin effects on intestinal smooth muscle and secretion cause dose-related diarrhea and cramping, the most common reason patients stop it. It also stimulates uterine contraction and is contraindicated in pregnancy when used for ulcer prevention.

Takeaway: Misoprostol prevents NSAID ulcers but commonly causes diarrhea.

whyNot.A: Black tongue and stool are caused by bismuth compounds.
whyNot.B: Constipation is typical of aluminum-containing antacids, not of a prostaglandin analog.
whyNot.D: Gynecomastia is linked to cimetidine, an H2 blocker with antiandrogen effects.
whyNot.E: Hypomagnesemia is a recognized effect of long-term proton pump inhibitor use.

items.objective: Recognize the main adverse effect of misoprostol.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer takes scheduled morphine for bone pain. Despite senna and polyethylene glycol, he has had one hard bowel movement in 5 days. Abdominal radiograph shows stool throughout the colon without obstruction. He is given a subcutaneous injection that produces a bowel movement within hours, without any change in his pain control and without symptoms of withdrawal. Which property of this drug best explains these effects?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of type 2 chloride channels in the intestinal epithelium

options.label: B
options.html: Agonism at guanylate cyclase C receptors on enterocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Agonism at serotonin 5-HT4 receptors in the myenteric plexus

options.label: D
options.html: Osmotic retention of water within the colonic lumen

options.label: E
options.html: Peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonism by a molecule excluded from the central nervous system

items.explanationHtml:
Methylnaltrexone is a quaternary derivative of naltrexone. The charged molecule does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it blocks mu receptors in the enteric nervous system and reverses opioid-induced constipation without affecting central analgesia or precipitating withdrawal. Like other peripheral antagonists, it is contraindicated in mechanical bowel obstruction.

Takeaway: PAMORAs relieve opioid constipation because they block gut mu receptors but stay out of the brain.

whyNot.A: Lubiprostone acts this way and is taken orally; it does not involve opioid receptors.
whyNot.B: Guanylate cyclase C agonists (linaclotide) are oral drugs that increase intestinal secretion, not opioid antagonists.
whyNot.C: Prucalopride is an oral 5-HT4 agonist used for chronic idiopathic constipation.
whyNot.D: He is already taking an osmotic laxative, and osmotic agents are oral.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of peripherally acting opioid antagonists.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old man completed a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for acute bacterial sinusitis 3 weeks ago. He now has jaundice and generalized itching. Serum studies show ALT 84 U/L (10-40 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 520 U/L (25-100 U/L), total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL) and direct bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL (0.0-0.3 mg/dL). Ultrasound shows no biliary dilation. Liver biopsy shows bile plugs in canaliculi with mild portal inflammation. Which best describes this liver injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Dose-dependent zone 3 necrosis from a reactive metabolite

options.label: B
options.html: Hepatic fibrosis from long-term folate antagonism

options.label: C
options.html: Idiosyncratic cholestatic injury attributed mainly to the clavulanate component

items.explanationHtml:
The R ratio here is (84/40) divided by (520/100), about 0.4, which is cholestatic. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a leading cause of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury, typically cholestatic or mixed, linked mainly to clavulanate and often starting after the course is finished. Most patients recover after the drug is stopped, although cholestasis can take weeks to resolve.

Takeaway: Delayed cholestatic jaundice after amoxicillin-clavulanate is classic idiosyncratic DILI.

whyNot.A: Dose-dependent zone 3 necrosis describes acetaminophen, with a hepatocellular rather than cholestatic pattern.
whyNot.B: Fibrosis from folate antagonism describes long-term methotrexate.
whyNot.D: Microvesicular steatosis is typical of valproate, aspirin in Reye syndrome and some antiretrovirals.
whyNot.E: Phospholipidosis is characteristic of amiodarone.

items.objective: Classify drug-induced liver injury and link it to amoxicillin-clavulanate.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma receives combined ipilimumab and nivolumab. Six weeks later she has 8 watery stools daily with cramping. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and other pathogens is negative. Colonoscopy shows diffuse erythema and ulceration, and biopsies show crypt abscesses and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which mechanism best explains her colitis?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of VEGF signaling causing mucosal ischemia

options.label: B
options.html: Direct toxicity of the drugs to rapidly dividing crypt epithelium

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complex deposition in colonic vessel walls

options.label: D
options.html: Overgrowth of a toxin-producing anaerobe after antibiotic exposure

options.label: E
options.html: Removal of inhibitory signals on T cells, allowing autoreactive T-cell activation

items.explanationHtml:
CTLA-4 and PD-1 are inhibitory receptors that limit T-cell activation. Blocking them enhances antitumor responses but also breaks tolerance to self and gut antigens, producing immune-related adverse events. Colitis is more frequent with CTLA-4 blockade than with PD-1 blockade and highest with the combination.

Takeaway: Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is autoimmune T-cell injury from loss of inhibitory checkpoints.

whyNot.A: Anti-VEGF drugs such as bevacizumab are linked to perforation and impaired healing, not immune-mediated colitis.
whyNot.B: Direct cytotoxicity to dividing cells describes conventional chemotherapy such as fluorouracil or irinotecan, not checkpoint antibodies.
whyNot.C: Immune complex vasculitis is not the mechanism of checkpoint-inhibitor colitis, which is T-cell mediated.
whyNot.D: C. difficile testing is negative, and she did not receive antibiotics.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman was admitted 8 days ago for cellulitis of the leg and treated with IV cefazolin, then switched to oral clindamycin because of a rash. For 2 days she has had 5 or 6 watery stools daily with lower abdominal cramping. She takes no laxatives. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse 92/min and blood pressure 128/74 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, mildly tender in the lower quadrants and nondistended. Leukocyte count is 13,200/mm3 (4,500-11,000/mm3) and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mg/dL). Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

options.label: D
options.html: Stool examination for ova and parasites

items.explanationHtml:
New diarrhea with 3 or more unformed stools a day in a hospitalized patient on antibiotics, without laxatives, is the indication for C. difficile testing by nucleic acid amplification or a multistep algorithm including toxin detection.

Takeaway: Test unformed stool for C. difficile when diarrhea follows antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Endoscopy is not needed to diagnose most cases and adds risk in an inflamed colon.
whyNot.B: CT is reserved for suspected complications such as megacolon or perforation, which her examination does not suggest.
whyNot.C: Antimotility drugs are avoided until C. difficile is excluded because they may worsen toxin-mediated colitis.
whyNot.D: Parasitic infection is unlikely in hospital-onset diarrhea after antibiotics.

items.objective: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected C. difficile infection.

items.stemHtml: Stool nucleic acid amplification testing and toxin immunoassay for C. difficile are both positive. Clindamycin is stopped and the cellulitis has resolved. Leukocyte count remains 13,200/mm3 and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. This is her first episode. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Leukocyte count below 15,000/mm3 and creatinine below 1.5 mg/dL make this an initial nonsevere episode. Current guidelines prefer oral fidaxomicin, which has lower recurrence rates, with oral vancomycin as an acceptable alternative.

Takeaway: Treat a first C. difficile episode with oral fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin).

whyNot.A: Microbiota therapy is reserved for multiple recurrences, not a first episode.
whyNot.B: IV metronidazole is used only as an add-on to oral vancomycin in fulminant disease.
whyNot.C: IV vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen in useful amounts and does not treat C. difficile.
whyNot.D: Antimotility agents without antibiotic therapy risk toxin retention and do not treat the infection.

items.objective: Select therapy for an initial C. difficile infection.

items.stemHtml:
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after swallowing a handful of acetaminophen tablets after an argument with her boyfriend. She took no other substances. She has mild nausea. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

TestResult
Acetaminophen, 4 hours after ingestion210 mcg/mL (nomogram treatment line at 4 hours: 150 mcg/mL)
SalicylateUndetectable
AST26 U/L (12-38 U/L)
ALT21 U/L (10-40 U/L)
INR1.0 (0.8-1.1)
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mg/dL)

Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat the acetaminophen level in 4 hours before treating

items.explanationHtml:
A single acute ingestion with a known time and a 4-hour level above the Rumack-Matthew treatment line requires N-acetylcysteine. Normal aminotransferases are expected this early; liver injury lags by a day or more. NAC is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion. Psychiatric evaluation follows once she is medically stable.

Takeaway: A post-4-hour acetaminophen level above the treatment line means start NAC immediately.

whyNot.A: Fomepizole treats methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.
whyNot.B: Hemodialysis is reserved for massive ingestions with acidosis or altered mental status; it is not first-line here.
whyNot.C: Suicide risk assessment follows medical stabilization; untreated, this level risks severe liver injury.
whyNot.D: A 4-hour level above the treatment line already mandates treatment, and delay beyond 8 hours reduces NAC efficacy.

items.objective: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to decide on N-acetylcysteine.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with severe hip osteoarthritis has had inadequate relief from acetaminophen and topical diclofenac, and his orthopedist recommends oral naproxen while he awaits arthroplasty. Three years ago he had a bleeding duodenal ulcer; Helicobacter pylori was treated and eradication was confirmed. He takes no other medications and has no cardiovascular disease. Which is the most appropriate strategy to reduce his risk of a recurrent ulcer?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a daily proton pump inhibitor

options.label: B
options.html: Add a standard-dose H2 receptor antagonist

options.label: E
options.html: Use antacids as needed for pain

items.explanationHtml:
Prior ulcer bleeding and age over 65 place him at high risk for NSAID-related ulcer complications. If an NSAID is necessary, co-prescribing a PPI is the standard protective strategy; in the highest-risk patients without cardiovascular disease a COX-2-selective drug with a PPI is preferred. Misoprostol is an alternative but is limited by diarrhea.

Takeaway: High-GI-risk patients who need an NSAID should receive a PPI.

whyNot.B: Standard-dose H2 blockers prevent duodenal but not gastric NSAID ulcers and are inferior to PPIs.
whyNot.C: Sucralfate has not been shown to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers.
whyNot.D: Enteric coating does not prevent ulcers, which result mainly from systemic COX-1 inhibition.
whyNot.E: Antacids relieve symptoms but do not prevent ulcers or bleeding.

items.objective: Prevent NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease in high-risk patients.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with prostate cancer metastatic to bone takes extended-release oxycodone with good pain control. He has had one or two hard bowel movements a week for a month despite taking senna and polyethylene glycol daily at full doses. He passes flatus and has no vomiting. The abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender with normal bowel sounds. Rectal examination shows soft stool without impaction, and an abdominal radiograph shows stool in the colon without dilated small bowel loops. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist

items.explanationHtml:
Opioid-induced constipation that persists despite adequate stimulant and osmotic laxatives, with obstruction and impaction excluded, is treated by adding a PAMORA such as naloxegol, naldemedine or methylnaltrexone. These block gut mu receptors without reversing analgesia.

Takeaway: Laxative-refractory opioid constipation calls for a PAMORA once obstruction is excluded.

whyNot.B: Alvimopan is restricted to short-term inpatient use for postoperative ileus after bowel resection.
whyNot.C: Docusate alone has little benefit in opioid-induced constipation and adds nothing to an adequate regimen.
whyNot.D: Metoclopramide is a prokinetic for the upper GI tract and is not a standard treatment for opioid constipation.
whyNot.E: His cancer pain is well controlled, and stopping the opioid would sacrifice analgesia when targeted therapy exists.

items.objective: Manage laxative-refractory opioid-induced constipation.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with ileocolonic Crohn disease started azathioprine 5 weeks ago. She has had 1 day of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with nausea and vomiting. She abstains from alcohol. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse 104/min and blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. Lipase is 1,620 U/L (0-160 U/L). Calcium is 9.3 mg/dL (8.4-10.2 mg/dL), and triglycerides are 140 mg/dL (reference: below 150 mg/dL). Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder without stones and a normal common bile duct. IV fluids and analgesia are started. Which is the most appropriate additional step?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute pancreatitis weeks after starting a thiopurine, with gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia and hypercalcemia excluded, is most likely drug-induced. Management is supportive care and permanent withdrawal of the drug; thiopurines should not be restarted, and switching to 6-mercaptopurine does not avoid the reaction. Another agent is chosen for Crohn disease.

Takeaway: Thiopurine-induced pancreatitis requires stopping the drug class permanently.

whyNot.B: ERCP is indicated for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, neither of which is present.
whyNot.C: Cholecystectomy prevents recurrence of gallstone pancreatitis, and she has no gallstones.
whyNot.D: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in acute pancreatitis without infected necrosis.
whyNot.E: 6-Mercaptopurine is the active metabolite of azathioprine and carries the same pancreatitis risk.

items.objective: Recognize and manage drug-induced pancreatitis.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer has received pembrolizumab every 3 weeks for 4 months. For 3 days he has had 8 to 9 watery stools daily above his usual one, with cramping abdominal pain. He has no fever or blood in the stool. Pulse is 98/min and blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and mildly tender. Stool testing for C. difficile and a gastrointestinal pathogen panel are negative. CT shows diffuse colonic wall thickening without perforation. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Hold pembrolizumab and start systemic glucocorticoids

options.label: D
options.html: Start infliximab as the first treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Seven or more stools above baseline after a PD-1 inhibitor, with infection excluded and CT showing colitis, indicates severe immune-related colitis. The checkpoint inhibitor is held and systemic (often IV) glucocorticoids are started. Lack of response within a few days prompts infliximab or vedolizumab.

Takeaway: Moderate to severe checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is treated by holding the drug and giving glucocorticoids.

whyNot.A: Antidiarrheals alone are appropriate only for mild diarrhea; this degree of colitis requires holding therapy and steroids.
whyNot.C: Surgery is reserved for perforation or refractory fulminant colitis.
whyNot.D: Infliximab or vedolizumab is added when colitis does not respond to glucocorticoids within a few days.
whyNot.E: Testing for C. difficile is negative, and antibiotics do not treat immune-mediated colitis.

items.objective: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with latent tuberculosis infection began isoniazid with pyridoxine 9 weeks ago. For a week she has had fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite and right upper quadrant discomfort. She drinks alcohol occasionally. ALT is 264 U/L (10-40 U/L), AST 231 U/L (12-38 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 112 U/L (25-100 U/L) and total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL). Hepatitis serologies are pending. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add rifampin to shorten the course

options.label: B
options.html: Continue isoniazid and recheck liver tests in 4 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Reduce the isoniazid dose by half

options.label: E
options.html: Stop isoniazid now and monitor liver tests

items.explanationHtml:
Isoniazid should be stopped when ALT exceeds 3 times the upper limit of normal with symptoms of hepatitis, or 5 times without symptoms. Her ALT is more than 6 times normal with symptoms. After liver tests recover, latent infection can be treated with a rifamycin-based regimen if appropriate.

Takeaway: Symptomatic isoniazid hepatitis with ALT above 3 times normal requires stopping isoniazid.

whyNot.A: Rifampin is also hepatotoxic and adding it now would compound the injury.
whyNot.B: Continuing the drug despite symptomatic hepatitis risks progression to fulminant liver failure.
whyNot.C: Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy and does not protect the liver.
whyNot.D: Dose reduction is not a recognized strategy; symptomatic hepatotoxicity requires stopping the drug.

items.objective: Apply stopping rules for isoniazid hepatotoxicity.
